text:
The Broken Heartland: Suicide and the Silence of the State in Kerala

They call it "God’s Own Country." It is a lush, vibrant lie. A postcard of backwaters, swaying palms, and impeccable literacy rates, sold with a seductive smile to the tourist trade.

But look past the emerald veneer, past the celebrated social indices that development consultants love to fawn over. Look at the shadows stretching across the state’s neat, painted schoolyards and its crowded liquor outlets. There, you will find a dark, weeping sore that refuse to be bandaged by policy papers.

Kerala, this beacon of progressive India, is hanging by a thread. It is a thread woven from desperation, indebtedness, and the crushing weight of impossible expectations. The state has long clawed its way to the top of India’s suicide charts, a gruesome statistic that mocks its high-minded rhetoric about social development.

This is not just a story of "mental health problems." That is the bloodless, sanitized language of global NGOs and pharmaceuticals. This is a story of a shattered heartland. It is a story of the systematic failure of community, the predatory nature of modern economy, and a state that offers rhetoric when its people are gagging for hope.

The Taxonomy of Despair: By the Numbers
To understand the crisis is to understand who the machine crushes first. Suicide is not an equalizer; it preys on the specific vulnerabilities of specific lives.

1. The Death of Youth (15-29 years)
The most luminous spirits, extinguished first. The age group of 15 to 29 is the single most vulnerable demographic in Kerala. These are the children of the "New India," the ones who were told they could have everything, provided they got into the engineering college, provided they passed the standardized tests, provided they secured the coveted "Gulf job" to send remittances back to their ambitious, consumerist families.

They are crushed by a lethal combination: an education system that is a factory of anxiety, not learning; a job market that demands subservience over skill; and a society that still views romantic love and social experimentation with deep, medieval suspicion. When the test fails, when the VISA is rejected, when the lover marries someone else chosen by caste and cash, the darkness is absolute.

2. The Debt of Life (30-49 years)
This is the "sandwich generation." The men and women, but mostly men, who are expected to bear the world on their shoulders. Between 30 and 49, the stressors change but the pressure intensifies. They are the ones borrowing massive, paralyzing sums of money—to build a "show house" they don't need, to pay outrageous dowries that further entrench the very oppression they claim to fight, to finance failing businesses that were supposed to be the ticket to wealth.

The state’s other great pandemic—alcoholism—rears its ugly, brutal head here. Kerala may drink less per capita than some states, but it drinks for the sole purpose of annihilation. Alcoholism is not a habit; it is a tool of slow-motion suicide, and when the money runs out or the family fractures, the final, swift act becomes the only logical conclusion to a life spent drowning.

3. The Isolation of Age (60+ years)
And finally, the old. The forgotten ones. Kerala’s elderly population is booming, but its capacity for compassion is shrinking. This is the tragic dividend of the "Gulf Syndrome." Children live in opulent isolation in the GCC or the West, sending money but withholding themselves. The parents are left as gilded ghosts, rattling around enormous houses they cannot maintain, facing the Twin Terrors: chronic, expensive physical illness and a bottomless, soul-eating loneliness. For many, suicide is the last act of sovereignty, a way to declare that they will not wait to be a burden anymore.

Before Laporta’s puppets start rewriting history, remember exactly WHO Xavi Hernández is and what he gave this club.

Xavi arrived at La Masia as a kid and dedicated practically his entire footballing life to FC Barcelona. 17 seasons with the first team. 767 official games. 85 goals. Captain. 25 major trophies.

He was at the heart of the greatest team ever, part of both treble-winning sides, and represented Barça’s football and identity for an entire generation.

And when the club was struggling financially and sitting NINTH in La Liga, who came back? Xavi.

He could have protected his reputation and stayed away from the mess. Instead, he accepted one of the hardest Barça jobs imaginable, took the team from ninth to second, then won La Liga in his first full season with 88 points, finishing 10 points ahead of Real Madrid, while also winning the Spanish Super Cup after beating Madrid 3-1.

And then there is LA MASIA.

Lamine Yamal was brought into the first team under Xavi and debuted at FIFTEEN. Fermín López, Pau Cubarsí, Héctor Fort and Marc Casadó were all given opportunities under him. 

After returning from his loan at Linares, Fermín has explained that his plan was actually to leave Barça because he had offers from Segunda División and believed that was the right next step. Instead, he was convinced to do preseason with the first team, Xavi gave him his opportunity and everything changed. Fermín later said of Xavi: “Without him I wouldn’t be here.” 

A huge part of the young core people celebrate today was trusted, developed or established while Xavi was the coach.

Was Xavi perfect? Absolutely not. But you cannot ignore what he did. You do NOT erase decades of service because your clown of a president wants you to move on from someone. And this is exactly where my problem with Joan Laporta starts.

Xavi announced that he was leaving. Laporta then spent weeks convincing him to continue. On April 25, Laporta publicly celebrated Xavi’s decision to stay and talked about stability, continuity and confidence in him. He had previously said Xavi “doesn’t deserve to be sacked.”

Then, less than ONE MONTH later, he fired him.

That was embarrassing treatment of a club legend. If Laporta no longer believed Xavi was the right coach, fine. Presidents are allowed to change coaches. But then have the courage to make the decision properly.

Do not convince a club legend to reverse his resignation, publicly celebrate his continuity, and then humiliate him weeks later.

Xavi deserved honesty. Xavi deserved clarity. Above everything, after everything he gave Barça, Xavi deserved RESPECT.

But apparently saying that now makes you “anti-Barça” according to Laporta’s little army of puppets online.

JOAN LAPORTA IS NOT FC BARCELONA.

He is the president of FC Barcelona. There is a massive difference.

Presidents come and go. Barça remains.

Supporting Barcelona does NOT mean switching your brain off and applauding Laporta.

His puppets behave as if their job is to protect Laporta from every criticism, excuse every contradiction, attack anyone who questions him and rewrite history whenever it becomes inconvenient.

That is not supporting Barça. That is supporting Laporta.

I will never let anyone tell me that defending Xavi Hernández after everything he gave this club makes me less of a Culé.

Xavi gave Barça more than Laporta’s internet puppets could ever dream of.

text:
There is a kind of movie that does not ask to be liked so much as endured, the way a fever asks to be endured, and The Keep from 1983 is that kind of movie. It stands in its field not because it is the cleanest horror picture of its decade and not because it is the most coherent war picture of its decade, but because it is neither of those things and still refuses to leave the mind. Other films about Nazis and the occult want the comfort of a costume, a relic, a whip, a tidy moral that says the uniforms are the whole of the darkness. This one puts the uniforms inside an older stone and then asks what happens when the stone answers back. That is why it is special. That is why it is unique. That is why, for all its scars, it became a masterpiece of atmosphere and a cultural icon for people who hunt the strange rather than the official.

What you are supposed to learn begins before you even understand the names. In 1941 a Wehrmacht unit under Captain Klaus Woermann climbs into the Carpathians to hold a mountain pass and takes quarters in an ancient citadel the locals call the Keep. The men are tired of war and hungry for anything that looks like loot. Two of them pry at a metallic icon set into the wall, one of the many crosses that seem to pin the place shut, and the Keep opens. A force named Radu Molasar comes out first as smoke and hunger and later as a body that drinks life. The lesson is not a jump scare. The lesson is that occupation itself is a form of prying. You do not have to believe in demons to see that an army which treats a sealed place as empty real estate is already performing the same gesture as the two fools with their hands in the wall. Greed looks small until the thing it wakes is older than the flag on the truck.

The film will not let you rest in the easy hatred of Nazis, and that is one of the reasons it stands apart from its field. Woermann is not a cartoon. He is a professional soldier who still has a conscience left in him, a man who can look at reprisals against villagers and feel the rot. Major Kaempffer arrives later with the SS logic that every unexplained death must be partisans and every village must pay. When the two men finally collide, Woermann says the monster hunting them is a reflection of what they have already become. You are supposed to take that away whole. Human systems of domination do not merely summon supernatural evil as a metaphor. They rhyme with it. The Keep does not excuse the Wehrmacht by giving one officer a soul. It uses that soul to show how little a soul can do once the machine is inside the stone. Strange mercy and strange condemnation live in the same frame.

Then the picture does something even rarer. It brings in Dr. Theodore Cuza, a Jewish historian dragged from the camps with his daughter Eva because the Germans need a translation they cannot perform themselves. Molasar heals the dying scholar and speaks of “my people.” Cuza, who has every earthly reason to want the Reich burned off the map, hears a promise that this ancient thing will destroy the Nazis if only the last binding talisman is removed from the Keep. Here is the lesson that makes the film a must watch and not a curiosity. Oppression does not automatically confer wisdom about power. A man who has been crushed can still be seduced by a larger crush. Revenge can wear the face of deliverance. The takeaway is not that Cuza is a fool. The takeaway is that the hunger to see the guilty punished is so clean and so human that an older hunger can hide inside it. Watch that bargain and you watch every later century in which the wounded are offered a weapon that will not stay pointed in one direction.

Opposite that bargain stands Glaeken, who arrives from occupied Greece as if the Keep itself had sent for him. He is not a speechmaker. He is an old duty walking around in a man’s skin. He tells Eva that when the evil is gone he will be gone too. The romance that blooms between them is abrupt because the movie as released is abrupt, but the idea underneath is not abrupt at all. Containment is not glory. Containment is a life spent watching a door. Good, in this cosmology, is not a shining army. Good is the refusal to let the thing in the wall become the weather of the world. You are supposed to leave the film knowing that some victories do not look like victory. They look like a light that spends itself sealing a hole, after which the sealer has no further use.

All of this sits under Tangerine Dream, whose score does not decorate the images so much as replace ordinary time. Synths crawl over 1941 the way fog crawls over slate. The music makes Nazis feel like they have driven into a dream that predates their uniforms. That collision of electronic future and medieval stone is one of the reasons the film became a cult object and then a legend. Other war horrors stay in period. This one lets the period leak. The opening descent of the convoy into the pass, engines and thunder braided together, is so hypnotic that later filmmakers have admitted the image never left them. A culture that keeps returning to that descent is a culture that recognizes something true: machinery can look holy and doomed at the same time.

Why it is a masterpiece even while it is wounded is the same reason it is a cultural icon. Masterpiece here does not mean perfect carpentry. It means a set of images and moral pressures that no later polish could have invented. Fog in a quarry dressed as Romania. A priest warning that dreams live in the walls. A scholar touching health that tastes like debt. An SS officer discovering that firing squads do not impress a thing that was already eating long before the Party learned how to print posters. An immortal who treats love as the last human heat he will be allowed before the work unmakes him. These are not plot beats offered for their own sake. They are teachings about thresholds. Do not treat sealed things as vacant. Do not assume your enemy’s enemy is your shelter. Do not confuse the destruction of a regime with the end of appetite. Do not wait for the universe to send a choir when it may only send one tired guardian and a glowing staff.

The Keep stands out among other movies in its field because its field is usually either pulp Satanism or prestige atrocity, and this film insists on being a fairytale for adults in which the fairies are terrible and the adults are already compromised. It is a must watch because most films tell you what evil wears. This one asks whether evil is a costume you can remove or a weather that moves into whoever opens the wall. It is a classic legend because legends survive damage. People passed it on in the years when it was hard to find, when the director would not speak of it, when the soundtrack rights tangled the home video fate of the thing, when the monster’s final body looked to some eyes like a bodybuilder wearing death. The legend is not that the film is flawless. The legend is that the film, even halved, still behaves like a sealed place. You put your mind against it and something answers.

Only after that pressure should the making of it be named, because the making is the last chamber, not the first. Michael Mann wanted an expressionistic grown fairytale, a long fever of blue light and religious hysteria, not a Saturday creature feature. He shot in Welsh rain and a quarry so deep the company had to lower the twentieth century into it by rope. The original assembly ran toward three and a half hours. The studio demanded two. Tests went badly. The picture that reached theaters in December 1983 was ninety six minutes, full of missing tissue, jumps in sound, and an ending far smaller than the tower battle once planned. Wally Veevers, who had helped will 2001 and Superman onto screens, died early in post production and took the map of the remaining effects with him. Mann finished hundreds of shots himself and still watched the climax shrink. F. Paul Wilson, whose novel had given the story its bones, found the film visually striking and otherwise nearly unreadable. Mann himself stepped away from the orphan. None of that cancels what remains. It explains the jaggedness. It also explains the cult. An incomplete cathedral can still make people whisper. The rights maze around the music, the director’s silence, the late restorations that still cannot resurrect a cut that may no longer exist as he imagined it, all of that only thickened the myth. Strange films about Nazis and older gods do not become icons by being easy. They become icons because they feel like something the century tried to bury and failed.

Watch it for the lesson the stone keeps repeating. Power will always offer itself as medicine. Armies will always call a prison a barracks. Scholars will always be tempted to trade a binding for a victory. Someone still has to stand in the doorway when the smoke learns a face. That is why The Keep remains a legend and a must watch. Not because it tells you the war in order. Because it tells you that the war was never the oldest thing in the room.

🔸 September 20 - Saint Eustathios 🦌 🔸

Today, we commemorate the Great-Martyr Saint Eustathios, along with his wife Theopisti and their sons Agapios and Theopistos. St Eustathios was born with the name Plakidas and was an illustrious military general of Rome during the reign of Emperor Trajan (98-117). Even before he knew Christ, he was known for his virtue and charity to the poor. One day, while hunting in the forest, Plakidas pursued a deer, and noticed a radiant Cross between its antlers.

A divine voice then spoke to him from the Cross saying, “I am Jesus Christ, Whom you do not know, but by your good deeds, you honor me.” The voice called Plakidas and his family to baptism, and prophesied that he would suffer many misfortunes like Job, but would conquer the devil. Plakidas was baptized with the name Eustathios (“Steadfast”). Soon, Eustathios was plunged into misfortune: all his servants died of the plague and his cattle perished, so he and his family boarded a ship to Egypt.

The ship owner, captivated by the beauty of Theopisti, threw Eustathios and his two sons off the ship, keeping the Saint’s wife for himself. In great sorrow, Eustathios continued on his way with his sons. While trying to take his sons across a dangerous river one at a time, one was snatched by a lion, and the other was taken by a wolf into the forest. Having now lost all his family, Eustathios wept bitterly. He did not know however that the shipowner who took his wife had died from a disease leaving her untouched, nor that shepherds had saved his sons from the beasts.

Eustathios returned to Rome and was restored to his former army rank. By divine providence, two young soldiers recruited to serve under him were his sons, and his wife was an attendant to the soldiers. And so during a Roman military campaign against barbarians, the family was miraculously reunited. After defeating the barbarians, the soldiers were ordered by the new emperor Hadrian (117-138) to offer sacrifice to the idols. True to his name, Eustathios steadfastly refused, declaring that he would only glorify Christ. The enraged emperor had St Eustathios and his family burned alive in a brazen bull.

🚨 ILLINOIS FOUND A WAY TO BUILD SOLAR FARMS WITHOUT TAKING OVER FARMLAND ☀️🏙️

While communities across the United States debate whether solar farms should occupy valuable farmland, Illinois is trying something different. Instead of searching for more land, the state is turning the rooftops of self-storage facilities into a massive network of solar power stations.

Through a partnership between Public Storage and Solar Landscape, 60 storage facilities are being transformed into community solar hubs, using around 5 million square feet of existing rooftop space. No new farmland is needed for these installations.

Once completed, the project is expected to generate 44 megawatts of clean electricity, enough to supply more than 6,000 homes. But the most interesting part isn’t just the energy being produced. It’s who gets to benefit from it.

People who cannot install solar panels on their own homes, whether because they rent, lack suitable rooftops, or cannot afford a private system, can subscribe to the community solar network. Together, subscribers are projected to save approximately $36 million on their electricity bills.

This approach could offer a different path for expanding renewable energy: using spaces that already exist instead of constantly competing for open land.

Illinois aims to reach 100% clean electricity by 2050. Whether rooftop solar can become a major part of that journey remains to be seen, but one thing is clear: the next solar revolution might not require more land. It might require us to look up. 🌍⚡

Source: Canary Media — Solar on storage units? Here’s how Illinois is making it happen.

Consider a hypothetical. Imagine you’re the American president and Canada begins developing an unusually close relationship with China. Chinese military advisers arrive. Investment pours in. Intelligence cooperation deepens. There are enormous Chinese-sponsored drone shows near Minnesota. Military infrastructure develops, discussions begin about hosting Chinese missiles, and Chinese investors start building resorts along the coast.

Investment, tourism, and drone shows north of Minnesota alone wouldn’t establish a military threat. But imagine them unfolding alongside a growing military and intelligence partnership, with paid media campaigns promoting the relationship and dismissing every security concern as paranoia. 

This develops gradually over years. Influence doesn’t require somebody knocking on your door and asking, “Can you please keep our missile at your house?” In this hypothetical, it could involve business opportunities, sponsorships, personal relationships, and payments to influential voices. For instance, even @patrickbetdavid and crew @VincentOshana I think were approached by a “Chinese charity” organisation and were offered money for some easy stuff. The guys rejected the offer because they understand what is going on.

How would a Washington that is genuinely concerned with American security respond? Would officials see an ordinary diplomatic relationship, or a potentially serious strategic threat developing next door? Would they suggest to open Chinese-Hollywood?

What often gets lost is how closely these societies are connected through history, geography, family, language, and culture. I have a Ukrainian father and family there myself. Ukraine has its own sovereignty and identity, but understanding Moscow’s calculations requires taking that relationship seriously.

For instance, even @patrickbetdavid and crew @VincentOshana I think were approached by a “Chinese charity” organisation and were offered money for some easy stuff. The guys rejected the offer because they understand what is going on.

How would a Washington that is genuinely concerned with American security respond? Would officials see an ordinary diplomatic relationship, or a potentially serious strategic threat developing next door? Would they suggest to open Chinese-Hollywood?

My expectation is that they would take it extremely seriously, even if Beijing kept saying, “This has nothing to do with America. We just really want to be friends with Canada.”

That’s the question about threat perception I’m asking people to consider. The analogy illustrates a way of thinking; it doesn’t establish that every allegation about Western activity in Ukraine is true.

Understanding that perception doesn’t give Russia ownership of Ukraine or make invasion inevitable. It helps explain the calculations involved. Ukraine’s own security concerns also have to be addressed.

If we want a settlement that lasts, we need to understand what each side actually believes, what it wants, and what arrangements could provide meaningful security. Then we need terms that can actually be verified and upheld.

Sunday, September 20, 2026 — 3:08 AM EDT

Ringwoodite can hold a lot of nitrogen **if you offer a reduced N-rich fluid**. That number is a **ceiling**, not the A1 charge. Solubility is what the lattice will accept at equilibrium. Packed native N is what we actually put in.

## What was measured

The useful dataset is Yoshioka, Wiedenbeck, Shcheka & Keppler (2018): multi-anvil, 14–24 GPa, 1100–1800 °C, near Fe–FeO, \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\)-doped \(\mathrm{NH_4NO_3}\) as the N source, SIMS on the recovered crystals.

| Phase | Typical N (µg/g = ppm wt) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Olivine / forsterite | few ppm; ~10 ppm max in Fo at 3.5 GPa / 1300 °C IW; ~37 ppm when coexisting with wad at 16 GPa / 1500 °C | Fo is the poorest silicate host of the family |
| Wadsleyite | ~8–250 ppm | hottest N sponge in the \(\mathrm{(Mg,Fe)_2SiO_4}\) series |
| **Ringwoodite** | **~10–150 ppm** in that paper; later citations push some runs to **~280 ppm** | T helps; P barely does |
| Bridgmanite | ~20 ppm | less than ringwoodite |
| Fe metal | up to ~1 wt% | steals N from silicates if metal is present |

Partitioning from coexisting pairs:

\[
D_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{wad/ol}} \approx 5.1 \pm 2.1
\]
\[
D_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{rw/wad}} \approx 0.49 \pm 0.29
\]
\[
D_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{brg/rw}} \approx 0.24
\]

So if olivine, wadsleyite, and ringwoodite sit together with the same fluid: **wad > ringwoodite > olivine**. Crossing olivine → ringwoodite does **not** dump N. It can keep it, and a wad-bearing path can even enrich the charge before the last step. Packed 0.5 ppm stays on the order of 0.5 ppm unless a fluid or metal steals or adds it.

## How T and P move the ceiling

In ringwoodite, **temperature is the main knob**. Pressure in the 14–24 GPa window is weak. One thesis cut: ~50 ppm at 21 GPa / 1200 °C vs ~100 ppm at the same P / higher T. Wadsleyite also rises with both T and P.

Our pairing anneal (8–15 GPa, 700–900 °C) is **colder** than those solubility runs. The ceiling at 800 °C will be lower than the 1400–1800 °C numbers — still tens of ppm if a reduced N fluid is in the capsule. A1 does not put that fluid in.

## How nitrogen sits in the crystal

Two pictures, both redox-tied:

- **Reduced (IW / Fe–FeO):** fluid is mostly \(\mathrm{NH_3}\). N enters the lattice as \(\mathrm{NH_4^+}\) (K-site analog) and/or nitride-like \(\mathrm{N^{3-}}\). That is why solubility jumps when \(f\mathrm{O_2}\) drops.  
- **Oxidized (Ni–NiO and above):** fluid is mostly \(\mathrm{N_2}\). Forsterite takes at most a few ppm, often below detection.

That is why A1 is Ni–NiO or more oxidizing: we are using redox to **keep the ceiling low**, not just a clean powder. A reducing Fe-metal buffer plus leftover air or ammonium salt is how you accidentally grow a 50 ppm bath.

Ringwoodite is a spinel: Mg/Fe on octahedra, Si on tetrahedra. N is not a documented “NV in diamond” substitution. We do not know the site of a useful color center. Solubility only says the lattice will **tolerate** N. It does not say N–V is the stable pair.

## What this does to the A1 lock

```text
solubility  = maximum the brick will accept if N is offered
packed N    = what SIMS said on the Fo powder  (0.1–1 ppm)
implant     = 1e11 15N / cm2, shallow
```

Three ways the press can still ruin the lean spec:

1. **Capsule leak / air / \(\mathrm{NH_4}\) salt** — offers a fluid; ringwoodite will drink it.  
2. **IW buffer + Fe metal** — raises solubility and can also pull N into metal, then dump it back on quench. Stay at Ni–NiO.  
3. **Wadsleyite detour** — if the P–T path parks in wad, \(D \approx 5\) versus olivine can concentrate N before the last conversion. Move through wad; do not soak there in an N-bearing fluid.

Metal in the capsule is a N magnet (\(D_{\mathrm{metal/silicate}}\) large). For A1, no Fe sponge sitting in the charge.

## Numbers to put on the wall

- Fo charge we pack: **0.1–1 ppm**  
- Ringwoodite **capacity** if we were sloppy and reduced: **10–150 ppm** (up to ~280 in some cited runs)  
- Ratio of those two: the press can multiply the bath by **10–100×** if we offer N  
- Natural mantle olivine: order **1 ppm** — already at our reject line if we used kimberlite grit  

A1 stays lean because we do not offer N. Solubility is the warning label on the capsule, not the recipe.

Sunday, September 20, 2026 — 3:12 AM EDT

There is **no published N–V spin center in ringwoodite**. No ODMR, no \(T_2\), no zero-phonon line assigned to nitrogen-plus-vacancy. What exists is a well-studied **iron color**, plus vacancy / hydroxyl chemistry. A1 is still a hunt, not a copy of diamond.

## What “color” in ringwoodite actually is

The famous blue is **not** an NV analog. Pure \(\gamma\textrm{-Mg}_2\mathrm{SiO}_4\) is colorless. A little Fe turns it deep blue. The bands are crystal-field and charge-transfer on iron, not a nitrogen-vacancy pair.

| Band (approx.) | Assignment | Where it sits |
|---|---|---|
| ~8600 and ~12 300–12 700 cm⁻¹ (~1.16 and ~0.78 µm / visible-NIR) | spin-allowed \(d\)–\(d\) of octahedral \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) | the green-window problem if Fe is in the brick |
| ~17 500–18 200 cm⁻¹ (~550 nm) | \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\)-\(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) intervalence charge transfer | the blue |
| ~30 000 cm⁻¹ edge | O → Fe ligand-to-metal charge transfer | UV wall |

Colorless grains of the same Fe content are read as **inverse spinel**: \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) on the tetrahedral Si site, one band near 12 000 cm⁻¹. Blue vs colorless is inversion + \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\), not a qubit. Heating in air turns blue → green → brown as Fe oxidizes and H leaves. That is pigment chemistry.

For A1 this is why the brick is Fo \(\ge 90\) and dry: Fe and OH are **optical and spin junk** next to a hoped-for defect. They are also the thing every mineralogist already sees.

## Defects that *are* documented

Ringwoodite is a normal spinel (\(Fd\bar{3}m\)): Si on tetrahedra, Mg/Fe on octahedra. At high T it partially **inverts** (Mg on Si sites, Si on Mg sites). That inversion is a built-in defect factory.

Known point defects, none of them ODMR-rated:

- **\(\mathrm{V_{Mg}}\)** and **\(\mathrm{V_{Si}}\)** — charge-balanced by H or by oxide vacancies  
- **\(\mathrm{V_O}\)** (oxide vacancy) — seen with hydroxyl work  
- **OH / \(\mathrm{[V_{Mg}(OH)_2]}\), \(\mathrm{[V_{Si}(OH)_4]}\)** — water up to ~2 wt% in hydrous runs  
- **Mg/Si inversion** — native, T-dependent  
- **\(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\)** on octahedral (and possibly tetrahedral after anneal)  
- **N** — soluble to tens–hundreds of ppm under reduced N-rich fluid; **site unknown**

That list is geology and catalysis. It is not a qubit catalog.

## What a “ringwoodite color center” would have to be

A useful center needs, at minimum:

1. A mid-gap electronic state that absorbs and emits  
2. A spin (usually \(S=1\) or \(1/2\)) that can be initialized optically  
3. Spin-dependent fluorescence or photocurrent (ODMR / PDMR)  
4. Neighbors quiet enough that \(T_2\) is not dead on arrival  

Diamond NV is \(\mathrm{N_C}\) next to \(\mathrm{V_C}\). MgO has a **computed** NV-like pair (N interstitial + Mg vacancy) with a predicted triplet — not yet a device. SiC has real NV and divacancy. Ringwoodite has none of those assignments.

Plausible pairs to hunt, in order of how close they sit to known chemistry:

| Candidate | Why it is thinkable | Why it may fail |
|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{N_O}\)–\(\mathrm{V_{Mg}}\) or N interstitial + \(\mathrm{V_{Mg}}\) | closest MgO analog; N is soluble | site unknown; band gap and level positions uncomputed for this host |
| \(\mathrm{N}\)–\(\mathrm{V_{Si}}\) | Si vacancy already exists via inversion | Si site is small; pairing geometry may not give a triplet |
| Isolated \(\mathrm{V_O}\) / F-like | oxide vacancies exist | often \(S=0\) or noisy; no N handle for hyperfine |
| \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) related | already optically active | spin bath, not a controllable qubit |
| Substitutional N only (P1 analog) | easiest to form | no vacancy, usually no convenient optical spin readout |

A1 (\(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) at \(1\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\) + pairing anneal) is built to make the first two. It does not guarantee they emit.

## What the first spectrum should look for

Do not hunt a 637 nm diamond ZPL. Hunt **anything that is not Fe**.

1. Unimplanted Fo-rich ringwoodite control — map the Fe \(d\)–\(d\) / IVCT baseline.  
2. Implanted + pairing-annealed A1 — difference PL at 10 K and 295 K, 400–900 nm.  
3. Same difference in EPR / ODMR 0.5–5 GHz (diamond NV is 2.87 GHz; MgO and SiC sit elsewhere; this host is unknown).  
4. \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) hyperfine as the fingerprint that the implant, not native Fe, is talking.  
5. Raman/XRD still saying spinel, not olivine.

If PL only follows Fe and ODMR is dark, the brick is still a mechanical host. The lid (hBN) remains the first real ambient spin.

## Honest status

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Ringwoodite is blue | yes — Fe IVCT / crystal field |
| Ringwoodite hosts OH, \(\mathrm{V_{Mg}}\), \(\mathrm{V_{Si}}\), \(\mathrm{V_O}\), inversion | yes |
| Ringwoodite dissolves N | yes, as a bath, site unknown |
| Ringwoodite NV with ODMR | **not observed** |
| DFT defect catalog for \(\gamma\textrm{-Mg_2SiO_4}\):N,V | **not in the public literature I can cite** |

A1 is how we start that catalog in the lab: lean Fo, known \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) spike, pairing under load, then look. The color the mineralogists named is iron. The color center we want has not been named yet.

Sunday, September 20, 2026 — 2:49 AM EDT

Lean. For A1, native \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\) is a bath we did not choose. Keep it under **1 ppm**. Prefer **0.1–1 ppm**. Do not saturate the capsule.

## Why not 10–50 ppm

That optional “N in the capsule” line was for a later ensemble path. It is the wrong first charge.

In diamond, Hahn-echo \(T_2\) falls as substitutional N (P1) rises: hundreds of microseconds at ~0.2 ppm P1, tens of microseconds at a few ppm. Type Ib at 100 ppm is a sensor brick, not a quiet register. Same logic here until a silicate spectrum exists.

Ringwoodite will **take** nitrogen if you offer it. N-saturated experiments put ~10–150 µg/g in ringwoodite and even more in wadsleyite (\(D_{\mathrm{wad/ol}} \approx 5\)). Forsterite itself only dissolves a few ppm under reducing, high-T fluids — about **10 ppm max** at 3.5 GPa / 1300 °C near IW; often below detection at Ni–NiO. So the danger is not “Fo cannot hold N.” It is “a wet N-rich capsule plus the ringwoodite field will load the brick.”

A1 uses implanted \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) at \(1\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\). That only wins if background \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\) is lower than the implant.

## Charge spec before the press

| Item | A1 (this run) | Later ensemble, only after ODMR |
|---|---|---|
| Native \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\) in Fo powder / crystal | **0.1–1 ppm**, SIMS reject if \(\ge 1\) ppm | 1–5 ppm growth-dope |
| Capsule fluid | dry, no \(\mathrm{N_2}\) source | metered \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) if we switch off implant |
| \(f\mathrm{O_2}\) | Ni–NiO or higher (keeps N out of Fo) | IW only if we *want* N in |
| Water | dry (wet + Fe drops the 1-atm tidy ceiling) | still dry if we can |
| Fe | Fo \(\ge 90\), Fe not in the implant volume | same |

High-purity synthetic forsterite, not kimberlite olivine, for the first cores. Natural peridot already carries Fe, H, and whatever N the mantle left. Rehearsal rock, not A1 charge.

SIMS or combustion-N on the powder **before** packing. If the lot is 5 ppm, we do not “dilute with hope.” We get another lot.

## What the press will do to that number

If the charge is 0.5 ppm in olivine and we cross into ringwoodite, N can stay in the spinel. Partitioning does not purge it. Wadsleyite would take more; ringwoodite less than wad, still not zero. So the number you pack is the number you approximately keep. There is no “the phase change burns off nitrogen.”

Air in a poorly pumped capsule is enough to spoil a sub-ppm spec. Pump, dry, weld.

## Run-sheet line

> Fo charge: synthetic Fo\(_{\ge 90}\), dry, SIMS \(^{14}\mathrm{N} = 0.1\)–\(1\) ppm (fail \(\ge 1\) ppm). No \(\mathrm{N_2}\) fluid. Capsule at Ni–NiO or more oxidized. Implant supplies the \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\). Raise native N only after A1 has a spectrum.

That matches the sparse gate. Native N is the floor of the spin bath. Implant is the controlled spike on top of it.

text:
This Irish girl absolutely NAILS IT

How did women today lose the ability to know the difference between men and women?

Have you found yourself a based wife like this?

Men and women are equal in worth, but they are very different. This is God's intentional design.

From the beginning, Scripture presents humanity as male and female, both made in the image of God, yet created with real differences that allow them to complement one another. Men are generally built with greater physical strength, size and ambition. Women are uniquely designed to conceive, carry, birth and nourish. Those biological differences are not small details. They shape how families, communities and civilizations have functioned throughout history.

A healthy view of masculinity does not mean domination. A man’s strength is supposed to become protection, provision, discipline, courage and sacrifice. His responsibility is not to demand service, but to spend himself for those entrusted to him. Christian leadership is modeled after Christ, who gave Himself for His people.

Likewise, femininity is not weakness. A woman possesses an extraordinary capacity to nurture life, create a home, form children, preserve relationships and bring warmth and order to a family. Motherhood in particular is one of the most physically demanding and spiritually significant callings imaginable.

Exceptions do not erase the larger pattern.

Modern culture often treats equality as though it requires sameness. Christianity offers something richer: equal dignity, different strengths, shared purpose.

A husband and wife are not competing versions of the same thing. They are two distinct parts of a whole, each bringing something the other cannot fully replace.

God did not make men and women different by accident. The differences are part of the beauty of creation. The goal is not to flatten them, but to order those strengths toward love, family, service and ultimately toward God.

How did we lose this simple truth in our society?

FREE SPEECH IS THE GOOD LIFE. FREE SPEECH IS EUDAMONIA 

No matter the economic gains accrued, if freedom of speech is eroded, governance cannot deliver happiness.

A society where people offer different opinions, revealing their psychological states and mental attitudes to the world, is a society born to accommodate happy, free, and dignified people.

The open society itself is a social good. Freedom of speech is an end in itself. Its value lies in the quality of life it offers members of society through freedom and individualism.

This is the democracy we imagined in 1992—the direct opposite of what was experienced under the PNDC dictatorship.

This is the society we collectively desired in 1956- the negation of the colonial grip and shackles to developing the African person born and nurtured in freedom.

Freedom and Justice. Not freedom or justice. We understand that freedom is necessary to secure a just society. Our independence was not only freedom from foreign domination.
It was also freedom to pursue a complete and total life from the overbearing demands of the State.

 “Free at last. Thank God Almighty, we are free at last.” 
Free to call our enemies our enemies. Free to praise our foes. Free to condemn our friends. 
Such is the kind of liberty our society protects. That “... over his body and mind, the individual is sovereign.”

Free speech is the principal right for securing the good life. The right that gives life to our darkest thoughts and frees us from being prisoners to the mind.

Secure, Protect, and Defend Free Speech. You will, by that, be securing, protecting, and defending YOUR DEMOCRACY.

“Ken Michaels Creative”(c)1988,2026 - "The Music Makers..." was my "community radio station" company’s name as a kid.

Hey there, it’s Ken Michaels, I was an 11 year old that wanted to be a "DeeJay"-AND- "weatherman." I ran into a few problems... I didn't have a drivers license and, well, I sounded like "a little girl!" (Haha!)

NOBODY WOULD HIRE ME!

With my Dad’s help, we found out that you could have a "Community Radio Station..." There was no age limit, you could play what you wanted to, and no "Federal License" was required if you only covered a small area. 

It's still referred to today, as a "PART 15 RADIO STATION" in the "rules and regulations" of The Federal Communication Commission, Washington, D.C.

We ordered a small FM Transmitter Kit, that you had to build yourself, "the kit" was made for this exact type of station.

He helped me turn an old storage shed into a small radio station building. I was able to buy old used studio equipment from a friend who did actually work at one of Meridian, Mississippi's biggest station as the engineer. First thing I needed was a mixer. Then, a mic 🎤 and two record players and a cassette tape player.

My engineer friend said that I needed to come up with a name for the station, decide on what type of music we'd play, and go from there! I named it, "POWER 88 Gospel!" ...and I wanted to put together the absolute best music collection. So... every weekend we went in search of records at yard sales. It worked out perfectly!

My engineer friend said that my music collection was "kind of, officially" known as the stations, "music format." -and since I was "the formats creator" and wanted to pick every song played, the format needed a name. I decided to name it, "Home Grown Gospel." ...And (haha) I was very picky about what songs played. I wanted to play the best, "Southern and Country style Gospel & Church Hymns!

I grew up, s l o w l y... but eventually was hired by one of the "BIG STATIONS" in Meridian, and decided to close my little community station. -But, I heald onto the company name: "Ken Michaels Creative"( and all of my records and tapes) -AND- kept my "music format name" with all of my notes as to what songs should play. I had future plans for my "Home Grown Gospel" format!

Since then, my "Home Grown Gospel" format became the musical format for a 50,000 watt FM station, and was heard all across two states... Later down the road, a guy called me and said, I own an AM and FM station in Meridian. 

I would love for you to bring your music collection and have "Home Grown Gospel" air on both the AM and FM station. I accepted the offer and became those stations, "Operations, Program and Music Director." 

My "Home Grown Gospel" format went on both the AM and FM...How long did they stay with me? 14 years...

As of a few weeks back (September 6th), it marked my 35th year in radio and weather. 

Today, my company "Digitally Kennected, LLC" has a "music format division" and not only is that division known as, "Ken Michaels Creative" but I not only still have "Home Grown Gospel" available, but I own almost 20 others that I have created. What about the weather? I'm a "Severe Storms Specialist" and have covered numerous stations across the South with my "LIVE" (non-stop) coverage.

And, without question... "Digitally Kennected, LLC's" 3rd division is, "Ken Michaels Weather." My (multi-year) weather partner is "Forbes Magazine ranked #1!" - "WeatherTAP" of Crossville, Tennessee.

I also have "Ken Michaels Channel" on Spotify. One of my most popular music shows is known as, "Home Grown Gospel!" text:
⛽ Why Global Chaos Controls the Cost of Your Commute: How Gas Prices Are Set

Even though the U.S. is the world’s top oil producer, your local pump prices are dictated by a massive global market. The retail cost of a gallon of gasoline is broken down into four core parts: about 50% to 60% comes from the raw cost of crude oil, 15% to 25% goes to refining it, 15% to 20% pays for government taxes, and 10% to 15% covers gas station operations and freight.

Because raw crude oil is a globally traded commodity, events happening thousands of miles away instantly change what you pay at the pump. Foreign nations like Saudi Arabia and Russia (leading the OPEC+ cartel) routinely coordinate to intentionally cut their oil production. By engineering these artificial shortages, they drive up global oil prices to boost their own revenues.

International conflicts—such as the recent Ukrainian drone strike on Moscow's Kapotnya refinery, or active military tensions choking off oil shipments in the Strait of Hormuz—spook energy traders and physically restrict supply. Because American refineries still rely on importing foreign oil varieties to keep their machinery running, any sudden geopolitical shock or intentional production cut overseas triggers a domino effect that forces local gas station owners to raise prices immediately to cover their next fuel delivery.

Because the global market heavily dictates crude oil costs, the U.S. government cannot completely control pump prices. However, Washington possesses a specific toolkit of short-term fixes and long-term policies to put downward pressure on fuel costs.

SHORT-TERM INTERVENTTIONS (IMMEDIATE IMPACT):

✅Deploy the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR): 
The White House can flood the market with crude oil by tapping into the nation’s underground emergency stockpiles.  A history of U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserves is provided below.

▶️Suspend Federal or State Gas Taxes: 
Congress can implement a "gas tax holiday" by temporarily freezing the 18.4 cents-per-gallon federal tax. Governors can similarly suspend state excise taxes, which provides instant relief at the pump, though it temporarily reduces funding for highway infrastructure.

✅Expand Biofuel Allowances (E15 Gas): The federal government can issue emergency waivers to permit the year-round sale of E15 gasoline (fuel containing 15% ethanol). Ethanol is typically cheaper than raw petroleum; expanding its use lowers production costs and stretches the domestic gasoline supply.

✅Ease Environmental and Refining Regulations: During supply crunches, the EPA can temporarily roll back specific environmental mandates or fast-track rules for domestic refiners. This allows refiners to produce more volume quickly, though it typically draws pushback over increased emissions.

LONG-TERM INTERVENTIONS (STRUCTURAL CHANGES):

▶️Increase Domestic Drilling and Infrastructure Permitting: 
The U.S. can lease more federal lands and offshore sites for oil exploration. Speeding up the environmental review and permitting process for new pipelines and refineries expands the country's long-term capacity to move and process crude.
✅Immediately upon returning to office, President Trump signed Executive Order 14156 ("Declaring a National Energy Emergency"), reversing previous administrative freezes on oil and gas leasing on public lands and offshore waters.
✅His administration has structurally streamlined environmental review processes under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), aiming to radically accelerate permitting times for domestic pipelines and fossil fuel infrastructure.

▶️Upgrade Refinery Compatibility: 
The government can offer financial incentives or tax credits to help domestic refineries retool their machinery. Upgrading them to process the "light, sweet" crude produced in modern American shale fields—rather than relying on imported "heavy, sour" foreign oil—would insulate the U.S. from overseas disruptions.
✅Under his "America First" energy platform, the administration has utilized economic incentives and regulatory rollbacks to aggressively onshore and expand heavy industrial processing capability.
✅Most notably, in March 2026, President Trump announced a historic $300 billion energy package to build the first major new U.S. oil refinery in 50 years, located at the Port of Brownsville, Texas. This initiative is designed specifically to upgrade domestic processing infrastructure, reducing reliance on foreign supply chains by allowing U.S. infrastructure to natively handle more domestic crude. 

▶️Diplomatic Pressure on OPEC+ Cartels: 
The administration can use geopolitical leverage, sanctions, or international trade negotiations to pressure major oil-producing allies (like Saudi Arabia) to ramp up their production quotas and lower global prices.

▶️Reduce Overall Oil Demand: 
Long-term reduction in fuel dependency directly lowers demand, which stabilizes prices. Governments achieve this by subsidizing public transit infrastructure, incentivizing remote work policies, and accelerating consumer transition toward electric vehicles (EVs).

text:
I'm doing something outside my comfort zone: I'm organizing a workshop where I'm not the one delivering the content.

Here's the story.

Our college cluster is great for the same reason it's unstable: anyone who asks gets sudo access. That freedom has caused real problems, like two separate Kubernetes installations running on the same machine and people killing other projects to free up a port. I think LLMs are a big part of it. Students follow whatever commands they're given without reading the explanation.

So we're planning to add restrictions. We want a log of who did what, so we can call out the person when something breaks, and we want to connect all the clusters across India behind one shared URL. Honestly, I haven't done the research or planning this needs. The plan is still clay.

The cluster already runs Kubernetes, and a central control plane already connects the clusters, but everyone still has raw access. To fix that properly, I needed to understand Kubernetes deeply.

I did what I always do and went to YouTube. The videos were good, but none of them gave me the confidence to say "I know Kubernetes."

Then the semester started, and we got a new faculty member for the DevOps class. On Krushn Sir's suggestion, I went to meet him, introduced myself, and asked if he could teach me Kubernetes. He was already teaching two students on Saturdays and invited me to join. The class was already midway, which made it hard to follow, but my YouTube background helped. He assumed I hadn't understood anything and offered to start a new class in parallel.

That first class earned my huge respect. I don't remember the exact question, but I remember how he answered it. Instead of giving a memorized answer, he showed us the internals and how it actually works.

The next weekend I asked when he'd start teaching me. His answer: "Find 50 students who want to learn it."

That was not my kind of work. I've always handed off anything that wasn't tech, writing code, or building projects. But most of my batchmates are busy with internships, and I wasn't familiar with the juniors. So I spent the next week finding 50 serious students. I stopped people walking by, asked if they wanted to learn Kubernetes, took their phone numbers, added them to a list, and finally created one common channel for everyone.

Then came the management lessons:

Class announcements have to go out at least 24 hours ahead so everyone is prepared.
I had to check that the room was free and the faculty was available.
Whenever the faculty needed something, the answer was "talk to Kanishk," so I had to start delegating.

I first gave the announcements to a junior. He had trouble getting Slack notifications, so we switched to WhatsApp. He still didn't manage it, and I ended up doing it myself.

The next class turned out to be controversial. It fell on Ganesh Visarjan, which was optional, but many students wanted to shift the class. I didn't want to make shifting classes a habit, so I held it that day. Attendance dropped, but we wanted serious students anyway.

The day after, I organized a revision class for those who missed it and retaught everything from the first class.

I'm still figuring out this side of things, but so far it's been a great learning experience.

text:
Someone was trying to convince me that this proves there's an AI bubble because they can't make AI smarter. 

No, there's still demand for AI. We've known mathematically that we can make AI more efficient and faster, but not much smarter. In fact, if we're not careful, AI will get dumber (for various different reasons that don't matter here). 

But there's still demand for the current capability. So saying there's a bubble because people aren't able to make cars go much faster and very few people need those high-end models is rather like saying that the automotive industry is a bubble because there's very little demand for NASCAR and Formula-1 vehicles. 

A bubble goes something like this: 
- "Wow, look at this Cool Thing!" 
- "The Cool Thing is clearly worth the attention, so let's charge more for it!" 
- "The Cool Thing is now REALLY expensive and worth a lot of investment!" 
- "Hey, do you see some people selling their investment over there?"
- "Dude, where's my market?"

By the way, those stages are called Displacement, Boom, Euphoria, Profit-Taking, and Panic. They're also called Minsky stages. 

There are a lot of people who point out similarities to a bubble, including high investment and buzzwords; but there are several anti-indicators. 

For example, bubbles run on debt. Other than government feeding troughs, there's hardly any debt involved here. 

There's also real, increasing demand, which can be easily seen in the arguments over data centers. 

There's also diversification. Bubbles tend to focus, hard. AI as an industry, however, is showing up in various different forms -- and, very tellingly, meeting different levels of demand. People aren't jumping on AI everywhere, all the time; they're picking and choosing what seems most useful. 

The closest you get to a bubble that I've seen so far are in two forms of behavior.  

The first is circular money flow. Here's how that works. Company A makes widgets; Company B makes sprockets. Sprockets are needed for making widgets, so Company B does really well if Company A does really well, so B invests in A. A then turns around and uses that money to buy sprockets from B, which allows them to produce more widgets. Both companies show increased profits even though a lot of money just went in a big circle. 

That's happening with a lot of tech firms. In fact, it was a good chunk of what was keeping SpaceX running at the pace it was for a bit there, because their biggest customer was Starlink . . . which, oh yeah, was developed and owned entirely by SpaceX. 

But the difference there was that Starlink was and continues to show real profits. And there is so much real demand for AI-powered products that they remain profitable. Which means the question is not whether it is a bubble . . . but whether the profit can be maintained. 

That might sound like a distinction without a difference. Instead, let me point you back to what I said about there being TWO behaviors that come close to bubble-like behavior. I only mentioned one. The other one rested in companies laying off human workforce because of the promise of AI automation. 

The big AI companies kept the prices as low as possible while developing their products. They wanted loyal customers (and their language data). That's not worked out as well as they thought (see my diversification point above), but it did result in a lot of bean-counting where people concluded they could save money by firing 5 people and having 1 person babysit the AI to do those other people's work. The problem there is that some of that calculus worked out . . . and some of it didn't. 

There are many different reasons, but I'll focus on two. One is institutional knowledge. I say over and over that AI is not an easy button, it is a QUICK button. You have to know how it works the long way in order to figure out how to use the shortcut. 

(And I don't even shortcut everything I could; every word of this post was pounded out with real meat-wearing fingers on a physical keyboard, just because I saw a post late at night and decided to springboard off it on a whim, because I enjoy the act of putting words on screen. I'm sure the typos will be hilarious.) 

But if you lose that institutional knowledge, you lose access to how to handle things that aren't in the rulebook, or maybe you even forget the rulebook covered that situation and you waste time trying to reinvent the procedure. 

The second reason I'll cover here is that the beans don't always add up to the same number every night. The math was based on the token cost for the AI to process the work of 5 former employees; but if anything has to be redone, it's not just a little fix on a spreadsheet. The whole thing has to be recalculated again. The tokens need to be spent again. That adds up. 

And that one employee has to be working without human feedback. Not just without a face to talk to, but describing things to a completely alien intelligence. You have to remind it to work in a particular way. You have to treat it like an overly-literal hyperactive child with the loyalty of a golden retriever and the personality skills of a lizard in a politician suit. That's exhausting. Reiterating and regenerating in weird phrases takes a toll. 

And so that 1 remaining employee, sometimes, isn't really working 1 workload. He's working 1.1 workloads, and it adds up. 

All the while, token prices rise. Suddenly that 1.1 workload isn't carrying 5 ghost employees. Now it's the equivalent cost of 6, and the beans aren't adding up right. 

There are companies now that are quietly hiring people back. Of course, a lot of the ones worth hiring back have already found other jobs. Employment numbers are surprisingly good considering the terrible inflation and various other economic issues we're having. 

So why are OpenAI and Anthropic crying doom and gloom? 

The answer is that they want to be regulated by the US government. But not just any regulation, no. They have very detailed suggested regulations, which all sound very reasonable and oh-so-technical. And which benefit them a great deal, since they have the money for lawyers and small startups don't. 

Nothing they offer has much chance of holding back what they say they're afraid of. About as much chance as a screen door holding back the ocean on a submarine, I'd say. 

And here's the reason why. United States regulation only affects the United States. 

"But Bowman, don't you realize that China's AI development is only as good as they can steal from US companies?"

That's not the full situation, but it's close enough. Sure. But development will still continue even under regs; and that lack of regs will really encourage the "black market" for open models. 

Which are already out there. Jailbroken models that are quite happy to tell any would-be "mostly peaceful" protestor exactly how to make a "mostly peaceful" present of a pipe filled with some screws and some unsilly putty. Or spit out the address of the guy he/she/it wants to gift said pipe to. 

The genie is out of the bottle. Not AGI (no such thing yet, and I personally doubt there ever will be), but the security vulnerability is there. And the best way to combat it is to have a massively distributed network of various different developers doing AI in different ways, rather than just a handful that become exploitable because they always do things the same way. 

And the funny thing about self-proposed regs is that you can always lead by example. You can say "We already play by these rules and we hope others follow them." 

They're not. They want the US government to do it for them. 

Who benefits?

Back in 1997 me and two other E-4s stationed at Pope would save up a couple months and trek it down to Myrtle Beach in my Ford Escort with sexy the automatic seat belt option. It was sexy because it choked you most of the time you tried to get out of the car.

Our first hit at Myrtle was Hooters, it was on a pier and you could get two dozen fresh oysters with a pitcher of domestic beer for five bucks.

We'd sit on their pier and enjoy the ocean, eat our snot and debate about what E-4s debated about. Louisiana hot sauce or Tabasco? Cindy Crawford or Kathy Ireland? Are the guys in Pearl Jam gay? You know, the usual. 

Tabasco and Ireland for the record. No idea about the PJ musicians.

We'd flirt with the waitresses and they'd flirt back for tips. Both parties knew this and were okay with it, we knew what was up. So did the goddess.

Then we would go cruise the strip in my Ford Escort with the sexy seatbelts. Yelling pick up lines to the local and tourist hotties running around. Strangely that strategy never worked. 😂😂😂

Between 8-11pm, nothing happened. We hung out on the beach or took a nap in the Escort. Seriously, nothing happened during those hours at Myrtle Beach in 1996-97.

But at 11PM, let's fucking go!!! Rolled up to Zannados or some other club and straight up partied. Hit on chicks. Drank. Partied then went to after parties. For an entire weekend. 

We never got a hotel either, slept in that sexy Escort or somebody would offer a couch or floor. An amazing Hooters server named Jennifer offered us a floor to sleep on, many times. Single mom and such an amazing person. I've tried to track her down but, sometimes strangers will forever be strangers. Jen, if you're reading this, love you girl, thank you for your floor. 

Those weekends were pure greatness. It's just the boys getting drunk and trying to get laid. 

Did we get laid, not as much as you think. The one brother had a 65% strike out, other one was  80% strike out. Me? I was 99.52% strike out. I had only lost my virginity two years before and was still terrified of women.

Talk to the two men today. All three of us are successful enough that money isn't an survival issue. Good to hear. Do we want to do it again, again no. We loved our youth but that is over. 

Hell, some hurricane destroyed the Hooters restaurant and the pier.

But history is good. Remembering those weekends and those men is fantastic. It's such a beautiful bloom of history in your life. Wonderful to remember.

It does remind you tho, if you life your life, memories will be made. Versus going somewhere to make memories.

text:
Channel 12 Video on the Yellow Line: Security Gap or Cover for Gaza Escalation?

By Mahmoud Khalil

Israel’s Channel 12 released footage of a Palestinian from Gaza crossing the Yellow Line, advancing toward a military site, walking among the vehicles and reaching the gate guard post before a soldier noticed him and looked toward his protruding head. The timing is not neutral. The Israeli army is intensifying killing and destruction in the Strip after Hamas accepted Trump’s 15-point roadmap to enter phase two of the Gaza deal, amid a heated Israeli election on October 27.

What the Tape Shows — and What It Does Not

The clip, after tight censorship according to coverage, records a surveillance failure more than an attack. The Israeli account itself says the man walked among the vehicles to the gate without being detected by systems or soldiers until the last moment. The public report, in the version circulating, offers no proof of a weapon, an explosive or gunfire. It offers one image with two readings: a worrying security breach for the army, or evidence that the Yellow Line is a gray zone where civilians are killed on the pretext of “approaching.”

The Yellow Line Is No Longer Temporary

The line was drawn with the October 2025 pullback as a temporary divide before a wider withdrawal. In practice it expanded. Satellite reports and agencies said Israel built an earthen barrier tens of kilometers long and widened its hold to about 60 percent of the Strip, with Netanyahu speaking of reaching 70 percent. The Washington Post and Associated Press documented Palestinians killed near a line that is not always clear, including children. The Israeli army says it fires to remove an immediate threat. Families say the markers are moved and people do not know where death begins.

The Deal on Paper, Escalation in the Field

Trump announced a 15-point roadmap for a second phase linking Hamas disarmament to a phased withdrawal and an interim Palestinian administration. Hamas announced its agreement and demanded Israel be bound by it. Netanyahu repeated that he will not withdraw from current positions before full disarmament. In September the Israeli army logged dozens of “violations” and answered with strikes, while Jared Kushner blamed a “crazy election” for making Israeli policy less rational. The Board of Peace, according to sources, does not expect real leverage over Israel before the October 27 ballot.

Is the Video a Justification for Brutality?

It is not legal proof of the man’s intent, and it is not a clean bill for wide bombardment. Its political function is clearer than its military content. In an election season in which the right competes to look firm on Gaza, a clip of “a man at the gate” becomes a ready argument for tighter rules of engagement, refusal to pull back to the original line, and tying any calm to a “security failure.” Palestinian coverage uses the same tape to show the slackness of the system used to justify an open-fire policy.

The analytical conclusion is that the video works both ways, but the balance of power decides who turns it into policy. Whoever holds the aircraft and artillery can say: look at the gap, so we continue the destruction. Whoever lives west of the Yellow Line pays twice: once when killed at a moving line, and again when the tape is shown to claim escalation is necessity, not choice. Phase two does not begin with a video. It begins with a ceasefire honored on the ground, not with tapes run through newsrooms before the polls.

text:
Saudi Arabia exited mBridge. It gave up a financial exit ramp, and with it the facade of sovereignty. 

For decades, Riyadh sold itself as the Arab world’s indispensable power: oil kingmaker, custodian of Mecca, counterweight to Iran, a partner Washington had to respect. The mBridge withdrawal exposes the gap between that image and reality.

mBridge was was a China-led central bank digital currency pilot involving China, Hong Kong, Thailand, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia. Its purpose was simple: create a cross-border payment channel that could reduce reliance on the US dollar and SWIFT.

That mattered. It was not a military alliance. It was not a binding break with the West. It was not even a sanctions-evasion tool by design. It was optional financial infrastructure for a multipolar financial future. Staying in it cost Saudi Arabia almost nothing.

Saudi Arabia still stepped back from the project. The official line - that it was always part of the plan - is a weak excuse. If it cost nothing to stay, why leave? 
Because Washington does not want its allies building dollar alternatives. And Saudi Arabia conmplied. 

That is not strategy. That is submission.

The BRICS angle is similar. Saudi Arabia was invited in 2023 but never formally joined. It attends as an observer and keeps its distance. So the story is not “Saudi left BRICS.” It is worse: Saudi Arabia was offered a place in a multipolar order and refused to take it, because the American security umbrella mattered more.

Saudi Arabia wanted to be treated as a regional superpower - independent, indispensable, able to balance between the US, China, Russia, and Iran. 
But when given a low-cost chance to diversify its financial options, it folded. It showed that its sovereignty is negotiable when Washington applies pressure.
Meanwhile, other Gulf states hedge. The UAE has diversified partners, left OPEC, and kept lines open to China, Russia, and Israel. Saudi Arabia has doubled down on US protection, signed a strategic defense agreement, and waits for the right moment to normalize with Israel. It has not built an independent deterrent. It rents one.

All in all, the mBridge exit is a small technical decision, but with a large meaning behind it. It says Riyadh is not the Middle East’s independent heavyweight. It is a client state that traded financial optionality for American approval.
A kingdom that once wanted to lead the Arab world now cannot even keep a payment pilot alive without permission. That is the real story. Not that Saudi Arabia left a project—but that it proved it never really had the sovereignty it spent decades projecting.

text:
The difference is which goal the story treats as legitimate: preserving an imperfect order versus exposing or breaking a rotten one. Everything else—who the antagonist is, how the plot is paced, and how the ending feels—follows from that.

Protagonist protects a flawed system
The hero is a guardian: cop, soldier, official, sheriff, superhero, or competent insider. The system has defects (bureaucracy, corruption at the edges, unequal application of rules), but the story treats those defects as preferable to the alternative the antagonist offers—chaos, terrorism, revolution, or a new tyranny. The antagonist is usually the person or force trying to smash or replace the order.

Narrative pattern:
A threat appears that exploits the system’s weaknesses.
The hero uses, bends, or personally embodies the system’s tools (law, force, expertise, tradition).
Climax is restoration or containment. Limited reform may occur, but the underlying structure remains.
Tone is often stoic, tragic-heroic, or “someone has to do the dirty work.” The audience is asked to accept that imperfect institutions still produce more safety and continuity than their collapse would.

Examples: Batman in The Dark Knight (Gotham’s justice is compromised; Joker wants to prove it is a lie), many Western lawmen, Die Hard, large parts of the Dirty Harry cycle (Harry despises red tape but still functions as the system’s sharp edge), most military and superhero films in which the hero saves “the world as we know it.”

Protagonist fights a corrupt system
The hero is a challenger: whistleblower, journalist, inmate, outsider, or reluctant insider who can no longer comply. The institution itself—its rules, incentives, and enforcers—is the primary obstacle. The antagonist is often not a single cartoon villain but the machine and the people loyal to it.

Narrative pattern:
Discovery or moral awakening.
Escalating institutional counter-pressure (cover-up, co-optation, punishment, violence).
Climax is exposure, sacrifice, escape, or a partial rupture. Total replacement of the system is uncommon in mainstream American stories; the usual payoff is that the truth comes out or one person refuses to be broken.
Tone is accusatory, paranoid, or bitterly inspirational. Victory, when it happens, is costly and incomplete.

Examples: Mr. Smith Goes to Washington, All the President’s Men, One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest, Erin Brockovich, Spotlight, The Matrix, much of 1970s New Hollywood (Chinatown, Network).

American stories frequently hybridize the two. The most common commercial version is the rebel insider: a hero who hates the system’s hypocrisy or incompetence but still defends its core function against people who would abolish it. That lets audiences enjoy anti-bureaucratic rage without endorsing actual systemic overthrow.

What U.S. film and popular story have favored
U.S. storytelling contains both templates because the national myth itself is split: the founding is a justified rebellion against a corrupt imperial system, yet once the republic exists, popular forms often treat further revolution as a threat to the experiment.

The balance shifts with institutional trust and the perceived alternative:

1930s Depression**: Both, with more room for the fighter. Gangster films and Capra often treat the system as failing ordinary people; outlaws or idealists can be sympathetic. Containment usually happens through individual success or family rather than collective revolution.
WWII through the 1950s**: Stronger “protect the order.” External enemies and internal deviance are the antagonists. Rebellion is frequently personal or adolescent and resolved by reintegration. Westerns and war films emphasize civilization being defended or imposed.
Late 1960s–mid-1970s*: High-water mark for “fight the corrupt system.” Vietnam, civil rights backlash, and Watergate produced *Bonnie and Clyde, Easy Rider, The Graduate, Chinatown, Network, One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest. Institutions are the problem; endings are often bleak.
Late 1970s–1980s*: Swing toward protection and restoration. Blockbusters (Star Wars, *Rocky, Raiders) and vigilante/cop films recast the hero as the person who makes the system work again, or who supplies the backbone it lacks. Bureaucracy is still mocked, but usually so the individual hero can save the underlying order.
Post-9/11 through the superhero peak**: Heavy emphasis on guardians. Existential or terrorist threats justify flawed security states and dark knights. Prestige films continue the critique; tentpoles mostly sell the feeling that competent heroes can keep civilization intact.
2010s–present**: Both run in parallel. Dystopian and awards-oriented work often make the system the enemy. Franchise action still treats world-ending disruptors as the villains. The same character (Joker, certain antiheroes) now gets competing readings: victim of a broken machine versus agent of chaos.

The commercial pattern is consistent. Mid-budget adult dramas can afford to let the system win or the hero lose. Large-scale popular entertainment more often sells a lone competent person holding a flawed but functioning world together. That is why the “protect the flawed system” story never disappears for long in the United States, even in eras that also produce sharp institutional critiques.

text:
Denmark's Prime Minister, Mette Frederiksen repeats it like a mantra. Greenland is part of the Kingdom, sovereignty remains intact. Formally, that's true. But she's leaving out the rest.

According to the White House, the US now has veto power over strategic investments in Greenland from countries it considers adversaries. A senior US official adds that the US can build new bases as needed.

Copenhagen and Nuuk insist sovereignty is intact. But sovereignty is about who makes the decisions. When another country can veto who invests in your land and build bases without asking first, you no longer decide alone. The keys are hanging somewhere else now.

So why doesn't she say it out loud? Because she can't. The entire Danish political class spent months whipping up a mood. Trump was cast as the enemy, the US as the threat, and the fear was milked for everything it was worth in the run-up to the election. The media played along, and large parts of the population followed like puppets without asking a single question. Emotion beat reason again.

Here's what the people ruled by their feelings missed. The White House never intended to invade an ally. The tariff threats, the talk of force, the offers to buy Greenland were leverage. Trump wrote the book on this decades ago, and anyone who looks for patterns instead of headlines could see where it was heading. You open with maximum pressure, you let the other side panic, and you close on the terms you wanted from the start. Look at what Washington walked away with: permanent basing rights, the freedom to build more, and a veto over who invests in the island. That was the goal all along.

And there's a reason for the hard hand. This administration is working to pull the West out of woke hell and away from the ideologues who spent decades hollowing out its foundations. You don't win that fight with kid gloves. You play the game it takes to win.

Now the same prime minister has to explain that she signed off on what she called unacceptable. So she talks about sovereignty and hopes nobody reads the fine print.

And to everyone outside Denmark: don't be fooled by the sudden love for Greenland. 

Denmark hasn't given a flying f*ck about Greenlanders for generations. They were only mentioned when the topic was drinking and social problems. In the '60s and '70s, thousands of Greenlandic girls and women had IUDs inserted without consent. Children were taken from their families to be turned into little Danes. The concern that suddenly blossomed this year was about ownership. Greenlanders themselves were an afterthought.

Greenland is still Denmark's on paper. That's the only place Denmark ever cared about it.

(Unsurprising from a movement that is part of the axis that has turned al-Aqsa into a replacement for the Qa'aba, which the Quran itself describes as the behavior of ٱلظَّـٰلِمِينَ, the wrongdoers)
One has to ask why it is that Hamas is so terrified of archaeological excavations. Why, if they are so sure of their position, would they fear the revealing of history? It is, of course, because they know what the evidence shows and what the Quran attests to. Jerusalem is the qiblah of the Jewish people. The Temple Mount, the part that holds significance for the Jewish people, isn't at al-Aqsa Mosque but in the more northern part, by the Dome of the Rock, a primarily political monument that even today isn't used consistently most of the year as a place of worship. That, at the end of the day, there is an easy and historically and religiously honest solution in which Jews and Muslims could both achieve a just agreement that can't even be described as a compromise because both sides would get the maximum of what they're actually demanding.
It is perhaps Yom Kippur that scares them so much because it is a holiday so intensely tied to the Temple Mount. A central part of the Yom Kippur service is the Avoda, the one time of year the Kohen Gadol would enter the Holy of Holies on the Temple Mount. Around the world, millions of Jews, even ones who wear keffiyehs in certain demonstrations, will recount how their ancestors gathered on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem in Israel in their masses and united around this singular event, and recite over and over again:
