text:
Inside the Outrageous Collapse of a ‘Montessori Ponzi’

A man with a vision set out to revolutionize preschool. It became a $440 million fiasco.

Ten years ago, a Montessori enthusiast named Ray Girn had a vision. He wanted to bring high-quality, child-led education to as many babies and toddlers as possible, with a chain of for-profit schools that would grow at the pace of a tech start-up. He spoke about doing for preschools “what ride-sharing apps or Airbnb have achieved,” and he raised $335 million from investors, including venture capital and private equity firms, to make it happen.

For a while, Mr. Girn’s schools, which operated under the brand Guidepost Montessori, appeared to be successful, with 150 locations that served tens of thousands of children. But they also ran up an astonishing $440 million in losses. The parent company, Higher Ground Education, filed for bankruptcy in June 2025 and shuttered about 60 schools.

In Oregon, parents received an email notification on a Sunday afternoon that their school effectively no longer existed. In Wisconsin, a father went to drop off his 5-month-old son at a Guidepost only to find it had closed. 

In California, a mother learned that her children’s Guidepost had been sold and that its Montessori curriculum would be replaced with artificial intelligence. Guidepost teachers and parents lit up Facebook and Reddit groups with horror stories — allegations of neglect and mistreatment that made a lot more sense now that everyone knew how mismanaged the company had been.

For-profit education ventures are notorious for disappointing investors and leaving parents fuming. But even in this context, the Guidepost story is striking. “Schools close sometimes, but usually not this many, and not all at once,” said Rebecca Winthrop, who directs the Center for Universal Education at the Brookings Institution.

What could have caused such a collapse? More than two dozen former teachers, administrators and corporate employees told me that they were deeply concerned by the company’s business model. Seven independently described it as a pyramid scheme. “We were calling it the Montessori Ponzi scheme internally,” said Alex Richardson, a teacher at Guidepost’s first school, in Orange County, Calif.

When Higher Ground opened new Guidepost schools, it often received large advances from landlords to improve their properties. As long as the company kept expanding, it seemed from the outside as if it were thriving. But when it came time to repay the landlords, and growth was no longer an option, the company collapsed. By the end, some Guidepost locations were losing $50,000 a month.

Mr. Girn is still active in the education industry. Last year, he and his wife, Rebecca Girn — the other founder of Higher Ground and its general counsel — welcomed me at a converted ranch-style house outside Austin, Texas, where they’ve already opened another school, called Fulcrum. Their three children are among the students.

Ray Girn adamantly disputed the Ponzi comparisons and said he is proud of what he built. “You can’t care about the people that are critics,” Mr. Girn said. “We’re not apologizing for this.”

When we met, Mr. Girn, 47, had a warm presence, a slightly nasal voice and a compelling smile. Ms. Girn, 42, was smaller, quieter and clearly used to being interrupted by her husband. They adamantly disputed the Ponzi comparisons and told me they were proud of what they’d built. “You can’t care about the people that are critics,” Mr. Girn said. “We’re not apologizing for this.”

We spoke for several hours, a conversation in which Mr. Girn referenced Julius Caesar, Plato, the founding fathers, environmentalism, Bismarckian Germany and Taylor Swift. As we talked, it became clear that the rise and fall of Guidepost was an only-in-America story of a charismatic founder who’s more confident than capable, and of the deep-pocketed investors who enabled him. But instead of an app that failed or a tech platform that went sideways, to the detriment of some customers, this time the casualties were children.Guidepost was not the first school chain that Mr. Girn had run at an unsustainable pace. 

Back in 2003, when Mr. Girn, a Canadian native, was a psychology and philosophy student at the University of Toronto, a friend suggested he come work at a school in Orange County called LePort Montessori. It was founded by a wealthy bariatric surgeon, Peter LePort, who sat on the board of the Ayn Rand Institute. Mr. Girn had no formal training in education, but he ran a Rand-focused club on campus. That was enough for Mr. LePort, who hired him to help start a new elementary school.

Mr. Girn became devoted to the Montessori method, which encourages children to direct their own lessons, with teachers as guides. “It’s as close to perfect as human education has ever gotten,” he once said at an Ayn Rand Institute conference. Traditional schools stifled children’s innate love of learning, he thought, and day care programs could be especially oppressive. “They’re literally putting the child behind bars, moving them from rocker to high chair to container,” he said. Montessori could free them.

In 2009, Mr. Girn became the chief executive of LePort. He envisioned turning the company into a national chain (“We had the opportunity to become the child care provider for SpaceX,” he said). But he was more focused on growth than Mr. LePort was comfortable with. In 2016, Mr. Girn was fired.

He resolved to try again, this time with a chain of schools that he could control. He and Ms. Girn formed Higher Ground and hired several of LePort’s corporate staff members. Some LePort parents soon followed, including Greg Mauro, a founding partner of Learn Capital, a venture firm known for backing education start-ups. Learn Capital invested about $1 million, and Mr. Girn opened his first two Guidepost schools. Within three years, the company had 27.

Guidepost employees describe these early schools as thoughtfully planned. White-walled classrooms were outfitted with charming, toddler-sized furniture made of pale, unfinished wood. 

“Everyone cared so deeply,” said Kiana Kometani, who in 2019 became the first head of school at a Guidepost in Folsom, Calif. Teachers spoke about fostering each child’s intellectual curiosity, of giving them agency before they could tie their shoes.

Mr. Girn was a skillful pitchman. He promised parents something rare: the rigorous education of a high-end preschool, but with the hours of a commercial day care. Most Guideposts were in wealthy places — Walnut Creek, Brooklyn Heights — and appealed to the kind of dual-income families who could afford the equivalent of a small sedan in preschool tuition.

“Guidepost catered to the elevated intellectual type,” said Emily Tkaczibson, who paid about $4,000 a month for her two children to attend a Guidepost in Tigard, Ore. “We would have recommended the school to anybody.” 

Matthew Espie, another parent in Tigard, considered himself “lucky” that his youngest child got off the waiting list after only 10 months.“On my first day they said, ‘Hi Alex, welcome to Guidepost, please go into the classroom,’” said Alex Richardson, one of the company’s former teachers. “They put me in during nap time for kids aged 2½ through 5. I had no clue what to do.”

There were signs, though, that the company was trying to do too much too soon. Mr. Girn expanded abroad, opening schools in Hong Kong and mainland China in 2019. Mr. Richardson, the Orange County teacher, said around that time, three Chinese toddlers came to his school for reasons that were never explained. None of them spoke English, and the Guidepost teachers didn’t speak Mandarin.

“One toddler would stand there and cry and say the same word over and over again,” Mr. Richardson said. “We learned later that she was yelling for her mom, but at the time we didn’t know. We couldn’t understand her enough to help her.”Running a preschool is expensive. Buildings need to be rented and renovated; classroom materials purchased; teachers and administrators hired. 

Until a Guidepost location enrolled enough tuition-paying students, the parent company, Higher Ground, had to prop it up financially.Labor was typically the highest expense. Laws vary by state, but businesses that deal with babies and toddlers are usually required to maintain certain ratios: one caregiver for every three to five children under age 2, and every eight to 10 preschoolers. And teachers with specialized Montessori training can command salaries that are tens of thousands of dollars higher than their peers’, and nearly double that of a day care worker.

There are two generally recognized Montessori training organizations, as well as other groups that help to uphold standards. But the label is not trademarked, and ultimately, any school that wants to call itself a Montessori can do so. Higher Ground created its own program, the Prepared Montessorian Institute. It allowed the company to hire conventional teachers and train them on the job, with primarily online lessons that could be taken, for free, during downtime.

The training program was accredited, but early Guidepost employees said that teachers struggled to get away from the classroom long enough to complete the lessons. “A bunch of us were enrolled in P.M.I.,” said Rhiannon Lentz, a former Guidepost teacher in Kansas, “but I don’t know anyone who finished it.”

In a 2024 podcast interview, Mr. Girn described this approach to hiring as a way to find “soul mates” — people who were good with children but lacked formal credentials. “I can walk into Chick-fil-A with my kids and really like the person and ask the cashier, ‘Do you like kids? You should consider becoming a Montessori teacher,’” Mr. Girn said.

The upshot was that some parents were choosing Guidepost for its Montessori marketing, unaware that their children were being taught by novices. Mr. Richardson, from Orange County, says he was hired as an assistant teacher in 2019 for $19.50 an hour with no experience caring for small children. 

“On my first day they said, ‘Hi Alex, welcome to Guidepost, please go into the classroom.’ They put me in during nap time for kids aged 2½ through 5. I had no clue what to do.”Even with these labor savings, it still took time for new schools to turn a profit. To help them out, when Higher Ground signed leases, it often asked landlords to front the company hundreds of thousands of dollars or more. Ms. Girn told me that this funded “not just the construction, but also the financial ramp-up, because the school loses money for two years.” Mr. Girn added: “We are literally not putting in a penny. We are just going to be paying higher rent in year three.”

But that plan works only if a school is smoothly progressing toward full enrollment. When the pandemic arrived in 2020, it nearly toppled the U.S. child care industry, and Guidepost was no exception. By the end of that year, many schools were only partly filled, and the company was $55 million in the red.The Girns are still active in the education industry, with a new school outside Austin, Texas, shown here.

Mr. Girn faced a choice. He could shrink his company, closing weak locations to focus on the best-performing schools, until the virus abated. Or he could open more schools and use the money fronted by landlords to keep operating. He opted to expand. “They were opening a school, then rushing to open more schools, get new capital,” said Diana Le Sieur, who worked for Higher Ground for five years in various capacities.

Ms. Kometani, who ran the Folsom Guidepost, said that Mr. Girn once explained the strategy in a regional staff meeting. “I remember him talking about how much money they got when they opened a new school,” she said. “It was in the millions.”

Employees started making Ponzi jokes. When I told Mr. Girn in Texas that several of his former employees claimed he’d effectively been running a pyramid scheme, he dismissed it as hyperbole. “The only ones that could be justified saying that would be some of the landlords,” he said. He acknowledged, though, that the approach was financially irresponsible. “We accelerated some openings to get some cash sooner,” Mr. Girn said. “This is part of the mistake.”I pressed him on a critical point: When landlords fronted the company money for a new location, were the funds ever used for other costs? “The new money was for the new school, but a portion of that was for overhead, and we didn’t have — we could cover more of our general overhead with that money,” Mr. Girn said. 

But he also said, “We did not take landlord money and give it to an existing school in the way that’s being described.”Kevin McDonald, a landlord in Missouri, said he doubted that the money he’d advanced for a new Guidepost was used entirely at that location. “In my opinion, they’re not ethical people,” he told me. “They borrowed from us to help them open up other schools. In our case in Ellisville, they asked for $1 million in tenant improvements. Not even a third of that went to that school.” 

He clarified that this was an estimate. “You can just figure it out,” he said. “They didn’t use the money. When I went to the school a couple of times, I saw it.”Mr. Girn wrote in a text message this month that he’d created “an incredible business model that is unfortunately very misunderstood,” adding: “Yes, the ‘float’ did impact the timing of our capital cycle, and there are legitimate criticisms one can make of our strategy, but it’s just plain false that we did anything negligent or nefarious.”According to bankruptcy filings, the company opened 33 schools in 2020 and another 21 the next year, while cumulative losses grew to $154.6 million.

Mr. Girn remained convinced that the pandemic presented an opportunity. So many preschools and day cares closed during Covid that there were now vastly more families in need of child care than there were places to serve them. Guidepost could fill the void.With that pitch, the company raised about $100 million from investors, much of it from either Learn Capital or Venn Growth Partners, a private equity firm that took a 7 percent stake and a board seat. In early 2022, Blackstone valued Higher Ground at $1 billion. 

By 2023 the company had opened another 50 Guidepost schools, getting another influx of cash from landlords.But Mr. Girn had not accounted for the post-pandemic labor market. Workers were demanding higher pay to keep up with inflation; at the same time, his investors complained that schools were spending too much on pay. By the end of 2023, losses had ballooned to $364.8 million. Higher Ground conducted two rounds of corporate layoffs. 

Some Guidepost schools offered tuition discounts if parents paid in advance. At one location, families who paid as much as $75,000 could win a trip to Paris. According to the Girns, they lent the company more than $5 million, while Ms. Girn deferred another $1 million in salary.

Mr. Girn maintains that his schools always had adequate resources. But Guidepost employees in multiple states told me their schools were regularly “out of ratio,” with too few teachers in the classroom.

Rylie Colvin, who ran a Guidepost in Washington State, said she was routinely told to combine toddlers from two classes into one room and send a staff member home for the day to keep payroll costs down. “We’re talking 1½-year-olds here. It’s illegal to have big ratios with kids that young,” Ms. Colvin said. “Never mind the fact that we’re telling families that we’re providing individualized Montessori lesson plans — and then just throwing them into whatever room.”

In Colorado, a regional manager had so many people quit at one of the schools she oversaw, in the Boulder suburb of Longmont, that for months she and an assistant had to run it themselves. She said that one day, only three Guidepost employees showed up to watch more than 100 children.

Ariel Baker, a Guidepost teacher in Scottsdale, Ariz., said her school became so understaffed that teachers stopped taking lunch breaks or regularly changing diapers. In one of the infant classrooms, an assistant teacher was fired for treating babies roughly. Ms. Baker said she asked if the incidents had been reported to the state. “I was told, ‘There’s nothing to report,’” she said.

Lucy Brooks, an assistant head of school at a Wisconsin Guidepost, said that an administrator accidentally stepped on a baby and lied to the parents about the cause of the bruise. In California, Mr. Richardson said, a toddler escaped and wandered around a nearby Walmart parking lot until someone finally noticed.

“There are cases where we made serious mistakes,” Mr. Girn said via text. “When I learned about an issue, I experienced it fully and as personally as if it was my own children, and made sure we faced it and fixed it.” He argued that with 150 schools, it was inaccurate “to assemble a few serious isolated incidents into a narrative that implies systemic negligence.”

But across the country, parents were becoming dissatisfied. According to company documents, in 2023, about 15 percent of Guidepost families were pulling out their children after just 90 days.The Girns could see that conditions were deteriorating. “People would sign up and then we’d lose them,” Ms. Girn said. She visited struggling schools and was appalled by what she found. “I’m going to school after school that I think is garbage and I’m like, this has to be completely rebuilt from scratch.”Guidepost offered parents something rare: the rigorous education of a high-end preschool, but with the hours of a commercial day care.

By 2024, the generous terms that Higher Ground had negotiated with landlords were rapidly coming to an end. “There was a timing issue,” Mr. Girn said. “We opened too many and it hit at once.”

In August 2024, Higher Ground stopped paying rent on all its schools. Two landlords, in Virginia and Texas, changed the locks on their buildings, causing schools to close with no notice. Other site owners sued. Over the next few months, many of Higher Ground’s executives quit. In February 2025, the Girns resigned. 

The company filed for bankruptcy that June, owing an additional $611 million in unpaid rent.Eventually, more than 80 Guidepost schools were sold to a new entity, Guidepost Global Education, which is based in Austin and employs many people who had been on staff at Higher Ground. The company’s investors include both Learn Capital and Steve Xu, a former investment banker who was involved in the earlier effort to open Guidepost schools in Hong Kong and the mainland.

About 60 other Guidepost locations closed. Mr. Girn told me that the process was orderly, with most families given at least a month’s notice. But according to several parents, that didn’t always happen. When a Guidepost near Milwaukee announced that it would close in five weeks, so many teachers quit that the school lasted just three more days. “I’m in the parking lot, calling my boss like, ‘I can’t come in because Tommy’s day care closed,” said Jake Boyd, whose 5-month-old had just started there a few weeks earlier. For months, he and his wife looked for another day care, but everywhere was full. 

Their mothers flew in and took turns babysitting so the Boyds could go to work.Guidepost Global partnered with a start-up called 2 Hour Learning. That company is the parent of Alpha School, a new for-profit chain where children are mainly taught by A.I. Under the agreement, Alpha and Guidepost Global would operate as separate entities in the same building, with Guidepost Global focusing on babies and preschoolers, and Alpha running elementary schools. But some schools that the Girns started already had an elementary program, and in those instances Alpha simply took over.

Parents were notified of this Montessori-to-A.I. switch just weeks before the start of a new school year. In California, Cecille Matsuo received an email inviting her to transfer her two children to Alpha for $50,000 per child. “I’m not paying $50,000 a year for a computer to teach my kid,” she said. She declined the offer.

In North Carolina, Cayla Guins also pulled her children after being told they’d be taught with A.I. She added up the tuition she’d paid Guidepost over the years — almost $200,000. She’d paid the money so her daughters could get a good education, but now she felt she’d been duped. Ms. Guins published an open letter to Mr. Girn on Substack, accusing him of “corporate hubris, broken promises, and the human cost of treating child care as a venture-backed commodity.”

Mr. Girn knows about the social media activity. He told me he’d read some of the posts. “A lot of people out there hate my guts and think I’m the devil incarnate,” he said. But he insisted his critics were wrong. Yes, his company had collapsed. Yes, children had lost their schools and their teachers. But, he argued, one of the reasons Guidepost had grown so big so quickly — and investors had been willing to give him so much money — was that it offered a service that was desperately needed.

Parents can’t work without child care, the economy can’t function without working parents and children deserve a quality education, he believed. And yet nationally this basic need remains unaddressed by both the government and the private sector. Guidepost had been Mr. Girn’s attempt to fix it. 

Thanks to him, tens of thousands of people had been exposed to what he believed was the best early childhood pedagogy. “I think that’s a victory,” he told me. “This is what it looks like to try to do something really hard.”Besides, he said, a majority of schools he’d opened still existed, just under new management. 

One, in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, was such a standout that last year Guidepost Global offered me a tour. The school did seem nice. A few months later, though, a teacher was recorded on video yelling at and pushing toddlers while on a neighborhood walk. And in June 2026, a different teacher accidentally left a 3-year-old at a playground. New York City’s Department of Health temporarily shut down part of the school.

Guidepost locations that initially survived the bankruptcy have continued to close. At the end of this month, three schools in Southern California, including the one that the Girns’ children once attended, will shut their doors. “This is right at the start of the school year, and now all these families are going to be scrambling for spots at other schools,” said Andrew Quillin, whose 2-year-old daughter was supposed to start at a Guidepost in Laguna Hills. “It’s insane.”

Mr. Girn and I talked about the demise of his old schools while sitting in the classroom of his new one. 

A few months after leaving Higher Ground, the Girns bought a property in Texas Hill Country and turned it into a five-room schoolhouse of sorts. Maps lined the walls, a bedroom had been converted into a library and the living room was now a classroom. Tuition is $23,000. The Girns are developing the curriculum themselves.The place seemed warm and inviting. And with four acres of surrounding land, there was plenty of room to expand — although Ms. Girn was adamant that she didn’t want to. 

When I asked Mr. Girn what he thought, he smiled.“We’ll be back,” he said. “We have a world to save.”

text:
Week 3 of college football was another eventful one spent at @TheRealCoach_JB TD Bar and Cigar Loung (tacos on the menu -- I had at least a dozen throughout the day) for Footballpalooza. Morning, noon and night it was all football. Some thoughts on what I saw..

- Ole Miss dominated early, LSU rallied in the third quarter, and then the Rebels won it late with a TD plus a two-point conversion. You can not underestimate just how big a win this was for Pete Golding. LSU and Lane Kiffin wanted the victory, the Rebels and their fan base needed it. 

Trinidad Chambliss right now is my early Heisman favorite. Sam Leavitt was both cold-and-hot this night. But that's who he is as a quarterback. His style of plays leads to volatile results.  Throughout this game it was Ole Miss that had superior QB play.

The status and health of Trey'Dez Green is a concern for the Tigers, who now look ahead to an SEC gauntlet.

Overall, this is a game and event that lived up to the hype. It was the best that college football and the SEC had to offer. It was incredible theater. Dare I say that this was the biggest win in program (Miss) history?

- NCState with a heart-breaking loss and Im not sure that Dave Doeren or CJ Bailey can overcome it. This enters the pantheon of Joe Pisarcik and Mario Cristobal and Miami not taking the victory formation knee vs GaTech a few years ago.

On that last play from scrimmage, Im not sure what Bailey was thinking. On those type of plays quarterbacks or punters are generally told to run to the far corner pylon and then get out of bounds as defenders get close. Bailey turned into defenders for some reason and then fumbled, which was recovered by Vandy for the game winning points.

It's one thing to blow a lead, it's another to lose a game like this.

- Look out for Louisville and Lincoln Keinholz, who outlasted SMU, 41-31 in an ACC shootout. But the Cards Brown Bros (Isaac and Keyjuan) run game was the story, they accounted for 230 combined rushing yards on just 20 carries. SMU moved the ball well, too, but they simply did not play a clean enough game. Brian Brohm has as good an offense as he's ever had.

SMU will still be a threat in the ACC title race. Kevin Jennings is a highly productive and exciting QB, but there's always a play or two that keep him from being truly elite. Ball security is still an issue with him.

- I am officially concerned about the USC Trojans defense. And once again, a Lincoln Riley coached tem struggles on the road in an east coast Big Ten game (still strange to type this out). Rutgers is a bad team, but on this afternoon in Jersey, Dylan Lonergan played fairly well, but his pick-six to Prophet Brown in the 3rd quarter as RU was about to take the lead was really the difference in the game.

But again, I kept thinking that the points USC had given up early this season was the result of playing young guys late in blowouts. This wasn't the case today. Rutgers actually had more first downs (27 to 24) and Rutgers had 460 total yards to 461 for USC. Next week, Oregon comes into the Coliseum after they survived 42-35 in New Brunswick.

-  Huge early win for Will Stein and Kentucky, who went into Kyle Field and out-played Texas A@M. Kenny Minchey played a solid, steady game behind center in leading the Wildcats to a convincing 31-21 win. 

Meanwhile, I think Marcell Reed is facing some heat from the Aggie fan base, even after leading them to a playoff birth last year. From what I saw, the heavy losses on both sides of the line of scrimmage have been a problem for Mike Elko. Regardless, he hasn't been accurate or protected the ball well enough.

- Weather delays were an issue in the Bama-FSU game, first it caused a 90 minute delay, and then another one right before half. Hard to say who it impacted more, but the Noles jumped out to a 21-6 lead, and they came out firing. Mike Norvell had his guys ready to play. It will be interesting to see if the Noles can play with this type of intensity again this season.

But it was the overall speed and talent of the Tide that took over. I'll say it right now, Keelon Russell is as athletically talented as any Alabama quarterback this century. He's a long, springy athlete with a live arm. This is a young superstar-to-be. I'm sure there will be some growing pains during SEC league play, but there's a reason why Kalen DeBoer hitched his wagon to this young man.

As for FSU, as well as they did offensively, once again the Tony White defense got gashed. They've given up over 1,200 total yards in two games vs SMU and Bama. Where have you gone Mickey Andrews?

- It was the story of two quarterbacks in Miss St-South Carolina. The Gamecocks jumped the Bulldogs early, building an early 16-0 lead, but over time it was MSU that just took over. Kemario Taylor kept getting better throughout this game (18 for 26, 251 yards and 4 TD's). The Bulldogs just kept gaining confidence as this game went on, while Lenorris Sellers shows that he's still a better athlete than quarterback. He still really struggles with intermediate throws. His two picks were key in the MSU turn around.

I get Steve McNair vibes with Taylor.

- Overall, I think as of now, UGA is the best team in college football. They cruised to a 45-17 win over a depressed Arkansas program. Steve Atwater and Barry Foster ain't walking through that door.

- Two first year coaches making an early impact at their gigs -- Jon Sumrall of Florida and UCLA's 'Bruin' Bob Chesney. Both of their teams remained undefeated as they won conference games in high-scoring affairs. I like the futures of both programs under their direction.

BTW, I get the sense that Buster Faulkner (Florida's offensive coordinator) will be the next hot commodity when the next cycle of head coaching hires begins.

- Finally, one of the best games this weekend took place on Friday night between Texas Tech and Houston in Lubbock. The Red Raiders squeaked by 28-26 as Conor Weigman came up just inches short on a late 2-point  conversion. But Houston was right with Tech, in fact they had more first downs (27-22) and yards (458 to 424).

The gap between TT and the rest of the Big12 isn't nearly as big as it was last season. As for the Coogs, they will continue to be a factor in this league moving forward.

I leave you with two pups who may not be with us for much longer…dumped in the ACC of NYC…the City that never sleeps…the Capital of Strays & Emaciated pups….

The sad boy behind his kennel bars is Balloon who was left in the care of his human’s parents, grand pup parents if you will, when his human moved out of the country…moved with no care about the wreckage they left behind…a big beautiful grieving pup who sits in a kill pound drooling behind the bars of his kennel…he’s completely shut down and they’ve issued his kill command….If no one comes for Balloon, if no foster or adopter through the rescue steps up, I’ll be writing his obituary tomorrow, Monday…whenever they decide to steal his shine ✨ 

And then there’s the beautifully bereft Raina…a Gorgeous white & sable Pibble girl who spent all four years of her life crated in a basement on bare concrete flooring devoid of bedding…she was never cuddled or touched or seen and she was almost never walked. A neighbor would spend time with her two times a week and when Raina’s human was evicted & abandoned her, this neighbor took her in to her small living space…Raina & the neighbor’s pup got into a scuffle  and hence her detainment at NYCACC….

Both pups are stunningly gorgeous. They deserve a shot at a real life with loyal humans. Balloon & Raina should be placed in a home where they are the focus of their new human. They need to be made to feel how special they are considering their trauma….

We’re looking for two good humans who do not have a pup or cat in their home…someone who wants to adopt or foster. If you know of anyone, please comment on my post.

This pound killed six healthy, beautiful, young pups on Friday night. It was an unholy slaughter of innocents….We can’t let them take Balloon and Raina…we simply can’t….

📚 Educational Saturday | Why the Clarity Act failed over ethics — not market structure

The payments and crypto industry spent 18 months negotiating a 635-page bill on how to regulate digital asset markets. It died on a question about President Trump's crypto income. Here's the plain-English explanation of what actually happened.

THE MARKET STRUCTURE PART (where both parties mostly agreed):
→ SEC oversees crypto securities. CFTC oversees digital commodities. Line drawn cleanly.
→ DeFi developers get a safe harbor (Section 604) from BSA obligations — disputed by law enforcement but included
→ Stablecoin yield/rewards framework — disputed by ABA, not fully resolved
→ 126+ Democratic amendments incorporated into the final Republican draft

THE ETHICS PART (where it fell apart):
→ Democrats demanded enforceable restrictions on government officials profiting from crypto while in office
→ Context: Trump and his family disclosed $1.4 billion in crypto income for 2025 — including the $TRUMP meme coin, World Liberty Financial, and Truth Social crypto products
→ Republicans' final offer (Sep 14): 2029 sunset on restrictions, DOJ enforcement
→ Democrats' position: that's a sunset that lets the current administration profit through 2028. Not acceptable.
→ Zero Democrats voted yes. Four Republicans also voted no — on the market structure merits, not ethics.

The result: 49–50. Eleven votes short of cloture. The strongest pro-crypto vote environment Congress has seen — and it wasn't enough.

What the SEC does next: Regulation Crypto Assets — its own offering framework — accepts public comments until October 20, 2026. If you want to shape U.S. digital asset rules, the comment period is now your legislative process.

text:
Judaism and the Sins of Israel: On the Essential Nature of Religion
Israel, an "artificial state" established by Zionists, has brought immense catastrophe to Palestine and the Middle East, exerting a profound and unsettling impact on the global order while severely jeopardizing humanity's faith in justice. To enable a clearer discernment of the true nature of Judaism and the state of Israel, distinguish right from wrong, and offer humanity a glimmer of hope to rectify deviations and restore justice, this article systematically delineates their multiple transgressions.
1. Blaspheming God and Serving the Devil
Does God exist? It is a question to which no definitive empirical answer can be given. Yet, for any religion, the existence of God is an absolute certainty—a Supreme Being who created the universe and will ultimately deliver it. Since God created the world, the Divine must be inherently grand, righteous, and impeccable. God cannot behave like an earthly despot who blurs the line between right and wrong, harbors blind favoritism, or instigates conflict that leaves the earth devastated and drenched in blood. Any entity that perpetuates such horrors must be the devil, not God. God would deem it beneath Divine dignity to broker arbitrary covenants, grant exclusive real estate titles to specific mortals, demonstrate absolute partiality toward a selective few, or engage in physical wrestling matches with humans—much like a human would never engage in such absurdities with an ant, and would find it reviling to hear an ant boast of such a relationship. Therefore, what Judaism worships is the devil, not God; consequently, Judaism itself is the true object of divine retribution.
2. A Total Syndicate Snuffing Out the Beacon of Humanity
The ultimate purpose of religion is self-interest, utilizing individual benefit as a mechanism to attract adherents. This self-interest can be bifurcated into two categories: temporal self-interest in the material world, and transcendental self-interest in the afterlife. While the vast majority of religions pursue the latter, the modalities of religious dissemination can be categorized into three paradigms: self-interest, altruism, and self-abnegation.
· Righteous Religions: Expand their doctrines through structural altruism to attain both temporal and transcendental self-interest (modern Protestantism, to a qualified extent, approaches this paradigm).
· Neutral Religions: Enjoin strict self-abnegation to achieve transcendental self-interest (authentic Chinese Mahayana Buddhism emphasizes high self-abnegation and moderate altruism; Tibetan Buddhism, however, deviates from this).
· Malevolent Religions: Disseminate their faith via raw self-interest to maximize both temporal and transcendental gains (Judaism fits this mold).
· Criminal Syndicates: When a group systematically inflicts harm upon external populations to secure transcendental self-interest, it ceases to be a religion and becomes a criminal enterprise (such as ISIS).
True righteous religion is singular; it must rely on altruism as its proselytizing engine to fulfill its dual self-interest. Judged by this criterion, Islam must also be categorized as a cultish entity.
When a religion becomes pathologically insular yet fiercely unified for collective self-enrichment, it must perpetually extract illicit advantages from the external world to fulfill its internal theological promises and suppress external criticism or interference. This manifests through predatory usury, monopolistic syndicates, the systematic deprivation of opportunities for outsiders, the monopolization of media to strangle freedom of speech, the utilization of ill-gotten wealth to manipulate foreign governments, and the deployment of collective intimidation against dissenters. Judged by any objective metric, this exhibits the classic hallmarks of a mafia.
Consider the contemporary world: we witness the collective intimidation of protesting students at Harvard, where syndicates coerced the university administration to surrender blacklists and threatened a total hiring boycott against student dissidents. Even in my own experience, when attempting to publish a critique of Israel, editors at major media outlets felt compelled to cautiously warn me to "ensure my personal safety." These multi-faceted realities reveal a chilling truth: when confronting Israel, the constitutional right to free speech is immediately compromised by physical and professional security anxieties.
Look at the sheer absurdity of our global reality: within the United States—the very nation that birthed the United Nations and once stood as a beacon of civilization—the government stands in obstinate, isolated solidarity with Israel, defiantly opposing the overwhelming majority of the international community on Palestinian sovereignty. Nearly all mainstream political figures line up in lockstep behind Israel, even when the comment sections beneath their public statements are flooded with denunciation from the populace. Are we to believe that every single American politician is a fundamentally malicious actor? Facing the spilled blood of the Palestinian people and the living hell of their homeland, have these politicians truly been possessed by demons to consciously walk in alignment with evil? No matter how compromised these politicians may be, it is impossible that this reflects the genuine, uncoerced intent of all of them. This unveils a profoundly horrifying reality upon closer reflection: the United States is rapidly transforming into a hollowed-out zombie, its sovereign soul thoroughly extracted by Israel and Zionist interest groups.
3. Bloodlust Masked by Hypocritical Dogma
We must remain hyper-vigilant against a common tactic employed by certain theologians and scholars who attempt to sanitize Judaism by citing altruistic laws within its scriptures—such as the Decalogue, commands to "give alms to the poor," or prohibitions against "oppressing the stranger." However, any insular, predatory interest group must inevitably weave a cloak of righteous justice to survive within secular society and deflect external scrutiny. As the ancient proverb goes, "there is honor even among thieves"—the most ruthless cartels in history eagerly built bridges and paved roads for their local neighborhoods, and the most extreme cults frequently used charitable handouts to buy public compliance.
These manicured facades are by no means the essence of the system; they are merely moral ornaments designed to deceive the world. In practice, "giving alms to the poor" stands in irreconcilable, parasitic contradiction with "predatory usury and capital monopoly." Through usurious practices and financial blood-sucking, they drive millions of Gentile families into destitution and ruin; then, they turn inward to distribute welfare within their enclosed circle, placating their own kin and delivering on the material benefits promised upon initiation. This closed-loop mechanism of "extreme external predation coupled with internal distribution of spoils" precisely validates its absolute identity as a mafia syndicate. To evaluate an entity, one must look past its ornamental garments and examine whose fundamental right to survival it has stripped away. Any appeasement of this profound hypocrisy constitutes an outright betrayal of human justice.
4. Actions Divorced from Modern Civilization
The foundational premise of modern civilization dictating that the Earth is the shared home of all living things; even apex species possess no arbitrary right to violently displace or dispossess other creatures of their habitats. If humanity lacks the ethical authority to evict monkeys from a mountain to claim it for ourselves, who under heaven possesses the right to strip the Palestinian people of their sovereign right to exist and reside in Palestine?
Following the conclusion of World War II in 1945, Jewish populations no longer faced an existential threat to their survival; what, then, justified their subsequent threat to the very survival of the Palestinians? text:
When I Returned Home After Nearly Eight Years

"እኛን ያስቸገረን በሁለት መንግስት እየተመራን መሆኑ ነው" ~  የወሎ ገበሬ።

Cry. Laugh. Mourn. Reflect. Those are probably the four words that best describe the past few weeks of my life.

After nearly eight years away, I returned to Ethiopia thinking I was simply going home for a while. Instead, the trip became something much deeper. It became a reset.

I started feeling that I was back in Ethiopia before the plane even landed. I was on an Ethiopian Airlines flight, surrounded by the familiar friendliness of the crew, Ethiopian music playing in the cabin, and an image of the mountains of Lalibela on the screen in front of me. I was still somewhere in the sky, but emotionally, I was already home.

Then I arrived in Addis Ababa.

The first thing I noticed was how much the city had changed. There were cleaner streets, new buildings, parks, recreation areas, business centers and, perhaps most noticeably, digital solutions everywhere. Money could be transferred digitally in ways that would have seemed unusual nearly eight years ago. Back then, cash was a necessity for almost everything.

I remembered the Addis I had left behind: streets filled with blue-and-white taxis, very few ride-hailing options, traffic that often felt chaotic, and old cars producing thick black exhaust. The Addis I returned to was visibly more modern.

I genuinely appreciated many of these changes. The corridor development, in particular, has transformed parts of the city. Some areas are cleaner, more organized and more pleasant to walk through. New public spaces and commercial areas have changed the appearance of the city considerably.

But the more time I spent there, the more I started noticing something beyond the new buildings and cleaner streets.

The people who used to be so visible on the streets seemed to have disappeared.

Of course, they had not actually disappeared. Many of the people I remembered from Addis lived in small, relatively inexpensive kebele houses. They ran tiny businesses or provided services that ordinary people depended on, often at prices accessible to those with limited incomes.

As parts of the city were redeveloped, many of those homes and businesses were demolished. The new buildings and commercial spaces that replaced them are often much more expensive.

So the people moved.

They moved further away from the parts of the city that were being transformed and celebrated.

That made me think about something important: a city can become cleaner and more modern without the lives of its poorest residents necessarily becoming better. Sometimes poverty has simply become less visible.

And then there was the cost of living.

I remember sitting in a café and paying several hundred birr for a cup of coffee. A simple lunch, something like a beyaynetu, cost several times what I remembered paying before I left. It wasn't just food. The same feeling appeared across many services and everyday expenses.

There were exceptions, of course. Internet access and digital services seemed much more widespread and, in some cases, relatively affordable compared with what I remembered.

But I kept asking myself the same question: how do ordinary people, especially people living on modest salaries, afford to live in Addis Ababa now?

After spending time in the city, I left for the north.

Lalibela was where the contrast became much more painful.

Lalibela is a place that has depended heavily on tourism for generations. But the COVID pandemic was followed by conflict in the north, and the consequences are still visible.

Hotels that once welcomed visitors are partially open or completely closed. Some of the larger hotels I saw were standing empty, with grass growing on their roofs and signs of nature slowly taking over buildings that had once been built with enormous investments.

Some investors appear to be keeping their hotels operating, even with very few customers, partly to keep workers employed. The tourist guides, meanwhile, have almost nothing to guide.

It was heartbreaking to see a place with such enormous cultural and historical significance struggling so badly.

And then I noticed something even more painful: the young people.

Many are leaving Lalibela as fast as they can. Some are looking for work. Some want to leave Ethiopia altogether. Others simply want to escape the uncertainty surrounding their lives.

Among those who remain, I saw young people sitting around the town with very little to do. At home, in the streets, in cafés - waiting. Waiting for something to change.

I also heard stories about young people dying from illnesses and problems associated with addiction, in addition to those who have died because of conflict.

These are not statistics when you are standing there. They are someone's son. Someone's daughter. Someone's brother. Someone's friend.

And after years of conflict, you can feel the exhaustion.

People are tired. Tired of losing people. Tired of uncertainty. Tired of hearing about fighting. Tired of not knowing when it will end.

Outside Lalibela, the situation felt even more real.

The countryside is beautiful, but traveling through some areas was not something I could take lightly. There were checkpoints and armed groups, and depending on the village, different groups appeared to have influence or control.

At one point, I decided that walking was safer than taking the road.

There was always the uncertainty of what might happen at a checkpoint - whether someone might demand money, try to take something from you, or worse.

And what I was seeing and hearing in Lalibela did not feel isolated to Lalibela. As I traveled through other parts of the Amhara region, including Bahir Dar and Gondar, I encountered similar stories and concerns.

And this is where I realized something important.

For people living there, conflict isn't something they watch on television. It is part of their daily lives.

A farmer doesn't necessarily care about political arguments. He wants to farm. He wants to feed his family. He wants his children to go to school. He wants to wake up tomorrow without worrying about what might happen.

But when there is conflict around you, staying outside it is not always an option.

I heard about young men being pressured to join fighting because they owned guns or were considered capable of fighting. Others could be pressured to contribute financially, regardless of whether they could afford it.

People who simply wanted to live their lives could find themselves pulled into something much bigger than themselves.

And yet, despite everything, something else remained remarkably consistent.

The people. The hospitality. The humor.

Everywhere I went, people offered food. On the road, people offered to carry my luggage. People joked with me. People laughed. People welcomed me.

It was almost strange to see so much warmth in places where people had experienced so much suffering.

Some had lost friends or relatives. Some had witnessed violence. Some had heard stories that would have sounded unimaginable to me nearly eight years ago.

And still, they offered food. Still, they laughed. Still, they joked. Still, they welcomed strangers.

That is something I will not forget.

text:
Chapter Thirteen
Both Rooms

Atar did not knock like Einar.
The pressure arrived in the sternum as a heading, not a greeting. No radio in the other room. No request to be friends. A vector: turn two points to starboard and keep the still place on the bow even when the still place looked like weather. Ramon did not inspect it. Chapter Twelve had already collected that fee. He set the vane and put his palm on the sole and let the friend steer the man who had once tried to steer the friend.
Mara took the heading as if she had been waiting for a city the way she waited for a creak.
Apprehension came on the same wind.
This was supposed to be home. He knew the word the way he knew Acre, which was to say as an assignment and a temperature, not as a street he could walk in the dark. He knew Atar. He did not know the rooms Atar came from. Four hundred years of kitchens, and the one that claimed him was a blank in his own file.
He stood the coaming and considered a mask.
First impression: the old vanity. Ramon the grocer, easy in the mouth. Elias the quiet American. The steward who puts glasses down. The man who left Nobody under a dog. Which face for a quay that might be Ithaca. He had ten lives and a habit of arriving as the smallest one that would pass.
Then the correction, clean as a click.
They already knew. Einar had had a file a hundred and fifty years. Brickell had been a flare on a hall-board. Verona had opened a door the size of a floorplan. The night-rumor, the small atlas, the enclosure — those were their courtesies, not his secrets. He was the one standing on an ugly steel cutter with no map of the city that had been feeding his flue since a house in the Adige’s damp agreed to be edited. They had the file. He had a heading and a boat that had fallen off paper twice.
The mask was a courtesy he would be performing for himself.
What is home, if the people in it can pick you out of a basin and you cannot pick the basin out of a sea.
What is trust, if the friend who knocks has steered you for centuries and you have never seen the street where he keeps his noon.
What is hope, if it is only the wish that a place which already knows your murders will still have a table.
What is loyalty, if you have been loyal to a spirit and a job and a hull, and the city now asks to be the noun those loyalties were always declining toward.
He did not answer the questions. He let them stand on the bow with him. Answers would have been another mask.
The heat-sheen thickened until it was not weather.
Atlantis did not rise like a coast. It assembled, as if the air had been keeping rooms for a city and had finally agreed to occupy them. First the harbor: a ring of water so still it held the traveling lamp without wrinkling, bronze going down a long way, piles that were not wood. Then the outer ring of the city itself — not a wall, a terrace, a circumference of quays and low halls facing the sea that was not the parish sea. Behind that, rings inward, each higher than the last, canals running not only around but up, water lifted in silent sheets along the faces of buildings that seemed to remember being stone and had decided to be more than stone. At the center, far in and far up, a noon that did not walk. The lamp of the greater earth went along the roof as usual. Atlantis kept a second light the way a body keeps a heart: inside, regular, not interested in dusk.
Towers stood in a spine along the third ring. One of them went up until counting became a joke. Glass that was not glass. Balconies like gills. A height with a number he would learn soon enough and not forget.
Mara slid into a slip that had been empty in the exact shape of a forty-one-foot steel cutter. No one ran. A woman on the quay took the line as if taking a line were a skill she had been paid to keep sharp. She said, “Ramon,” without testing the word, and then, milder, “Raimond, if you prefer the house,” and did not wait for him to choose. A man in a coat that drank light and gave it back as a thin gold edge asked whether the tanks wanted filling and whether the bilge had been a problem since the cave. He named the cave without naming the dog. Efficiency, here, included knowing. Friendliness included not requiring him to perform surprise.
Atar was a warmth at the edge of the flue, present the way a mentor is present when the student has finally reached the building. He did not take a body on the quay. He did not need to. The city was already his sentence.
“Three days,” the woman said. “The king will see you. Until then you are a citizen who has been away. That is the whole complication.”
She offered lodging the way the green harbor had offered tea, and it was not the same offer. Two keys, two kinds of light.
A villa on the outer ring, floor at water-height, a terrace that took the bronze harbor in one look, rooms that opened until the rooms were weather. A penthouse on the three-hundred-and-thirty-third floor of the spine tower, the city become a map, the still noon close enough to feel in the teeth.
“Both,” Ramon said.
He did not decorate the word. He had ten lives and a boat that was a room that did not flex and a memory of two identical chambers that had traded floors because he could not bear to leave one uninhabited. He wanted the sea and the height. He wanted to experience the instrument, not pick a favorite string on the first evening. Appetite that is not El Dorado looks like this: not gold, not a kettle. Two keys. A man who has been Nobody and a file and a steward and a guest, refusing to arrive as only one of those.
They did not blink. Both was a sentence the city could conjugate. A car that was not a car — a quiet slab, no performance of engine — would run him between the terrace and the three-hundred-and-thirty-third whenever he asked. Mara would stay in the slip that had been waiting in her shape. He put his palm on the mast once, privately, and said the old thing, and she did not have to answer. She had delivered him. That was the friendship for the day.
He walked.
The geography of Atlantis was a lesson you took with the feet. Outer ring: harbor, villas, the long terrace where the bronze water licked stone that had been taught to stay cool in noon. Second ring: workshops and body-wright halls, doorways tall enough for work that was not public, a smell like rain on copper and something sweet that was not tea. Third ring: the civic spine, towers, the canals lifting, bridges that did not boast. Inward of that, rings he did not yet have a right to, the still noon living in a court he could feel through the soles. The whole thing sat inside the inner ring of the greater earth like a heart inside a chest. Beyond the harbor, the sea that had been his first love went out toward kitchens he had passed and refused: gold, halls, green, cave. Atlantis had withdrawn from that pasture on purpose. It had not withdrawn from empire. Empire, here, meant the capacity to remain a noon while the parish was given dusk as a courtesy.
Architecture did not separate wall from water or floor from light. Facades took the traveling lamp and the civic noon both and sorted them the way a flue sorts a meal. Windows were not holes. They were decisions. Stairs existed for the pleasure of stairs; lifts existed for the height; neither apologized. Stone remembered being quarried from a place that was not on the small atlas. Metal remembered being taught. In the body-wright halls the walls were the color of inside-of-wrist. In the spine tower the corridors were cool and exact, numbered without anxiety. On the villa terrace the rooms opened until privacy was a choice you made with a pane, not a lock you inherited.
History lived in the joins.
They told it without a museum voice, which was to say the streets assumed you knew and then, because he did not, a plaque or a guide or a child on a bridge would give him a piece. Atlantis had been a noon civilization when the parish still had more than one story about the sky. It had kept the body-wrights when other kitchens kept axes or gold or withdrawal. When the small atlas was drawn — when the ice was taught to be a wall and the night was taught to be a rumor — Atlantis did not stay to steer the flock. It closed a gate and kept the lamp inside. Pride, if you wanted the unkind word. Hygiene, if you wanted the civic one. Valhalla stayed and watched who could end a life. El Dorado stayed and watched appetite. Atlantis stayed itself. The empire was not a conquest of the 1%. It was the refusal to become a rumor in the 1%. For centuries the city refined the only expansion that interested it: how a body could carry noon, how a room could be edited, how a people could remain friendly and efficient without turning either quality into a kettle.
He was of that people and not of it. The draught had been a door. The streets were the house. He had lived in rented rooms on the other side of the fence and called the fence the world.
Home, walked like this, was not a feeling that arrived and sat. It was a set of facts that did not yet include him: a slip in his boat’s shape, a woman who knew both his names, a king in three days, two keys. Trust was the heading he had not picked apart. Trust was also the unease that a file so complete might be another column, prettier ink. Hope was the still noon remaining still when he looked at it. Hope was also the future he could not sketch — upgrades Atar had mentioned in a twenty-minute sleep, a body that could carry more lamp, a job that might not be only the glasses. Loyalty was the palm on the mast. Loyalty was the friend who had come when two rooms traded floors. Loyalty, now, would have to decide whether a city could be added without betraying the hull, the dead shopkeeper, the boy who had not run.
He did not decide on the first afternoon.
He went up to the three-hundred-and-thirty-third because height is a kind of honesty. The penthouse was one floor of quiet air. The city lay under it in rings you could count. The harbor was a bronze coin. Mara was a dark hyphen in the slip. Beyond the outer terrace the greater sea faded toward weather he knew better than he knew this. He stood at the pane and let the still noon press his teeth and thought: all right. Then he went down and out to the villa and opened every room that would open until the bronze came in across the floor like a guest who had been invited.
Both rooms. He would sleep in one and wake in the other until he understood what the difference was for, or until he understood that the difference was the point.
Evening in Atlantis was a civic decision. The traveling lamp went long along the roof; the city did not go dark. It went precise. Streets took a cooler light. People came out as if the street were a room they had paid for.
He walked and watched.
Manners: no one blocked a bridge. No one performed hurry. Greeting was a small lift of the face, not a hug and not a stare. They knew him and granted him the dignity of not being stopped for it. A child looked at his rust-stained hands with interest and was steered past without being shamed for the interest. Efficiency included leaving a returned citizen a little uncollected.
Fashion: cloth that behaved like a decision. Edges that held a thread of the civic noon. Jackets that drank the traveling lamp and gave it back as a line at the cuff, the throat, the seam along a calf. Hair cut as architecture. Bare arms on people who did not fear the feast. A man in a coat the color of inside-of-wrist; a woman whose dress morphed once, slowly, from harbor-bronze to the gray of Mara’s bruise, as if the city had already told the cloth there was a new ugly boat in the slip. No one wore a mask that he could see. That might have been the most expensive garment they had.
Hyper-futuristic, if you needed the parish word: an empire that had kept every century it wanted and invented the ones it lacked. Ancient in the joins. New in the lifts. A people who had had time to make friendliness into infrastructure.
Ramon walked until his feet had a map that was not Atar’s heading. He did not look for a courtyard. He did not look for a king. He had three days. He had two keys. He had a boat in a slip that had been waiting in her shape, and a future that was no longer only away from the kettle.
Home, tonight, was a word he could walk through without agreeing to it.
He agreed only to the next street.
The city, which already knew him, let him pass as if that were the first gift: not a mask, not a file read aloud. A pavement. People. The chance to look before he was looked at in a throne room.
He put his hands in his pockets because the pockets were his, and he watched a cuff take the light and give it back, and he thought of Nicolò’s coffee-stained wrists in a city that had never heard of a 333rd floor, and he did not make the two cities fight.
Tomorrow he would take the other key and sleep in the other room.
Tonight he let Atlantis happen at street level, efficient and friendly and older than his ten lives, while he learned, one doorway at a time, how little of his home he had ever seen.

text:
RESMED $RMD FELL 37% ON DRUGS THAT HAVE NOT REPLACED IT YET. THE FDA RULES ON ONE FEBRUARY 28:

The Quality-Value Len5 is watching Resmed, ticker RMD, at $224.99, -$3.43 / -1.50% at the September 18 close, 14th of 59 on that Len5. The San Diego company makes the machines and masks that hold the airway open for people whose breathing stops and restarts through the night.

The verdict: the argument is about the machine, and the machine is not where this business grows. Last year Resmed sold $2.89B of devices and $2.09B of masks and accessories - the cushions, straps and tubing that wear out and get bought again. The second number is the smaller one and the faster one, and it is the one the next report has to defend.

The fall first. From $284.87 on October 8, 2025 the shares slid to $180.27 on June 2, -36.7%, and sit 21.0% under that high now. Over the same stretch the fiscal year ended June 30 brought revenue of $5.653B, +10%, and adjusted profit - earnings with one-time items stripped out - of $11.17 a share, +17%. Each of the last seven quarters came in above published expectations. The reported numbers never went the way the price did.

The worry has two halves: weight-loss medicines, which treat the apnea by shrinking the patient, and a pill aimed at the breathing itself. Only the second carries a date. Apnimed submitted its once-nightly pill AD109 to the Food and Drug Administration in April, the agency accepted the filing on July 14, and the target date for an answer is February 28, 2027. Two late-stage trials cut the count of breathing interruptions per hour of sleep against a dummy pill.

Apnimed at $29.02, +$0.91 / +3.24%, is the other side of that argument, priced in the open since July 31, when the Cambridge, Massachusetts company sold shares at $16. It is worth $1.21B with no approved product and nothing yet to sell. Resmed's free cash flow last year - the cash left after running the business and buying equipment - was $1.65B, so one year of it outweighs the entire challenger. Apnimed fits none of the six Len5es: a clinical-stage company with no revenue offers neither the settled earnings the value styles want nor the record of growth the rest need.

Which is why the refill line matters more than the machine line. A machine is prescribed once and kept for years; a mask wears out and is replaced on a schedule an insurer pays for. In the June quarter devices grew 8%, to $750M, and masks and accessories grew 11%, to $542M. That refill line is where a pill shows up first, because patients stop reordering long before they stop owning.

One quiet number sits in the same quarter. On June 25 Resmed told customers that a leaking component inside its Astral 100 and 150 ventilators can push the machine into a fail-safe state and stop delivering therapy. Regulators class it at the most serious level, it covers 168,069 devices, and both products are unavailable to order. The response cost $41.9M - which is why reported profit per share rose 2% that quarter while the adjusted figure rose 16%.

The same company, six ways of looking:

- QUALITY-VALUE - STRONG, and the Len5 watching it. Hunts a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought under its worth. The rebuild half is the setup: a diagnosis, a prescription, a fitting, then years of routine reorders - and Resmed kept 62.4 cents of every sales dollar after making the product last year, 2.4 points more than the year before. The weak half is the price, about 21.6 times the $10.43 it reported and 4.9 times book value, its net worth on its own books. Cheaper than this company usually is, not cheap. CHANGE IT: two or three quarters of masks growing slower than devices, which would say the installed base is leaving rather than refilling.

- DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS - PARTIAL, and the second Len5 holding it. Hunts settled earning power bought under a careful estimate of its worth, or a sound business knocked down by a fixable problem. Both knocks are dated - the slide into June 2, the $41.9M recall response - and the earning power never blinked. What fails is the discount: the price came down to reasonable and stopped there. CHANGE IT: a fall back toward $180.27 with the quarters still compounding.

- MOMENTUM - NOT A FIT. Hunts a price at or near its one-year high where the short climb and the long climb agree. They argue: 21.0% under October's high, 24.8% above June's low. CHANGE IT: a close above $284.87.

text:
He wrote that he had panicked about the pressure of marrying into my family. He claimed Jessica offered him emotional stability and legal protection during a confusing time. He said he loved me, but feared losing himself in the Alden world. He said he never meant to hurt me.

I read the letter twice.

Then I handed it to Helen.

She read it once and said, “He confesses beautifully to nothing useful.”

That was exactly right.

There was no real apology.

No full truth.

No clear accountability.

Just elegant fog.

I did not reply.

For months, I lived quietly.

That surprised people.

Some expected me to become a public symbol overnight. Some wanted interviews. Some wanted me to write an essay. Some wanted details they had no right to know. I declined everything.

I returned to work at the foundation.

At first, walking into board meetings felt unbearable. I imagined people looking at me and seeing the canceled wedding, the mistress-wife, the million-dollar scandal, the bride in blue. But serious work has a way of rescuing you from your own reflection.

There were grants to review.

Programs to fund.

Budgets to approve.

Families to support.

The legal aid fund from the wedding-that-wasn’t became the beginning of something larger. Six months later, we launched the Alden Women’s Legal Resilience Initiative, supporting women facing financial deception, coercive debt, divorce complications, and emergency legal needs. We partnered with organizations across Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, and Wisconsin.

The first year, we funded 1,200 consultations.

The second year, more than 3,000.

Whenever someone asked why I cared about the issue, I gave the professional answer.

“Because legal access can determine whether a crisis becomes a life sentence.”

That was true.

It was not the whole truth.

The whole truth was sitting in the bridal suite at the Peninsula, wearing a robe, staring at a photograph of her fiancé holding another woman’s marriage certificate.

The whole truth was understanding how quickly love becomes leverage when money, reputation, and silence are involved.

One afternoon, nearly a year after the canceled wedding, Megan and I returned to the Peninsula for lunch.

She suggested it.

I resisted.

Then I agreed because I was tired of letting buildings keep my ghosts.

We sat near the window overlooking Michigan Avenue and ordered salads that cost too much. For a while, we talked about her work, my foundation, her terrible dating life, and whether my father would ever learn to text without sounding like a subpoena.

Then Megan said, “Do you ever miss him?”

I looked down at my water glass.

“No,” I said.

Then I corrected myself.

“I miss who I thought he was.”

Megan nodded.

“That counts.”

“I miss the future I planned.”

“That counts too.”

“I don’t miss the man who showed up.”

Megan reached across the table and squeezed my hand.

“That’s the part that saves you.”

Outside, Chicago moved on.

So did I.

Not quickly.

Not cleanly.

But honestly.
Two years after the canceled wedding, I wore the midnight blue gown again.

Not because I wanted to recreate anything.

Because the Alden Women’s Legal Resilience Initiative was hosting its annual benefit at the Art Institute of Chicago, and Megan told me if a dress survives a scandal, raises millions, and still fits, it deserves a second public appearance.

She was right.

The benefit was smaller than the wedding had been, but more meaningful. Two hundred guests. No imported rose forest. No engraved champagne glasses promising forever. No groom waiting at the end of an aisle with another wife hidden in the paperwork…..

text:
The historic Vera Coking House in Atlantic City, New Jersey, squeezed between the unfinished steel frameworks of a planned casino development around 1991...

Vera Coking bought the three-story boarding house at 127 South Columbia Place with her husband in 1961 for $20,000. In the 1970s, Penthouse publisher Bob Guccione offered her $1 million for the land. Later in the 1990s, Donald Trump attempted to acquire the property through eminent domain to build a limousine parking lot for his nearby casino.

... .... 

In early 1990s, Atlantic City was a battleground between real-estate ambition and personal resolve. This photo shows the home of Vera Coking, a widow who refused to sell her three-story boardinghouse despite pressure from Donald Trump and city officials. Her small white home, wedged defiantly between rising steel frames of Trump Plaza, became a national symbol of resistance.

Trump had offered Coking $1 million for the property to make way for a limousine parking lot connected to his casino. When she refused, New Jersey’s Casino Reinvestment Development Authority tried to seize the house through eminent domain. Public outrage followed. In 1998, a state judge ruled in Coking’s favor, halting the project and preserving her right to stay.

Coking lived in the house for nearly 35 years, watching Atlantic City’s fortunes rise and fall around her. Long after Trump’s casino closed, her home remained, a physical reminder that not all things could be bought or bulldozed.

Vera Coking finally sold her house in 2014 for just $530,000, far less than Trump’s original offer, but she had kept her principles intact.

text:
BitMEX shuts down on Wednesday. 04:00 UTC. All remaining positions force-closed.

The exchange that invented the perpetual swap in 2014. 100x leverage. Arthur Hayes. The wild west. It's done.

Moscow Exchange launches perpetual crypto futures on Tuesday.

BTC. ETH. SOL. XRP. TRX. One-day contracts with automatic rollover. Cash-settled in rubles. Restricted to qualified investors — but 72,000 of them have already traded MOEX crypto products since last November. RUB 600 billion in volume.

Two events. Two days apart. Same product.

The perpetual swap was born on BitMEX as a crypto-native invention — a way to hold leveraged positions without expiry dates. No regulator approved it. No exchange listed it first. BitMEX just built it and the market adopted it globally.

Eleven years later, the product has been absorbed by the system. A state-controlled exchange in Russia offers the same mechanism inside a regulated wrapper. The invention outgrew its birthplace.

BitMEX isn't shutting down because of a hack or a ban. The board decided. The business model couldn't sustain itself in a market where every major exchange — Binance, Bybit, OKX, CME, now MOEX — offers the same product with deeper liquidity and regulatory cover.

The market BitMEX created ate it alive.

For BTC specifically: the perpetual swap is now an institutional instrument. MOEX joining means Russian capital gets a regulated on-ramp to crypto exposure. Not direct Bitcoin ownership — cash-settled futures — but price exposure through the country's largest stock exchange.

The product BitMEX built to bypass the system is now part of the system.

That's not good or bad. It's just what happens when a genuinely useful financial innovation hits escape velocity. The inventors get left behind. The infrastructure keeps going.

text:
This segment features an interview with Vivek Ramaswamy, an Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate and former biotech executive, on Fox & Friends Weekend. 

The discussion covers several key topics, namely;

1. AI Regulation: Ramaswamy criticizes the push by progressive politicians, specifically mentioning California Governor Gavin Newsom, for increased government control over AI. 

2. He argues against "AI hysteria" and suggests that tech companies calling for regulation might be seeking to entrench their position against smaller startups.

3. Data Centers: The discussion pivots to the local impact of data centers. Ramaswamy outlines a plan for Ohio where data centers would only be built if they offer tangible benefits to local communities, such as lowered electric bills, reduced property taxes, and the use of abandoned industrial sites.

3. Midterm Elections and Political Rhetoric: Ramaswamy addresses his race for governor and the broader political landscape. The segment includes a clip of Spencer Pratt speaking at a campaign event, framing the election as a choice between "American success" and "socialist/communist" policies. 

4. Ramaswamy concludes by emphasizing individual responsibility and the importance of voter participation.

Credit: @RCamposDuffy @CharlesHurt @GriffJenkins @VivekGRamaswamy

Isaiah 66:
Thus says the Lord:
“Heaven is my throne,
    and the earth is my footstool;
what is the house that you would build for me,
    and what is the place of my rest?

2 All these things my hand has made,
    and so all these things came to be,
declares the Lord.
But this is the one to whom I will look:
    he who is humble and contrite in spirit
    and trembles at my word.

3 “He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man;
    he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog's neck;
he who presents a grain offering, like one who offers pig's blood;
    he who makes a memorial offering of frankincense, like one who blesses an idol.
These have chosen their own ways,
    and their soul delights in their abominations;
4 I also will choose harsh treatment for them

Acts 7:48-50
"However, the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands... Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me?" 

Acts 17:24
"The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples built by human hands."

No more need for a temple 

Hebrews 9:
11 But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come,then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation) 

12 he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption. 

13 For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, 

14 how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.

15 Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.

 16 For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established.

 17 For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive.

 18 Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood. 

19 For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, 

20 saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” 

21 And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. 

22 Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.

23 Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these

. 24 For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf.
