GREEN BAY #PACKERS AT NEW YORK #JETS
#KALSHI #NFL SCAN —
September 20, 2026 | NFL Week 2 | Quote snapshot 07:46 AM PDT

ASSESSMENT: PACKERS WINNER LEAN; WAIT FOR FINAL INACTIVES
Kalshi asks Green Bay 62c / Jets 39c. Green Bay is the favorite, but the current ESPN sportsbook benchmark puts its fair probability close to the pre-fee price. Estimated fees eliminate that small apparent advantage. Older previews show a stronger Packers lean but are not synchronized with current quotes. No independent calibrated win-probability model was run. No trades were placed.

GAME CHECK [1,2]
Green Bay (0–1) at New York Jets (1–0), MetLife Stadium, East Rutherford, New Jersey.
Sunday September 20: 1:00 p.m. EDT / noon CDT / 10:00 a.m. PDT. FOX.
ESPN game ID 401872936. Outdoor venue. ESPN's game-weather snapshot lists cloudy conditions and 68°F. Wind and precipitation risk were not independently verified; clouds alone do not establish an under advantage.

LATEST INJURY CHECK [3,4]
Green Bay: Javon Hargrave (knee/concussion) and Warren Brinson (calf) are out. Aaron Banks and Zach Bako-Bewele (knees), plus Benjamin St-Juste (hamstring), are questionable. The September 19 update clears Lukas Van Ness from the concussion protocol and removes his game designation; older reports listing him questionable are superseded.
Jets: Minkah Fitzpatrick (groin), Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle), Kene Nwangwu (back) and Joseph Ossai (foot) are out. Will McDonald IV (ankle) is questionable. The Jets announced Cooper's injured-reserve placement September 19. D'Angelo Ponds has no game designation after full Thursday and Friday participation.
Final game-day inactives were not verified. Recheck approximately 11:30 a.m. EDT / 8:30 a.m. PDT, about 90 minutes before kickoff, particularly Green Bay's offensive line and McDonald.

MATCHUP INTERPRETATION
Green Bay's missing interior defenders could help Breece Hall sustain drives. Questionable Packers linemen make pass protection an important swing factor; McDonald's availability affects the Jets' ability to exploit it. Fitzpatrick's absence creates a concern in New York's secondary against Jordan Love's downfield passing. These are qualitative football considerations, not measured point adjustments. Public injury information may already be in the price.

WEEK 1 EVIDENCE [2]
Packers lost 39–22 to Minnesota. Jordan Love completed 21 of 42 for 387 yards, two touchdowns and one interception. Christian Watson had six catches for 147 yards and two touchdowns. MarShawn Lloyd ran 13 times for 37 yards.
Jets beat Tennessee 23–10. Geno Smith completed 19 of 24 for 215 yards; Breece Hall ran 22 times for 102 yards and one touchdown; Garrett Wilson caught six for 79 yards.
Love generated explosive yardage but completed only half his attempts. New York's run production and efficient passing offer a path to shortening the game, but one week's outcomes do not establish durable team strength. Preseason results were excluded; no opponent-adjusted offense, defense or scoring model was calculated.

WINNER MARKET [5]
Event: KXNFLGAME-26SEP20GBNYJ
Green Bay YES bid 61c / ask 62c.
Jets YES bid 38c / ask 39c.
Ordinary win pays $1, loss pays $0. A tie pays $0.50 for each team's YES contract. Both asks total 101c before fees; buying both is not an arbitrage, including in a tie.
Quotes can change before execution. Displayed size is not a guaranteed fill, and order-book depth was not independently checked. Volume and prices cannot establish who is betting or prove informed money flow.

SPORTSBOOK / MODEL CROSS-CHECK [2,6]
ESPN's DraftKings feed shows Packers -185 / Jets +154, Green Bay -3.5 and total 44.5. Proportional removal of the moneyline margin gives Green Bay 62.25% / Jets 37.75%.
A September 16 FanDuel preview lists -215 / +180, equivalent to approximately 65.65% / 34.35% after normalization, and attributes a 64% Packers forecast to numberFire. The older price and unaudited model are reference points, not live consensus.
At 62c plus an estimated 1.65c fee per contract for 100 contracts, Green Bay costs 63.65c. Even the cited 64% model leaves only a tiny margin before uncertainty. Jets cost 40.67c at 39c plus fees, above the ESPN benchmark. Neither is a robust edge.
Sportsbook moneyline tie rules may differ from Kalshi's 50c settlement. An exact comparison requires a tie probability; normalized moneylines are only an approximation to expected payout. Different timestamps and sources do not establish a verified historical line move.

FEES / PAYOFFS [7]
Live winner, total and spread series metadata reports multiplier 1 and quadratic fees with maker fees. Confirm the actual ticket; passive orders are not necessarily free.
Estimated taker fee = round upward to a cent [0.07 × contracts × price × (1-price)], with price in dollars.
Packers: 100 YES at 62c = $62.00 principal + $1.65 fee = $63.65 cash risk. Win profit $36.35; loss $63.65; tie net $-13.65.
Jets: 100 YES at 39c = $39.00 principal + $1.67 fee = $40.67 cash risk. Win profit $59.33; loss $40.67; tie net $+9.33.
Expected profit per contract = P(win) + 0.5 × P(tie) − all-in cost. Break-even expected payout is therefore 63.65c for Green Bay and 40.67c for the Jets in these examples. Small or split orders may round differently. Early exits add spread costs and possibly additional fees.

CONDITIONAL STRATEGIES
1. Default: wait for inactives and updated wind/rain conditions. Refresh Kalshi and multiple sportsbooks before relying on a small price difference.
2. Packers watch price 58c: 100 contracts cost $59.71 with estimated fees. IF independent analysis supports a 64c expected settlement value, hypothetical edge is 4.29c per contract. That is an illustrative assumption, not an endorsement of the older model.
3. Jets watch price 35c: 100 contracts cost $36.60. IF justified expected settlement is 40c, hypothetical edge is 3.40c. The underdog thesis needs evidence that New York can exploit Green Bay's missing interior defenders while protecting its own weakened secondary.
4. Limit orders and a predefined maximum total cash loss help control execution and sizing. The 100-contract examples explain mechanics, not recommended allocations. Winner and spread positions on the same team overlap.

TOTAL / SPREAD CHECK
Over 44.5 YES 49c; over 43.5 YES 54c; over 45.5 YES 46c. Over 44.5 requires at least 45 total points. Buying 100 YES at 49c costs about $50.75 with fees; a 50% probability would not cover the cost.
Green Bay by over 2.5 YES 56c; over 3.5 YES 47c; over 6.5 YES 40c. The first two require wins by at least three and four points. The nine-cent difference highlights the importance of an exactly three-point margin; it is not an independently calibrated margin probability.
NO on Green Bay over 3.5 corresponds to Jets +3.5 in ordinary completed-game outcomes: a Jets win, tie or loss by up to three qualifies. It is not equivalent to Jets moneyline or a sportsbook +3 with a push.
Without a scoring distribution and final injury information, no positive-value total or spread is established. Week 1's Packers score does not automatically justify an over.

SETTLEMENT
Winner rules pay 50c per team for a tie. If postponed but started within 48 hours of the original start, the market resolves using the official final result. If not started within that window, it resolves to a fair price, not necessarily a refund. Injuries do not automatically void the team-winner contract. Read total/spread terms separately for abandoned or rescheduled games; the short API descriptions do not cover every contingency.

text:
Replacing social media with a video game controller could be a major boost to your mental health.

 New long-term studies reveal that gaming beats social media scrolling when it comes to both stress relief and emotional well-being.

For years, digital screens have been lumped together as a monolithic threat to mental well-being, but pioneering research is rewriting that narrative. An 11-year study from the University of Cincinnati and Northwestern University tracking over 183,000 U.S. adults found a damning correlation: exceeding 150 minutes of daily social media use significantly elevates the risk of depression. 

This passive, algorithmic scrolling traps the mind in a loop of social comparison and cognitive fatigue. Unlike other screen activities, mindless scrolling acts as a primary driver of adult depressive symptoms, leaving users feeling emotionally depleted.

In stark contrast, video games are emerging as a powerful, interactive tool for cognitive enhancement and emotional regulation. A study by the Boston University College of Communication highlights that video games offer structured, goal-oriented engagement that actively supports stress management and builds mental resilience. Rather than draining cognitive resources, gaming demands decision-making, puzzle-solving, and social teamwork, triggering a healthy state of mental flow. By shifting from the passive consumption of social feeds to the active engagement of gaming, users can transform their screen time into a restorative and purpose-driven break.

source: Breiter, H., Block, M. L., et al. (2026). Social media use and depression across 11 years of U.S. adult data. npj Mental Health Research.

text:
Three years after Azerbaijan restored its sovereignty over the whole of Karabakh, Irish historian and political analyst Dr Pat Walsh offers a thought-provoking analysis of the events that led to September 2023 and of the strategic choices made over three decades.

Dr Walsh, whom — together with other esteemed historians — FATSR had the pleasure of welcoming to the Palais de Rumine in Lausanne in 2023 for our conference marking the centenary of the Treaty of Lausanne [https://t.co/J5Ub15aCwY], argues that the outcome in Karabakh cannot be understood without examining the successive miscalculations of Armenian governments and the leadership of the separatist entity.

His analysis highlights several points:

▪ The persistence of maximalist territorial objectives despite the absence of international recognition for the self-proclaimed “Artsakh”;

▪ The failure to fully implement the November 2020 agreement, including the withdrawal of Armenian armed forces;

▪ The reliance on external powers to preserve an increasingly unsustainable status quo;

▪ And, finally, the rejection of opportunities for a political accommodation within Azerbaijan’s internationally recognised borders.

Particularly striking is Walsh’s account of the proposals discussed in 2023 for the Armenian population of Karabakh.

These envisaged safeguards for their language, religion, cultural identity, education and private property within Azerbaijan.

According to Walsh, their rejection represented one of the last opportunities to reach a different outcome.

History deserves to be studied not merely to assign responsibility, but to learn from mistakes.

Perhaps the most important lesson today is therefore addressed to Armenian political leaders — both in Armenia and within the diaspora: A serious examination of the strategic choices of the past three decades, including the consequences of maximalism and dependence on outside powers, could help prevent the repetition of past errors.

Such introspection should not be regarded as a defeat. On the contrary, it can be the foundation of a more realistic and peaceful future as @NikolPashinyan seems to currently implement. 

Armenia and Azerbaijan now have an opportunity to turn the page on decades of confrontation.

We sincerely hope that wisdom and political courage will prevail, allowing Armenians and Azerbaijanis (and by extension 🇹🇷) to build a durable peace based on internationally recognised borders, mutual respect and regional cooperation.

That would ultimately place all the peoples of the South Caucasus on the right side of history.

text:
THE FIRST BOOK OF 
SAMUEL 
1
1 Now there was a certain man of Ramathaim-zophim, of the hill-country of Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephraimite:  2 and he had two wives; the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah: and Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.  3 And this man went up out of his city from year to year to worship and to sacrifice unto Jehovah of hosts in Shiloh. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, priests unto Jehovah, were there.  4 And when the day came that Elkanah sacrificed, he gave to Peninnah his wife, and to all her sons and her daughters, portions: 5 but unto Hannah he gave a double portion; for he loved Hannah, but Jehovah had shut up her womb.  6 And her rival provoked her sore, to make her fret, because Jehovah had shut up her womb.  7 And as he did so year by year, when she went up to the house of Jehovah, so she provoked her; therefore she wept, and did not eat. 8 And Elkanah her husband said unto her, Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons? 
9 So Hannah rose up after they had eaten in Shiloh, and after they had drunk. Now Eli the priest was sitting upon his seat by the door-post of the temple of Jehovah.  10 And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto Jehovah, and wept sore.  11 And she vowed a vow, and said, O Jehovah of hosts, if thou wilt indeed look on the affliction of thy handmaid, and remember me, and not forget thy handmaid, but wilt give unto thy handmaid a man-child, then I will give him unto Jehovah all the days of his life, and there shall no razor come upon his head. 
12 And it came to pass, as she continued praying before Jehovah, that Eli marked her mouth.  13 Now Hannah, she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard: therefore Eli thought she had been drunken.  14 And Eli said unto her, How long wilt thou be drunken? put away thy wine from thee.  15 And Hannah answered and said, No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I poured out my soul before Jehovah.  16 Count not thy handmaid for a wicked woman; for out of the abundance of my complaint and my provocation have I spoken hitherto.  17 Then Eli answered and said, Go in peace; and the God of Israel grant thy petition that thou hast asked of him.  18 And she said, Let thy handmaid find favor in thy sight. So the woman went her way, and did eat; and her countenance was no more sad. 
19 And they rose up in the morning early, and worshipped before Jehovah, and returned, and came to their house to Ramah. And Elkanah knew Hannah his wife; and Jehovah remembered her;  20 and it came to pass, when the time was come about, that Hannah conceived, and bare a son; and she called his name Samuel, saying, Because I have asked him of Jehovah. 
21 And the man Elkanah, and all his house, went up to offer unto Jehovah the yearly sacrifice, and his vow.  22 But Hannah went not up; for she said unto her husband, I will not go up until the child be weaned; and then I will bring him, that he may appear before Jehovah, and there abide for ever.  23 And Elkanah her husband said unto her, Do what seemeth thee good; tarry until thou have weaned him; only Jehovah establish his word. So the woman tarried and gave her son suck, until she weaned him.  24 And when she had weaned him, she took him up with her, with three bullocks, and one ephah of meal, and a bottle of wine, and brought him unto the house of Jehovah in Shiloh: and the child was young.  25 And they slew the bullock, and brought the child to Eli.  26 And she said, Oh, my lord, as thy soul liveth, my lord, I am the woman that stood by thee here, praying unto Jehovah.

text:
A guy I went to high school with bought a house for $71,000 in March. Last week the bank wrote him a check for $101,250 and he still owns the house

I made him send me the closing statement. It checks out

March: a 3 bedroom in Toledo listed at $84,900. Estate sale, carpet older than he is, three kids who wanted it gone. He offered $71,000 cash with a 9 day close. Somebody else offered $80,000 with a mortgage. The family took the cash

April: $24,000 of work in 5 weeks. Paint, vinyl plank floors, new cabinet doors and counters, both bathrooms

May: rented at $1,295 a month

September: a lender sent out an appraiser. $135,000. They loaned him 75% of it

Line by line:

Purchase: $71,000
Rehab: $24,000
Card processing fees: $2,850
Refinance closing costs: $3,200
Total in: $101,050
Loan check: $101,250

He's up $200 and owns a house worth $135,000 with a tenant in it

The $95,000 up front came off 0% business credit cards. He has about $160,000 in limits. A payment processor turns card limit into money in his LLC's checking for about 3%, the title company gets a wire, and nobody at the closing table asks where the cash started. Holding $95,000 for six months cost him $2,850

The refinance lender never asked for a W-2. That type of loan gets decided on one question, whether the rent covers the payment. $1,295 coming in against $985 going out. Approved

The risk is the appraisal. If it comes in low, some of his money stays stuck in the house while the 0% clock keeps running. So he only buys where three houses within half a mile have already sold at the fixed-up price, and he starts the refinance with 5 months of 0% still left

The cards are back at $0. The house pays him about $310 a month. He closes on the next one Friday, same cards

text:
I watched a sommelier fail to identify a Cabernet when a customer asked him to blind taste it.

Upscale steakhouse. My wife and I are finishing dinner. Table next to us orders wine. Sommelier comes over with the full performance, describing terroir and vintage characteristics.

"This Napa Cab shows beautiful cassis notes with hints of cedar and tobacco. Exceptional structure."

Opens it, pours a taste for the customer. Customer nods, approves the bottle.

Sommelier pours glasses for the table. As he's leaving, customer calls him back.

"Since you know this wine so well, would you mind blind tasting something for me?"

Sommelier looks uncertain but agrees. Customer pulls out a different bottle from his bag, something he brought for later.

Pours a small amount in a fresh glass. "Tell me what you think."

Sommelier swirls, sniffs, tastes. Goes through the whole ritual.

"Interesting. I'm getting... Pinot Noir? Oregon, maybe? Cherry notes, lighter body..."

Customer turns the bottle around. It's Cabernet Sauvignon. Same variety the sommelier just served them, different producer.

"It's Cab. From Napa. Literally the same wine type you just described in detail."

Sommelier's face goes red. Starts backtracking about how blind tasting is difficult, similar profiles, his palate being off today.

Customer's not mean about it, just matter-of-fact. "You charged us $120 for a bottle and gave us a whole speech about what we'd taste. But you can't identify the basic variety blind?"

Manager comes over. Offers to comp their wine. Customer says comp the whole meal or he's posting this interaction.

They comp'd it.

My wife and I looked at each other. We'd paid $95 for our bottle based on the same sommelier's recommendation.

Suddenly tasted a lot more like marketing than expertise.

text:
Have been reading about extinct countries.

In 1893 James Harden-Hickey of San Francisco declared himself “James I, Prince of Trinidad” and claimed Trindade Island as his very own state. (The island is volcanic, roughly 700 miles east of Brazil, and completely unrelated to the Caribbean island of Trinidad)

He tried to construct the apparatus of a real state. He designed a flag and coat of arms, issued postage stamps, established an order of chivalry called the Cross of Trinidad, appointed officials, opened a diplomatic office at 217 West 36th Street in New York, and began selling government bonds to finance settlement of the island. One scheme offered purchasers of ten $200 bonds free passage to Trinidad if they agreed to remain there for at least a year, and early settlers were enticed by the prospect of becoming part of the principality’s future aristocracy and, if you bought all-in to the promotional material, buried pirate treasure.

But self-proclaimed Prince James’ was relying on a dubious claim of terra nullius when Europeans had known the land since the Portuguese voyages around the time of Columbus. And James had never actually set foot there.

Then the British arrived and claimed sovereignty, hoping to connect telegraph cable to Brazil. Prince James’ “government” protested and appealed to the United States, which was hilarious because Brazil was simultaneously doing the same as an actual recognized nation state.

Today Trindade belongs to Brazil and has a permanent Brazilian Navy presence.

Prince James never recovered his kingdom. His finances and personal circumstances deteriorated, and in 1898 he died by suicide in El Paso, Texas.

But despite James’ tragic end, it must be said that this was a remarkable project. Its downfall was caused not by the ridiculousness of the venture but by actual great-power imperial politics.

Before E10 came along, people had to actually buy little cans of alcohol to add to gasoline with brand names like HEET or DRY GAS in winter for gas-line antifreeze.

Ethanol is an oxygenate which greatly reduces gasoline's toxic, carcinogenic, and dirty exhaust emissions all while being a very cheap and non-toxic concentrated octane booster.

We could and should refine natural gas, oil, and coal into pollution free non-toxic ethanol.

China, Indonesia, India, and others are using and/or looking at an efficient and economical process to do that from a Texas company named Celanese with their TCX Technology.  https://t.co/hVKmPzDIwO

With enough ethanol we could have 99%+ pollution free hyper efficient ethanol optimized engines with more power and more mpg than gasoline,even more mpg than diesel engines (at half the size/twice the power).

Here is an excerpt about the ethanol optimized engine Ricardo built and drove around for GM.  Better fuel economy than their diesel engine. 

FROM RICARDO:   The new federal CAFE standards are calling for a doubling of fuel mileage performance, which, Vint says, is going to send OEM’s looking for high octane numbers to improve efficiency and ethanol is the best source. Ricardo, an engineering firm with over 100 years in the business of engine design, has developed an extreme boosted direct injection engine (EBDI) to optimize ethanol blends. The 3.2 V6 gasoline engine rivals the power and torque of a much larger GMC Sierra 6.6 diesel, he said, and it delivers 3.5 percent better fuel economy than the diesel.   https://t.co/p86HQhEJQx 

Ford's first prototype EcoBoost engine was optimized for E85 and achieved 15 to 20% better fuel economy on E85 than with E0 with load performance similar to a diesel engine.  https://t.co/whEWz7A19K

Scania has sold a heavy-duty ethanol engine for years which they say has power and fuel economy on par with their diesel engines.
https://t.co/efjkWs9jVA

Note that ethanol makes a wonderful fuel for fuel cells, much farther range than with dangerous hydrogen.

Fuel Cell technology offers many advantages over Lithium-ion batteries, not the least of which is that hydrogen used in fuel cells has the energy to weight ratio ten times greater than lithium-ion batteries.

That said, the volumetric energy density of ethanol is over five times greater than hydrogen.

Ethanol has five times higher volumetric energy density (6.7 kWh/L) than hydrogen (1.3 kWh/L) and can be used safely in fuel cells for power generation.

Source: https://t.co/BXHf68KXB6

In 2016 Nissan drove around a fuel cell powered electric vehicle in Brazil using the already existing E100 fuel infrastructure.  

The fuel cell can even use ethanol with enough water in it so as to be non-flammable.  Making an already safe fuel even safer.

https://t.co/kFtNeAqx47

Advanced and ultra quiet large military submarines in Europe and India use ethanol fueled hydrogen fuel cells for propulsion today.

Alcohol fuel cells are sold in RV/sailboat power, backup power systems, and even small enough for computers and very long-range drones.

Show Us the Request: Trump’s Triumphal Arch Has Suddenly Become a Sniper Base

Donald Trump wants a triumphal arch in Washington.

Not merely an arch anymore, apparently.

Now it's a military installation.

On September 20, President Trump announced that his proposed 250-foot monument near Arlington Memorial Bridge would become what he called a “top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch,” capable of housing large numbers of drones, positioning snipers on its roof and plaza, and storing substantial quantities of sniper ammunition.

And Trump supplied the sentence upon which the entire new justification rests:

This was done, he said, at the “strong request” of the United States military.

Fine.

Then show us the request.

Because at the moment, that is the missing piece of the story.

The Pentagon told the Associated Press that it had no information beyond the president's statement. Reuters separately reported that a U.S. military official said the Defense Department had nothing to add beyond Trump's social-media post.

That does not prove Trump's statement false.

It does something journalistically more useful:

It leaves an extraordinary presidential claim conspicuously uncorroborated.

And this particular claim deserves corroboration.

The president isn't saying that somebody at the Pentagon thinks the arch would look nice.

He is saying the United States military strongly requested that a monumental structure beside one of America's most symbolically important military landscapes become an operational facility involving drones, sniper positions and ammunition storage.

That should leave paperwork.

There should be an originating organization.

There should be an operational requirement.

There should be threat analysis.

There should be planning.

There should be somebody whose name appears underneath the recommendation.

There should, at minimum, be an answer to the simplest question imaginable:

Who asked for this?

A Monument Acquires a Mission

The chronology makes that question more important.

The arch was already Trump's project before Sunday's military rationale appeared.

It has been proposed as a monumental structure commemorating America's 250th anniversary. It has moved through federal architectural and planning processes. It has generated enormous public opposition. Veterans and an architectural historian have sued over it. Preservationists have objected to its effects on historic landscapes and sightlines.

The project has also encountered questions about whether congressional authorization is required.

And now, amid that controversy, the monument has acquired a national-security mission.

Maybe that mission is legitimate.

If so, documenting it should be straightforward.

Produce the military request.

The Geography Makes the Question Stranger

The proposed location isn't some undefended wilderness.

Reuters notes that Memorial Circle is approximately a mile from Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall and roughly two miles from the Pentagon.

Retired Marine Col. Mark Cancian, now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, questioned the military rationale on precisely those grounds. He also raised practical questions about storing ammunition at the monument and about the usefulness of placing snipers there.

Those are not partisan questions.

They're logistical ones.

If Washington needs a new drone-response facility at Memorial Circle, what capability does it provide that nearby military infrastructure cannot?

What threat is it designed to defeat?

Why does that threat require sniper positions on a triumphal arch?

Why does the facility require ammunition storage at the monument itself?

Why this location?

Why this architecture?

And why now?

Trump's announcement supplied none of those answers.

CHIMERA Finds the Missing Key

This is almost comically well suited to the new CHIMERA methodology in the EFMW Zoo.

CHIMERA does not ask whether a statement sounds crazy.

It asks where the information came from.

The president has created a durable public record.

C: Classical record.

The project has moved through public opposition, litigation, administrative review and now a changing public justification.

R: Recursive feedback environment.

Then comes the crucial claim:

“At the strong request of the United States Military.”

That statement asserts the existence of another record.

CHIMERA calls that the missing key.

Who made the request?

Where is it?

What does it say?

Can another observer independently recover the provenance of the president's claim?

Until those questions are answered:

K: withheld.

The claim that a key exists is not itself the key.

Don't Diagnose Trump. Audit the Government.

It is tempting to look at a president proposing a gigantic triumphal arch containing drones, snipers and ammunition and ask whether something has gone terribly wrong with the man proposing it.

That's the less useful question.

Journalists are not Trump's psychiatrists.

Congress isn't Trump's psychiatrist.

The Pentagon isn't Trump's psychiatrist.

They don't need to be.

The United States government operates through authority, appropriations, planning, documentation and accountability.

So forget amateur diagnosis.

Audit the claim.

If senior military officials genuinely concluded that national security requires an armed drone-and-sniper installation incorporated into a triumphal arch at Memorial Circle, the public deserves to know why.

If military planners generated the proposal, identify them.

If the Secret Service generated it, say so.

If NORTHCOM generated it, document that.

If another organization produced a threat assessment, disclose what can safely be disclosed and acknowledge the classified remainder.

If the president received an oral recommendation, identify who made it and when.

But if nobody can identify the supposed “strong request,” then the absence becomes significant.

Not proof of insanity.

Not proof of corruption.

Not proof of some hidden motive.

Something much simpler:

a major presidential national-security assertion without publicly demonstrated provenance.

And There Is Already a Legal Fight

This isn't happening on a blank sheet of paper.

The project has faced litigation from veterans and an architectural historian who argue that the arch requires congressional authorization and would damage the historic relationship between Arlington National Cemetery, Memorial Bridge and the Lincoln Memorial.

Earlier this month, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ordered the administration to provide 48 hours' notice before activity at the site. The project still lacks final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission.

Meanwhile, the National Park Service's preservation process has found adverse effects on historic resources, and enormous numbers of public comments have been submitted during the review.

The military justification therefore arrives not at the conception of an uncontested defense project, but during an existing fight over a monument the president already wanted built.

That chronology does not establish that the national-security rationale is pretextual.

It makes its provenance important enough to demand.

Congress Has a Very Short Question to Ask

This does not require a 400-page investigation.

Send a letter to the Department of Defense:

Please identify the office, command, official or component that made the “strong request” referenced by President Trump on September 20, 2026, and provide the date, nature and documentary basis of that request, subject to appropriate handling of legitimately classified information.

That's it.

The answer could vindicate the president's account.

Perhaps there really is a detailed military requirement. Perhaps planners have identified a vulnerability around Memorial Circle. Perhaps the architecture offers some advantage not apparent from the outside.

Then show the evidence that can safely be shown.

But the alternative matters too.

If the Department of Defense cannot identify who strongly requested this thing, journalists should stop repeating “at the request of the military” as though it were an independently established fact.

Attribute it correctly:

Trump says the military requested it.

Because today, that's what the evidence establishes.

Show Us the Request

This is bigger than whether anyone likes Trump's arch.

Presidents routinely possess information unavailable to the public. National-security decisions sometimes necessarily depend upon classified intelligence.

But “classified” cannot become a magic word that transforms an unsupported public assertion into an established fact.

And the Pentagon hasn't even publicly invoked classification here.

So the question remains almost embarrassingly elementary.

The president says the United States military strongly requested an enormous new armed facility embedded inside his triumphal arch.

Which part of the military?

Who requested it?

When?

For what operational purpose?

On the basis of what threat assessment?

And where is the record?

Donald Trump has supplied the claim.

Now somebody needs to supply the receipt.

text:
SAUDI ARABIA EXITS CHINA’S DIGITAL PAYMENT PROJECT

DECODE CONFLICT ASSESSMENT

Saudi Arabia has ended active participation in mBridge, a China-led platform designed to settle cross-border payments through central-bank digital currencies.

This is not a withdrawal from China’s CIPS network or an end to Saudi trade with Beijing. Riyadh joined mBridge in 2024, completed its proof-of-concept work by May 2025 and quietly departed under what the Saudi Central Bank described as a predetermined plan.

The project offered faster and cheaper payments with less dependence on dollar clearing and SWIFT. That also raised concerns that mBridge could eventually help governments reduce exposure to American sanctions.

Saudi Arabia had several reasons to proceed cautiously. The riyal remains pegged to the dollar. Saudi oil, investments and reserves remain deeply connected to dollar markets. The kingdom also depends on American weapons, intelligence and security cooperation.

Riyadh may also be unwilling to exchange dependence on Washington for dependence on a financial platform heavily influenced by Beijing. Questions remain about sanctions enforcement, transaction privacy, cyber resilience and who ultimately controls the network.

THE DECODE

Saudi Arabia wants Chinese trade, American security and financial flexibility. Leaving mBridge allows it to preserve all three without becoming the symbol of a Chinese challenge to the dollar.

China can build an alternative payment platform.

It cannot yet reproduce the trust, liquidity and security relationships supporting the dollar.

Saudi Arabia tested Beijing’s system but declined to anchor its financial future inside it.

Jeff is great for finance, but he has a lot to learn about international relations. It is way more complex than how expensive things are and how good the offer is.

Letting Iran fall is an absolute disaster for China:

1. It gives US full control of Persian Gulf resources that China needs, which includes oil. After China lost Venezuela, they can’t afford giving US such control.

2. It breaks China’s centrury project - Belt and Road - that relies on Iran NOT being under US’ control.

3. It gives US control over too much cheap resources, harming longer term competitiveness of China in the battle of world powers.

So, best Trump can do is somehow persuade Xi to help Iran a bit LESS ACTIVELY by offering huge concessions on Taiwan or by applying pressure on Europe to allow free flow of Chinese high tech to Western Europe.

Last time, Taiwan seemingly was the concession - not supply arms in exchange for China stopping maritime oil import and using reserves.

text:
The stock rips +4% after earnings.

Your call is still red.

That’s not bad luck.

That’s IV crush.

Before the print, the market pays for uncertainty.

After the print, the uncertainty is gone.

Front-month IV often drops 30–60% tech closer to 35–55%, biotech even harder.

Across large samples the average crush is ~38%.

Four types trade the same event differently:

Retail income Iron condors or credit spreads outside the expected move. Defined risk. Less credit. 

You survive the 30% gap. Vol-seller Short strangle/straddle 1–2 days before, often closed at the next open. More premium. Undefined risk. 

Only makes sense if the stock historically moves less than the straddle is pricing. Pro / market maker 

Calendar: short the expensive earnings week, long the back expiry. Or inventory fade, delta-hedged. They are not betting beat vs miss. They are betting vol is wrong. 

Ownership Cash-secured put on a name you would hold through a drawdown. The crush can help the short put after the print. That is not why you sold it. You sold an offer to buy the stock. If earnings is in the window and you do not want the gap, you stay flat. That is the rule I actually run. 

The filter that decides the trade not the feeling:

• IV rank/percentile high (above 70 crushed harder on average, ~44%)

• Historical earnings move < ~80% of today’s implied move

• Tight spreads, liquid chains

• Size so an ugly gap does not kill the book

Without the filter, “sell the crush” is a slogan.

With the filter, it is an edge with a nasty tail.

This week includes AZO, COST, DRI, GIS, PAYX.

Not all of them are crush trades. COST often prices a tight move. 

That does not automatically mean short vol.
I sell premium for income.
I often stay flat through earnings when spreads, skew, or the implied move do not fit.

Not a trade idea.

Just the mechanics before Q3 really starts.

Which type do you play through the print?

A Iron condor

B Strangle

C Calendar

D CSP / ownership

E Flat until after the open

text:
OpenAI scales back features for stability

As we kick off another week of tech news, let’s dive into something that caught my eye: OpenAI’s recent announcement. So, what’s happening? Well, it turns out the big player in artificial intelligence is making some significant changes to their platform. But why now, and how does this affect you?
What Exactly Changed?

OpenAI has announced several key adjustments:
• Feature Scaling Back: They’re reducing the scope of certain advanced features that were causing performance issues.
• Data Handling Adjustments: There’s a new emphasis on data privacy and security. This includes stricter controls over user data storage and processing.

These aren’t just minor tweaks; they represent a strategic pivot in how OpenAI operates its platform. For instance, some of the high-end analytics tools that were previously available are now limited or removed entirely. These exclusions aim to address performance bottlenecks and regulatory concerns.
Why Now?

The timing isn’t random. OpenAI has faced increasing scrutiny from regulators around the world regarding the handling of sensitive information. They’re also dealing with internal challenges like resource constraints and competing priorities. By scaling back, they can focus on what’s truly necessary for their core services.

But why would a company known for pushing boundaries suddenly pull back? It’s likely that OpenAI has realized they need to prioritize stability over innovation in certain areas, at least temporarily. This shift is partly driven by the need to comply with stricter data protection regulations and ensure that their platform remains reliable and secure.
How Does It Work?

Let's break down how these changes will impact you:
• Performance: The reduced scope means less strain on the system, which should lead to more stable performance.
• Privacy: Enhanced data security measures mean your information is better protected. This includes stricter access controls and regular audits.

But what about users who rely heavily on those advanced functionalities? How will they adapt? For example, if you were using OpenAI’s predictive analytics tools for business forecasting, you might need to find alternative solutions or workarounds within the platform's new limitations.
What Is Stored?

OpenAI’s changes include stricter guidelines for storing user data. They’re implementing more robust encryption methods to protect sensitive information. Additionally, the company has announced that it will no longer retain certain types of personal data indefinitely.

However, this doesn’t mean all your data is gone; rather, OpenAI is being more selective about what they keep and how long they store it. This shift aims to reduce the risk of data breaches while still providing necessary services. For instance, if you’ve been using OpenAI’s chatbot for personal finance management, rest assured that your sensitive financial information will be encrypted and stored securely.
What Is Excluded?

The changes also involve excluding certain features that were previously available. For instance, some advanced analytics tools are now limited or removed entirely. These exclusions are designed to address performance bottlenecks and regulatory concerns.

But what does this mean for users who relied on these features? Will they find alternative solutions elsewhere, or will OpenAI provide workarounds? If you’ve been using the predictive text feature for writing reports, you might need to explore other tools that offer similar functionality.
User Controls

One of the most significant changes is an increase in user control over their data. Users now have more options to manage how their information is used and stored within the platform. This includes granular settings for privacy preferences and clearer opt-out mechanisms.

However, these controls come with a learning curve. Will users take advantage of them, or will they remain largely unused due to complexity? For example, if you’re not tech-savvy, navigating through new privacy settings might be challenging. OpenAI needs to ensure that the user interface is intuitive and easy to understand.
Availability

The changes are rolling out gradually across different regions and user groups. OpenAI is prioritizing updates based on regulatory requirements and internal resource availability. This means that not all features may be affected simultaneously.

But how does this staggered rollout impact users who need consistent access to their preferred functionalities? Will they experience downtime or inconsistencies? For instance, if you’re a heavy user in Europe where data protection laws are stringent, your access might change before it affects users in other regions.
What This Does Not Prove

While these changes are positive steps forward, it’s important to note what they don’t prove:
• Regulatory Compliance: The measures may not be enough to satisfy all regulatory bodies concerned about data privacy.
• Long-term Stability: While the immediate performance improvements are promising, long-term stability remains uncertain.

And here’s where it gets tricky: OpenAI is walking a fine line between innovation and compliance. They need to keep pushing the envelope while also ensuring they’re not overstepping legal boundaries. For instance, if they continue to innovate too aggressively without addressing regulatory concerns, they risk facing stricter penalties or sanctions.
Practical Takeaway

So what’s in it for you? Better security and more reliable service, at least initially. But don’t get too comfortable—this is likely just the beginning of a series of adjustments as OpenAI navigates an increasingly complex landscape. As regulations evolve and technology advances, expect to see further changes that balance innovation with compliance.

text:
@BillAckman @Uber
My nephew—an NYPD officer and Navy Reserve officer—got married yesterday. He arranged 100 Uber vouchers so guests could get home safely after the reception. Validity window: 9:30 PM Saturday to 12:30 AM Sunday.
Only 6 of 100 vouchers worked.
Uber Support offered no usable fix. Almost everyone paid out of pocket. A few people had no backup and family members had to leave the reception to retrieve them.
The room included many members of the NYPD and guests from all four branches of the U.S. military. These are people who plan, show up, and expect systems to work when they say they will.
A product sold for events—especially one meant to get first responders and service members home safely—should not fail at a 94% rate with no recovery.
This is not a small glitch. It is a broken promise at the exact moment people needed the service most.
Respectfully requesting that someone with authority look at this event, make the guests whole, and explain what failed so it does not happen to the next wedding, fundraiser, or shift change.

text:
Celebrating India’s Growth Story | Ep. 3 - Mukesh Ambani

On 1 September 2016, at a Reliance AGM, voice on a phone network became free.

Not cheaper. Free. Data thrown in on a welcome offer that made every other operator rewrite the tariff board. Within a year India went from a back-marker in mobile broadband use to the country that eats the most of it. That is not a branding line. That is what happened to the network in your pocket.

Mukesh Ambani did not invent the mobile phone. He spent a decade and a brutal amount of capital building a 4G-only network, missed dates, and then used price as a weapon. The idea, he has said, sat in the house first: Isha home from Yale, internet at home was bad, Akash talking about a world where voice would not be the product.

Before that, he was the son who actually poured Jamnagar.

Born 19 April 1957 in Aden. Dhirubhai’s elder son. Chemical engineering at the Institute of Chemical Technology, a short Stanford MBA, then home to build plants. The split with Anil in 2005 left him with the refining and petrochemical machine. Anil took the first telecom bet, and it did not become Jio. Mukesh came back to the sector later and did.

What the file actually contains:
1. Jamnagar is the unfashionable masterpiece. Late-90s grassroots refinery, then doubled, until one site was among the largest integrated refining-and-petrochem complexes on earth. That cash built the later bets. No Jamnagar, no Jio war chest.
2. He is an operator more than a pitchman. Dhirubhai was the market. Mukesh was the project. People still get that backwards.
3. Jio was a price shock sitting on a greenfield network. Free voice. Cheap data. A stack of apps. Rivals merged or shrank. Users did not ask permission from the old ARPU religion.
4. Retail is the quiet third leg. Thousands of stores, JioMart, a distribution machine that looks boring until you need it in a tier-2 town.
5. The house is not a morality play you can finish in one tweet. Political access, spectrum, and scale are part of Indian telecom. So is the fact that a 4G data plan stopped being a luxury good. You can hold both.

We love a founder who “disrupts.” We get shy when the disruptor already owns a refinery. That shyness is not analysis. Jio used hydrocarbon cash to subsidise a digital habit for a country that could not have paid US prices for data. That transfer is the growth story.

Settled: Jamnagar made Reliance a global energy node. Settled: 2016 repriced Indian internet. 
Not settled: that this is only genius, or only capture. A network that large is always both.

If your India story starts at a startup dinner in 2018, you are standing on a tower someone else paid for.

Next episode tomorrow, 9 PM.

text:
So days after Prime Minister Mark Carney denied a Wall Street Journal report that Canada was exploring becoming an “associate member” of the European Union, EU President Ursula von der Leyen invites Canada to become its first “associate member.”

Once again, as occurred with the Gordie Howe Bridge controversy, American media — in that case, it was Bloomberg — seem to know more about what’s going on inside the Carney government than Canadian media.

They reported, based on what Carney and Canadian officials were saying, that contrary to the WSJ report, Canada was not seeking associate membership with the EU, but a “unique alliance.”

But whatever it’s called, nobody knows what it means.
That includes Canada’s Parliament, which doesn’t return from its summer break until Monday.

Meanwhile, Carney has been making trade deals in Canada and abroad — many of them offering Canadian taxpayers’ money to “catalyze” private investments — with few details provided to date.

A key concern is how this new trade deal with the EU, if it happens and whatever it’s called, will impact Canadian sovereignty on the issue of trade.

In that context, one of the reasons Carney said he called off trade negotiations with the U.S. was that the Americans wanted control of Canada’s trade deals with other countries.

In that context, full EU members do not negotiate individual trade deals with non-EU countries such as the U.S. Rather, the EU negotiates with them on behalf of its 27 member countries.

Canada already has a free trade deal with the EU known as the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) which in practical terms is in effect, even though only 17 of its members have fully ratified it.

In the wake of von der Leyen’s offer to “dear Mark”, as she referred to Carney in her speech, some EU representatives said they were blindsided by the proposal and concerned the term “associate member” has no legal definition within the EU.

They also expressed concerns about any special deals made for Canada on trade that could negatively impact trade in their own countries.
Given that many of Carney’s trade and investment decisions will involve the use of taxpayers’ money to prime the pump, they have a right to know what they’re paying for.

text:
A friend of mine came home late one night and everyone in the house was already asleep. The next morning she went to wake her 19-year-old son for work, opened his bedroom door and found his 18-year-old girlfriend asleep in there with him.

She immediately closed the door and stood in the hallway trying to decide how to handle it. They’d been dating for a while, they were both adults, and she didn’t want to turn breakfast into some giant interrogation. So when they eventually came downstairs, she acted completely normal. She offered the girl coffee, asked if she wanted something to eat and basically tried to make the whole situation as unremarkable as possible.

The girlfriend looked absolutely mortified. She kept apologizing and wouldn’t accept anything. Apparently they’d fallen asleep and hadn’t planned on spending the night. Eventually her son drove her home.

Then he came back and was furious with his mother.

Not because she’d found them. Because she’d been TOO casual about it.

Apparently the girlfriend left convinced that his mother hadn’t even been surprised to find her there, which made her assume her boyfriend regularly had girls sleeping over.

His mother was trying so hard not to embarrass them that she accidentally made her son look like a complete menace.

text:
Trump's Top 25 Achievements:
- Rod D. Martin

Donald Trump doesn't have an accomplishment problem. Republicans have an information problem. Each of us must change that.

With the midterms coming, an astonishing number of Republican voters cannot name three things President Trump has accomplished. Which is remarkable, considering Donald Trump has accomplished more in a year and a half than any other president ever did in four.

Indeed, he has accomplished so much, so fast, across so many fronts that most people cannot keep up. The Enemedia buries the victories, while Republicans do an abysmal job of explaining them.

So here is the cheat sheet. It barely scratches the surface. And yet every item here is a game-changer, and your befuddled black-pilling friends need to know it.

This is not a list of promises. It's a list of laws enacted, cases won, policies implemented, agreements secured, and measurable results.

You don't have to memorize all 25. Learn five. And when somebody says Trump "hasn't done much," show them the receipts.
Trump Restored American Safety and Sovereignty

1. He made the border a real border again.
In months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, "Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.

2. He reversed mass migration.
America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest "self-deported.”

Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President's innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegal aliens to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.

3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegal aliens arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.

Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.

4. History's biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.
According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent; robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.

This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America's poorest.
Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle

5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.

Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.

6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the "one" was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump's entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.

Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama's 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam's vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans' freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.

7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That's nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump's America.

No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it's just getting started.

8. He made "reshoring" and "reindustrialization" real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery driving the boom.

9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.

10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world's largest energy importer — "exporting" $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.

Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.

11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.

Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.
Trump Made Elections Matter Again

12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated "States' independent" agencies from voters' control.

Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the "Deep State".

Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.

13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse.
In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that's exactly what they've done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.

In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy's favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.

14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.

Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?

15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.

What's more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees "worked" from home. The Trump Administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, "you can work from the office, or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”

16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that "fighting discrimination" requires the federal government to discriminate.
He Defended Faith and Family

17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump appointed the judges who overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.

Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden's weaponized Justice Department.

He's also done everything within the Executive Branch's power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.

No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.

18. He got men out of women's sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.

Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women's sports and ruin girls' lives, Trump's Administration protects women and girls again.

19. He enacted America's first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President's One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America's first nationwide school-choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.

That's on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America's future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn firsthand about free markets and future orientation.

20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.
He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First

21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old 2 percent of GDP spending target with an enormous 5 percent by 2035.

Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner, not a dependent.

22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.
China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro's Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.

Beijing's planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.

23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months.
In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. No other President has matched this record.

24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.
Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.

Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more coming once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.

25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.
After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America's atrophied industrial base.

Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they're showing up en masse.
Now, Act As It Matters

Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they're just the top 25: I could give you hundreds more.
