text:
THE DIGITAL DAILY LEDGER
A Truthwright Review

September 20, 2026

They trained neighbors to watch the immigration police. Then they sent them to watch the vote.

When the watcher becomes the faction
By Craig Drelas

    January, a Minneapolis street. A woman in ordinary clothes holds up a phone. She has been told to keep her distance, say little, film the officers, and warn the block if a raid is moving. She may be a mother. She may be retired. Reporters who rode with these crews said the rooms were full of both—people who, in another year, would have been pouring coffee at a precinct (Rosales, 2026). That is ICE watch: civilians tracking the federal immigration police.

    September, a training room. Some of the same networks are handed a different packet. The subject is no longer a raid. It is a polling place. The job title has changed to election monitor. Early voting has already opened in parts of the country. Minnesota, one of the two named pilots, began on September 18. Election Day is November 3.

One person. Two offices. That is the story.

    Natalie Winters, a White House correspondent, found the sentence that makes the story undeniable. On May 19, Movement Voter Fund—a group that raises money and sends it to local organizations—published a plan for the 2026 midterms. Midterms are the vote in which Americans choose the national legislature: all of the House of Representatives and one-third of the Senate. States, not Washington, run the polls. The plan’s training line is plain: “training ICE watch volunteers to be election monitors—like we are seeing in Minneapolis and North Carolina.” Winters published it. It is not a rumor. It is their language (Winters, 2026; Movement Voter Fund, 2026a).

Two jobs that are not the same

    Natalie Winters, a White House correspondent, found the sentence that makes the story undeniable. On May 19, Movement Voter Fund—a group that raises money and sends it to local organizations—published a plan for the 2026 midterms. Midterms are the vote in which Americans choose the national legislature: all of the House of Representatives and one-third of the Senate. States, not Washington, run the polls. The plan’s training line is plain: “training ICE watch volunteers to be election monitors—like we are seeing in Minneapolis and North Carolina.” Winters published it. It is not a rumor. It is their language (Winters, 2026; Movement Voter Fund, 2026a).

    An ICE watcher follows officers, records them, warns neighbors, and sometimes helps lawyers build a file. A poll watcher is a person state law allows to stand near the casting and counting of ballots. In some states that person may be inside the room; in others, only near it. The law of the state decides the doorway. The work, if it is honest, is dull: watch the clock, watch the scanner, watch that every lawful ballot is treated like every other. You do not campaign. You do not instruct the clerk. You do not decide whether the result was “honored.” You watch whether the rules were followed.

    Those offices can exist in the same country. They cannot be treated as the same training course without changing what “monitor” means.

The field test is not theoretical

    Two weeks before the May 19 pitch, Movement Voter Project wrote the strategy in the open: turn networks built to answer immigration raids into networks “to protect our democracy.” In April, Unidos MN trained 700 of its MONARCA observers—people raised for raid response—on “democracy defense,” and offered the model to other cities (Movement Voter Project, 2026).

    Minnesota’s Democratic Party chair told Axios the party itself had trained 10,000 “constitutional observers” during the winter enforcement surge. Other groups, he said, trained another 60,000. That pool was to be retooled as door-knockers and “poll protectors” (Van Oot, 2026).

    North Carolina is the second named pilot. Siembra NC organizer Andreina Malki said the group had trained more than 5,000 ICE watchers statewide (News & Observer, 2026). A federal complaint filed September 10 describes Common Cause there pairing with immigrant-rights groups to recruit verifiers, widen poll presence, set up “safe sites” near voting places, and point monitors toward locations where immigration officers would cause the most fear (Complaint, 2026). North Carolina’s in-person early voting does not open until October 15; absentee ballots began moving on September 4 (North Carolina State Board of Elections, 2026).

    Training is happening now. The vote is not a winter problem. In Minnesota, it has already begun. The money sits in the background on purpose. Movement Voter Fund still sends much of its charitable cash through Tides Foundation—a legal mailbox. Donors write a check to a fund; the public sees a neighbor in a vest. The conversion of street watchers is one line, $450,000, inside a program of several million dollars for turnout and for “securing” results (Movement Voter Fund, 2026a, n.d.). The training partners named in the pitch are Freedom Trainers, the Horizons Project, and States at the Core. Their paperwork runs through other mailboxes: Community Change, New Venture Fund, Hopewell Fund. Horizons traces back in part to philanthropy tied to Pam Omidyar, whose fortune began with eBay (Winters, 2026). None of that is a crime. It is distance. Distance is how a doctrine arrives without a face.

The world already wrote the rule

    Every serious election-observation system on earth draws one line: the observer may watch; the observer may not join the fight.

  In 2005, at the United Nations, governments and groups including the Carter Center issued a code now used by European Union missions and by the OSCE’s election office. Observers must “maintain strict political impartiality at all times.” They must not do anything that could reasonably look like partisan gain (United Nations Electoral Assistance Division et al., 2005). That is the rule the world wrote down, in one sentence. American rules are messier—each state writes its own—but even a congressional observer sent by Washington is barred from advocating for a candidate or interfering with the count (52 U.S.C. § 21083a).

    A person trained first to shadow police is not, by that training, an impartial observer. Merging the jobs may not break a statute. It breaks the office. One job treats the state as an adversary to document. The other treats the count as a public trust that has to survive the adversary.

    Readers who have watched “citizen observation” captured by a ruling party, an opposition machine, or a well-funded civic brand will not need the point explained twice. The vest is local. The curriculum travels.

What the packet does after the last ballot

   Freedom Trainers teaches “pillars of support” and mass noncooperation, with lessons from Serbia, Chile, Poland, and the Philippines (Freedom Trainers, n.d.). The Serbian chapter is Otpor: students who helped push Slobodan Milošević from power in 2000, then taught the method abroad. The American scholar Gene Sharp had catalogued the tools—strikes, boycotts, withdrawal of consent—long before that. Later research found that, against authoritarian regimes, disciplined nonviolent campaigns often beat armed ones (Sharp, 1973; Chenoweth & Stephan, 2011).

   That history is real. It is also the wrong filing cabinet. Tools built to make a dictatorship unworkable are being labeled “election protection” in a country that still certifies results through local officials who add the totals and sign that they are done, then through courts and legislatures. The People’s Election Playbook puts the filing error in order. First the ordinary work: register, vote early, staff Election Day, watch the count. Then Stage 6. If “election results are not honored,” leave work, leave school, stop shopping. The packet points to Indivisible and May Day Strong and calls this “the escalation tool of last resort” (Freedom Trainers, 2026).

    Who decides that a result was not “honored”? In law: a court, a recount statute, a legislature acting under the Constitution. In the packet: the movement. This is not a thought experiment. On May 1 those same networks ran a national day of no work, no school, no shopping, and called it a test of the muscle (Helmore, 2026; Levin, 2026; Hunter, 2026). Vote. Count. Certify. Or walk out. That is the ladder they published. Certification is a legal act. “Honored” is a faction’s verdict. When a training packet lets the second word overrule the first, observation has ended.

The other table

    Organizers are not inventing the fear from nothing. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said ICE will not patrol polling places, and will appear only for a specific threat or to serve a warrant already in motion (Bazail-Eimil, 2026). Civil-rights groups and some lawmakers say even that possibility keeps eligible people home, and they point to an old federal statute against stationing armed force at the polls except to stop an armed attack (18 U.S.C. § 592; Ingram, 2026). Courts will decide that fight.

    Take their fear as sincerely as it is offered. It still does not turn a faction into an observer. A first-time voter, eighteen and new to the booth, needs a clerk who is boring. A poll worker of sixty-eight needs a room that stays a room, not a second front. A father who only wants the totals to close needs the same rule applied to every vest. Fear of the state does not cancel the world’s rule: watch; do not become a party to the fight.

     This brief does not say parties may not appoint watchers. They have for a century. It does not say filming police is a crime. It does not say the foundations are illegal. It says a public count cannot be staffed as a continuation of street doctrine. Winters found the conversion in writing. Minnesota and North Carolina are the pilot. The playbook is the doctrine after the last ballot. The 2005 observer code is why a serious country would refuse the merger.

     The method would be just as illegitimate if a nationalist street cadre printed a Stage 6 of its own.

November 3, then Monday

    The clock is short. Minnesotans are already voting. North Carolinians may vote absentee now and in person beginning October 15. The rest of the country follows, then Election Day on November 3. After that, local boards add the numbers and sign. That signature is the promise: lawful work at the booth will still count tomorrow.

    An election is not a mood. It is a book. If the people standing over the book were recruited from a rapid-response war against the same government that must certify the result, the promise is already under strain. Vote as you wish. Do not confuse a training manual with the law of the count.

     Read Winters. Read the May 19 plan. Read the playbook. Read the 2005 United Nations observer code. Then call the office that runs elections where you live and ask two questions: who accredits the watchers, and what training did they take?

Final thoughts

    Do not let “honored” replace “certified.”Question everything until the books prove otherwise. “The friend of popular governments never finds himself so much alarmed for their character and fate, as when he contemplates their propensity to this dangerous vice.” Madison was naming faction: several citizens, united by passion or interest, adverse to the rights of other citizens or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community (The Federalist No. 10). He did not say factions would vanish. He said a republic must so arrange its offices that no faction is allowed to become the count.

    The Constitution does not leave that arrangement to a training packet. Times, places, and manner of congressional elections are given to the state legislatures in the first instance, subject to Congress (U.S. Const. art. I, § 4). The people choose. Officers of the states administer. The courts hear contests. Each house of Congress is “the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members” (art. I, § 5). Nowhere in that chain is a movement licensed to decide whether a result has been “honored,” and then to withdraw from work, school, and commerce until the books agree with the movement. That is not review. It is a second sovereignty applying for a job this Constitution does not advertise.

    Washington, leaving office, put the same thought in a plainer tense. The people have a right to alter their Constitutions of government. “But the Constitution which at any time exists, till changed by an explicit and authentic act of the whole people, is sacredly obligatory upon all” (Washington, 1796). An explicit and authentic act is an amendment, a statute, a judgment. It is not Stage 6.

    A promise is not a mood. Locke called political power a trust: it is held for a purpose, and it is forfeited only by a breach the community may prove, not by a curriculum that declares the breach in advance (Second Treatise, chs. 11, 19). What cannot be willed as public law cannot be dressed as civic virtue. An observer who has already chosen sides is not observing. He is campaigning under a borrowed title.

    Law is less lyrical and more exact. A congressional observer may not advocate or interfere with the count (52 U.S.C. § 21083a). State watcher statutes, however they differ at the doorway, assume presence without command. None of these texts answers every fear now in circulation. All of them answer the question this brief has been asking: who may stand over the book, and by what warrant? Juvenal’s line—Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?—is not a slogan against police. It is a warning against any watcher who will not himself be bound.

   Madison, on money, wrote that the ways and means ought always to face the public engagements. The franchise is an engagement of the same kind. Work at the booth today must still purchase a lawful result tomorrow. Credit unused is weakness. Credit abused is bondage. A watcher unused is a vacant chair. A watcher who arrives from a rapid-response war against the certifying government, carrying a sixth stage in his packet, is bondage dressed as protection.

Look at the document first.
Then look at the two offices.
Then look at the two states.
Then look at the code the world wrote down.
Then look at Stage 6.
Then look at Article I. That is the only honest order.

    The question in September 2026 is not whether one party is holy. The question is whether the dull machine of self-government—registration, the clerk, the signed return—is still compounding faster than the factions that would consume it. Markets are not oracles. Governments are not gods. Training manuals are not constitutions. They are instruments.

Keep the house. Demand the books.

text:
I am incredibly excited and humbled to share with you all that I have finally rented a dedicated physical space for our independent grassroots book club.

It feels completely surreal because just a year ago, the formal idea of running a physical reading hub had never even crossed my mind. 
The entire movement started organically during my regular, quiet evening walks where I routinely made it a conscious habit to strike up conversations with everyday Nigerians that I stumbled upon streets. 
During these informal encounters, we would analyze breaking political events, debate government decisions, exchange contact information, and I would encourage them to message me directly on WhatsApp whenever a confusing national development required deep systemic explanation. 

Initially, I did not create a generalized group chat for them. The individuals I met did not know each other, operated in complete isolation, and did not even know me by my real name. But one deeply disturbing, recurring pattern emerged across all my conversations that forced me to call a general assembly to unite them under one roof. I noticed that every single one of these youths harbored an identical, deeply entrenched, and internalized racist belief that "the Black man is inherently wicked, cursed, and evil." While this self-hating sentiment is completely irrational and absurd (considering that they themselves are Black and are neither wicked nor evil), I could completely understand the psychological trauma driving this delusion. The sheer scale of systemic corruption, institutional looting, and state cruelty in Nigeria is so astronomical, violent, and vomit-inducing that an uneducated citizen has virtually no other way to emotionally explain their daily suffering without concluding that the Black race is biologically defective. 

Over 180,000 innocent people die every single year in Nigeria from easily preventable malaria. A standard pack of basic Amartem softgel capsules used to treat uncomplicated malaria costs around ₦3,000 to ₦4,000 (roughly $2 to $2.50). On paper, this sounds like pocket change, until you remember that over 65% of the Nigerian population, more than 133 million human beings, is actively condemned to survive in extreme, multidimensional poverty, meaning that buying a basic blister pack of antimalarials is an impossible financial luxury. 

If the infection degenerates into severe cerebral malaria, oral pills no longer work, and you are forced to purchase injectable Artesunate, hospital drips, and so on, which is easily 5-10 times more expensive. How can anyone logically explain why malaria treatments are not 100% free in an oil-producing nation that generates billions of dollars in petroleum revenue? The Nigerian political establishment has spent billions of dollars in scarce foreign currency purchasing military-grade cyber-surveillance software, phone-hacking tools, and spyware packages from American and Israeli defense contractors, strictly to track phone calls, monitor citizens, and violently suppress political dissent. Yet, they flatly refuse to spend that same money to subsidize and distribute life-saving medicine for an endemic disease that slaughters nearly 200,000 of their own citizens every single year. When you add this daily medical tragedy to the wanton looting of public funds, collapsed roads, and starving communities, I completely understood why these desperate youths felt that the leaders of their own race must be inherently evil. 

However, as emotionally comforting and popular as this "wicked Black man" conclusion may seem, it completely fails to explain why corruption actually exists. So, for the very first time, I gathered all the scattered youths I had been quietly mentoring and educating in isolation, and we held our inaugural general meeting sitting together on the grass of an open community field. 

I stood before them and methodically explained why systemic corruption thrives in Nigeria, proving that it is a direct consequence of institutional collapse rather than a genetic defect of the Black race. To break this down, I introduced them to the foundational political philosophy of Thomas Hobbes in his 1651 masterpiece, "Leviathan." 

I began by explaining how human society functions in a baseline societal setting. 
Hobbes argued that before the establishment of a formal, civilized government, humanity existed in an ungoverned, pre-political condition called the "State of Nature." In this state of nature, there are no established laws, no public courts, no property protections, no police forces, and no collective security. Because every individual is driven by raw self-preservation and competing for scarce resources, human life inevitably degenerates into a perpetual, terrifying "war of all against all", where existence is famously solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. To escape this violent anarchy, rational human beings collectively enter into a profound "Social Contract": they voluntarily surrender their individual monopoly on violence and submit to a supreme, all-powerful sovereign authority known as the "Leviathan", the state. In return, the Leviathan is contractually obligated to maintain absolute law and order, protect citizen lives, enforce justice, build public infrastructure, and guarantee collective survival. 

Once they understood this societal model, I brought the analysis straight home to Nigeria: what happens when the state completely fails to act as a functional Leviathan? 
The Nigerian state has broken its end of the social contract. Its public institutions are frail, compromised, corrupt, and structurally extractive, completely failing to guarantee basic healthcare, clean water, quality education, reliable electricity, stable pensions, or physical security. When the state institutions are this catastrophically weak, society is violently dragged right back into a modern, dog-eat-dog State of Nature. In this artificial jungle, systemic corruption and wanton looting are not born out of genetic "Black wickedness".
 Because there is no functional state to catch you if you fall, both the political class and the everyday citizen operate in a state of perpetual panic, knowing that if they do not aggressively grab, hoard, loot, and privatize public resources today, the state will abandon them and their families to starve to death tomorrow. 

This Hobbesian dynamic also perfectly explains why Nigerian politicians shamelessly, perpetually cross carpet to defect to whatever ruling party happens to occupy Aso Rock at any given moment. These politicians fully know, see, and understand that the Nigerian state is not an impartial, constitutional arbiter governed by the rule of law. They know that our judicial systems, regulatory agencies, and anti-graft bodies are weaponized instruments of coercion. In such an unjust environment, surviving in the political opposition leaves your business vulnerable to sudden state crackdowns, selective EFCC investigations, frozen bank accounts, and revoked government licenses. To survive politically, protect their looted assets, and advance their careers, these politicians perform their own grotesque version of the Hobbesian contract: they abandon their political parties, swallow their shame, and completely surrender their loyalty to the supreme Leviathan sitting in Abuja in exchange for federal protection and continuous access to the national treasury. 

After that lengthy philosophical lecture(which was much more detailed and consumed 1hr30mins), I was deeply moved by their remarkable level of comprehension, intellectual hunger, and profound appreciation. Every single one of those young men confessed that this materialist, institutional model was infinitely more accurate and logical than the cheap tribal and racial myths they had been taught. This breakthrough brought a deep sense of accomplishment to my heart, but more importantly, it permanently shattered the elite lie that the average Nigerian is stupid or incapable of deep thought. The average Nigerian is exceptionally brilliant, hungry for truth, and genuinely loves learning; the tragedy is that he is perpetually, maliciously fed intellectual poison by a colonial educational curriculum and a compromised corporate media apparatus. 

What our people desperately need are the critical analytical tools to dissect their own material reality. To this end, whenever our study group meets, instead of gossiping about politicians, or engaging in surface-level banter, we rigorously study the political philosophy of Plato, examine how human societies organize, and dissect the underlying mechanics of how the state actually functions. 
I constantly train them never to fall into the childish, emotional trap of merely insulting Nigerian politicians. The ruling politicians are obviously as guilty as charged, but if you continuously think in terms of "bad people" instead of "extractive systems," you will perpetually fall into the naive delusion of believing that once you replace one corrupt politician with another, everything will magically be fixed. Throughout the tragic history of Nigeria, we have witnessed bad leaders removed, military dictators overthrown, and corrupt politicians voted out countless times, yet the country keeps violently reverting to its default settings of economic plunder and resource extraction, simply because the underlying neocolonial system was left completely untouched. 

So, I made it crystal clear to them that our newly rented book club is absolutely not a political clubhouse where people gather to emotionally insult Tinubu or blindly campaign for Peter Obi. 
It is strictly, unapologetically engineered to be an intellectual fortress of mass political enlightenment. Our primary, non-negotiable mission is to decolonize the mind, equip the youth with systems thinking, teach them to critically analyze their geopolitical environment, and build the intellectual acumen necessary to spearhead the greater African Revolution to rescue our continent from the parasitic clutches of global imperialism. 

If you are interested in actively supporting this organic, grassroots movement, we would deeply appreciate your solidarity. Physical books and academic manuscripts are what we desperately, urgently need right now. If you possess the financial means to purchase, order, and ship classic literature, political economy texts, and philosophy volumes, please kindly indicate in the comments or direct messages, and I will personally reach out to provide our delivery address. 

If voluntary financial contributions are what you are able to offer, your support will be immensely appreciated and transparently deployed. Every single kobo will be put to direct use toward fully equipping our physical learning facility with durable wooden bookshelves, comfortable study chairs,high-resolution projector screens, and reliable solar-powered backup generators to ensure uninterrupted power supply. 

Thank you for reading!

text:
A Peshmerga Fighter and his Bulletproof BMW.
A small army of ISIS militants launched their coordinated attack on Kirkuk on the morning of October 21st, 2014. In the opening stages of the battle, over 100 civilians and Peshmerga security forces were killed or severely wounded. Many more people were left trapped due to the indiscriminate firing carried out by ISIS.
Abdulrahman refused to sit idly and let this happen and, like many Kurds, decided to leave his wife and four children to head to the frontline and take ISIS head-on. To do this, he knew he needed protection. At a car auction in Kirkuk, he handed over $10,000 for a bulletproof BMW from the early 1990s. At the time, Ako Abdulrahman didn’t realize that the vehicle would end up saving the lives of dozens of people.
To assist the trapped civilians and security forces, Abdulrahman drove his armoured BMW through the besieged city, returning again and again to collect the injured, as ISIS fanatics sprayed the vehicle with assault rifle rounds and narrowly missed it with RPGs.
Despite bullets bouncing off the bulletproof windshield and almost killing him, overall, he had saved over 70 people from being killed by ISIS as well as retrieving the bodies of many of those who had died.
The heroic actions of the Peshmerga fighter were summed up in a poignant and refreshing statement that offered a glimpse of hope in an Iraq torn apart by sectarian violence: “In my car, I carried Sunni, Shiite, Kurds, Turkmen, and Christians. I felt like I was truly Iraq, and this is who everyone should be”
The actions of Abdulrahman were not only recognized in Iraq. BMW heard the story of the heroic Peshmerga fighter and his bulletproof car and offered him a brand-new BMW model in exchange for his trusty, bullet-riddled 1990s version, which they wanted to display at the BMW headquarters in Munich. But Ako was not interested. Instead, he chose to repair his battlefield-tested car so he could keep using it.

text:
Ralph Manley, 101st Airborne Division veteran at the grave of his twin brother Roland in Springfield National Cemetery. The two enlisted together halfway through their final year of high school in Springfield, Missouri, but the Army wouldn't allow twins to serve in the same division, so Roland was sent to the 82nd Airborne while Ralph went to the 101st.

Roland never made it to the invasion his brother would later fight in. He was killed in July 1943 during the invasion of Sicily, his plane shot down over the Mediterranean. The Army offered to send Ralph home after his brother's death. He chose to stay in.

Ralph went on to jump into Normandy on D-Day, June 6, 1944, and fought again that September during the invasion of the Netherlands. Over his service he earned two Bronze Stars, five Purple Hearts, and a Presidential Unit Citation. He died in 2019 at 95 years old, and is buried in Springfield's Hazelwood Cemetery.

A photo widely shared online has often misdated this moment to D-Day itself and misspelled the family name, but the real story is no less powerful for the correction, one twin who came home from the war, kneeling at the grave of the one who never got the chance to fight beside him. Lest We Forget.

text:
The Valley View estate at 1801 Foxhall Road NW in Washington, D.C., was a prominent 17-acre property.  

History & Architecture
 Origins: Built in 1935–1936 by Elinor Morse Ryan Brady, granddaughter of Wall Street financier Thomas Fortune Ryan. She commissioned renowned architect William Lawrence Bottomley to design a ~13,000-square-foot Georgian-style mansion featuring over 25 rooms.  
 High-Profile Tenants: Because Elinor travels frequently with her husband, Rear Admiral Parke Howell Brady, the family leased the estate to prominent figures. Notable residents included cereal heiress Marjorie Merriweather Post (who housed her Fabergé collection there), financier Richard King Mellon, and former Secretary of War Dwight F. Davis.  
Sale & Demolition
 Later Ownership: After Elinor Brady passed away in 1993, the estate was sold and eventually acquired by philanthropist Betty Brown Casey (Mrs. Eugene B. Casey) in 2001.

text:
**AM I WRONG FOR WHAT I DID? 👀**

My cousin came over last weekend and asked if she could borrow a few things from my pantry because she was “running low.”

I told her, “Sure, take whatever you need.”

I didn’t think much of it.

About ten minutes later, I walked into the kitchen and found her filling a large shopping bag. 😳

She had flour, rice, cooking oil, sugar, spices, canned food… basically half my pantry.

I stared at her and said, “Uh… what are you doing?”

She looked confused.

“You said I could take whatever I need.”

I said, “I meant a few things. Not enough groceries to survive the apocalypse.” 😂

She immediately got offended.

She said I was being selfish and that I clearly “didn’t mean it” when I offered to help.

I told her she could take a reasonable amount, but I wasn’t giving away a month’s worth of groceries.

She dropped the bag on the counter and said, “Forget it. I don’t need anything from you.”

Then she left.

Later that evening, my aunt called me and said my cousin was telling everyone that I had embarrassed her over “a few groceries.”

Apparently, she thought because I said **“take whatever you need,”** she was allowed to take whatever she wanted.

Now some of my family thinks I should have just let her take it.

But honestly…

If someone tells you to take what you need, do you really take enough to empty their pantry?

**Am I wrong? 👀**

text:
For those who don't pay close enough attention to the daily shenanighans... oops, sorry, 'activities' of Colorado's Attorney General's office, I would offer the following link to an article in last Thursday's Complete Colorado. 

In it, the author brings home the point that not only is Philby (slur intentional on my part) Weiser a hypocrite (after all he is both a 'modern' Democrat and an elected politician - 2/3'ds of the trifecta required for Dante's 9th circle of hell) but is also intentionally seeking YOUR personal information specifically in regards to groups and positions that he opposes.

Now, don't get me wrong - if the AG is seeking to root out corruption, fraud, abuse, true criminal behavior then I understand investigating and looking for evidence. But these 'demands' (a purely legal term, I assure you) for overreaching access to individual's non-public information (if it was public, Philby would already have it) are not for those heinous purposes listed above. No, it is to provide a 'defense' on behalf of the state of newly passed laws. Granted, this is the AG's job. However, challenging actions, laws and Executive Orders in court is part of what makes our system work - as Philby likes to point out on the CO AG website (not his 'main' campaign site). But part of Weiser's lawsuits are based on decrying government 'overreach' for seeking access to state maintained data - a point which, while being debated, raises the spectre of the core issue: what is public and what is private? When data is collected by the government, regardless of level and that collection and maintenance of that data is paid for by resident's tax dollars, one can make a logical (if not legal) cae that the data should be 'public' meaning protected but not hidden. Yet by Philby's seeking specific individual data concerning private organization's data, paid for by individuals who make voluntary contributions or payments (vs the mandated taxes and 'fees' of the state), that data should be considered 'private' and held to a stricter standard for disclosure.

But the bottom line, regardless of whether the data should be shared or not, is that Philby doesn't mind speaking out of both sides of his mouth.

To close out this rant, I will simply state that we have a mess on our hands here in Colorado this election cycle. This is not a breaking news flash. And, like the Complete Colorado article that admits the probability that we will see Governor Philby sworn in next year, I too am not optimistic about how this election will go. But, regardless of who sits in the Governor's Mansion come next January, we - the public, the taxpayers and the citizens of Colorado - MUST call out this blatant double dealing by our elected officials.

Here's the article for those who care and who have not seen it: https://t.co/2vXuUbfubb

text:
For centuries, in the service of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, the scarlet cord would miraculously turn white as a sign of purification: that which was red had to become white, a powerful image of the atonement for sin. But the Talmud records something profoundly significant: during the forty years preceding the destruction of the Second Temple, the cord stopped turning white. Scripture had already announced this image: “though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18). From a Messianic perspective, this event takes on an extraordinary prophetic weight, as it coincides with the year Yeshua gave His life. This sign points to a greater reality: the atonement that the sacrifices foreshadowed was reaching its definitive fulfillment.

For bulls and goats could point toward atonement, but they could not accomplish it eternally. Yom Kippur was a shadow; Yeshua is the fulfillment. He entered not with the blood of others, but by laying down His own life; not to repeat the sacrifice year after year, but to offer Himself once and for all. The scarlet cord reminds us that sin demands atonement, but the blood of the Messiah proclaims that the price has been paid. The blood that could not be replaced by rituals found its fulfillment in the Lamb. Blessed be Yeshua HaMashiach, our High Priest and our perfect sacrifice: by His blood we are cleansed, by His death we have life, and by His renewed covenant we have hope in YeHoVah, the God of Israel. To Him be all the glory, forever and ever!

text:
The honest case against Wheaton — the one the bulls don't post.

Heavy reliance on a few core assets. A finite pipeline of new projects.

Those two facts mean production growth is not guaranteed — especially if metal demand weakens, or if regulations raise costs at the partner mines Wheaton depends on.

Concentration is the flip side of quality. The same discipline that keeps 80%+ of production in bottom-half-cost mines also means the portfolio isn't broad. Antamina alone delivered 2.3 million attributable silver ounces in Q2. If BHP has a bad year there, Wheaton feels it directly.

And every stream has a term. When they expire or step down, Wheaton needs new deals — at whatever prices are on offer then.

Record margins. Real concentration. Both true.

text:
Why Memphis is quietly the ultimate hard-engineering capital for multi-gigawatt compute
​Most people think xAI chose Memphis simply for available industrial footprint and fast TVA grid hookups. But sitting directly beneath Elon’s Airstream is a geological and industrial convergence that feels like it was designed by a first-principles engineer.
​Beyond the fast permit timelines and warehouse space, here are three high-velocity engineering advantages in Memphis that make it uniquely suited for scaling AI infrastructure:
​1. The 100-Trillion-Gallon Geothermal Heat Sink
Memphis sits on top of the Memphis Sand Aquifer a massive subterranean reservoir holding tens of trillions of gallons of pristine water filtered through 500 feet of natural quartz sand. It sits at a constant year-round temperature of ~62°F (16.7°C). For next-generation GB200 and GB300 liquid-cooled GPU clusters running at gigawatt thermal density, this geological setup offers an unprecedented natural thermal advantage. Closed-loop geothermal heat exchangers tapped into this region provide steady-state cooling delta-Ts that standard atmospheric chillers can’t touch during humid Southern summers. The main reason Memphis has the cleanest water in America . Our water even taste good .
​2. The Electrical Steel Engine Next Door
The biggest bottleneck to scaling multi-gigawatt data centers isn’t GPUs it’s transformers, switchgear, and grid inductors. Just up the Mississippi River in Mississippi County Arkansas  sits the heaviest concentration of advanced steel production in North America (including Big River Steel). They manufacture the high-permeability grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) that forms the literal cores of the massive step-down transformers and Megapack components feeding Colossus. The raw material supply chain for the entire grid expansion is effectively in the backyard.  The place is massive.
​3. High-Throughput "Velocity" Culture
Building a supercomputer campus in 122 days requires a local labor pool conditioned for high-speed logistics. Because Memphis hosts the world’s largest cargo sorting hub (the FedEx Superhub, which cycles millions of packages through a 4-hour nightly window), the local industrial ecosystem operates on high-throughput, zero-latency execution. Moving 720+ Megapacks and hundreds of thousands of GPUs into position overnight isn't an anomaly here—it matches the city's operational rhythm.  
​Silicon Valley supplies the code, but the Mid-South provides the raw physics, high-grade metallurgy, and thermal capacity required to run it at scale.

text:
Caravaggio’s famous 1596 oil painting Bacchus was removed from the Uffizi Gallery in Florence after a flash flood leaked rainwater directly onto its protective glass case... 

Flash flooding sent rainwater cascading over Caravaggio’s Bacchus at the Uffizi Gallery in Florence 🇮🇹. A sudden downpour caused a window to leak, flooding the protective glass case housing the painting, one of the museum’s most significant holdings. The painting was removed from display as a precaution shortly afterwards, though museum officials said it sustained no actual damage.

The storm hit the Tuscan city in the early afternoon, dumping nearly two inches of rain in a single hour, the type of sudden, torrential burst that tends to overwhelm even well-maintained infrastructure. Footage shared online from inside the gallery shows water streaming steadily from a window directly above the painting, running down over the glass case protecting it. Six other works hanging in same room of 17th-century art were apparently untouched by the leak, which remained confined to section directly beneath the window.

In a statement, Uffizi described the incident as a minor leak, emphasising that the protective glass covering meant Bacchus was never directly exposed to water. The painting’s removal from the gallery, the museum said, was purely precautionary, a standard response rather than an indication that any actual harm had occurred. What the museum did not offer was much clarity on the underlying cause. Asked why the leak happened in the first place, or what steps might prevent something similar in the future, officials declined to comment further.

The disruption was not limited to the Uffizi alone. Rain damage was also reported at the nearby Pitti Palace, where water reached parts of the galleries, suggesting the problem was broader across the infrastructure connecting Florence’s cluster of museum buildings rather than being isolated to a single roof or window. Investigators are still working to establish exactly where the failure originated.

Bacchus occupies an unusual place within the Uffizi’s collection, a museum otherwise crowded with instantly recognisable masterpieces like Botticelli’s Birth of Venus and a substantial run of Titians. The painting itself sat unrecognised in storage for years before being rediscovered in 1913, and was later identified by art historians Roberto Longhi and Matteo Marangoni, who spent the following decade examining it closely before concluding it was an early Caravaggio. Their attribution held up, bolstered by stylistic parallels with other works from the same early period in the artist’s career.

Caravaggio painted Bacchus around 1596, when he was roughly twenty-five years old, on commission from Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte, one of his earliest and most important patrons. The painting eventually made its way into Medici collection, likely as a gift to Grand Duke Ferdinando I of Tuscany, and is documented there as early as 1618, giving it a fairly continuous provenance stretching back more than four centuries.

The painting offers a familiar subject, the Roman God of wine reclining amid grapes, goblet raised toward the viewer in a gesture that reads somewhere between invitation and challenge. What made it significant to art historians was not the subject matter itself but the treatment, an early sign of Caravaggio’s growing interest in rendering mythological and religious figures with a distinctly human, almost uncomfortably physical presence. That instinct would eventually harden into the dramatic chiaroscuro the artist became famous for, the sharp collisions of light and shadow that defined Baroque painting for the following century.

text:
Charlotte's Brain Tumour Journey
Diagnosis to Death: 951 days
Age 19
18.2.97 - 24.2.16

13 years ago:
18th  September 2013
 
Charlotte had a bath earlier this morning.
She cried as she got into it.
Then she turned to me and said,
“I’m a disabled person in a young person’s body.”
My heart broke.
She was so terribly miserable.
“Why me?”I felt so helpless.
 There were no answers I could give her.
She was only 16 years old and was enduring all of this.
It was incredibly painful to see. 

Only a few months earlier, she had been a young woman with her whole life ahead of her. Now she needed help getting in and out of the bath.
Her eyes were becoming increasingly blurred, and she was very concerned about her sight.

Later in the day, the consultant asked us to come into a private room without Charlotte.
They explained that achieving a long-term cure for disseminated anaplastic astrocytoma that was unresectable would be extremely difficult.
Given how much Charlotte had deteriorated clinically, they had decided to use radiotherapy combined with chemotherapy.
Their exact words were:
“We have a window of opportunity for radiotherapy in the hope of getting on top of the tumour."

They also explained that another option was symptom care only,  given the poor prognosis. We chose radiotherapy and chemotherapy which Charlotte also wanted. It was our only hope. We hoped that the treatment would at least control Charlotte's symptoms and, hopefully, prolong her life long enough for other treatments or therapies to become available that might offer further benefit. 

We would have to travel every weekday, Monday to Friday, for six and a half weeks. Charlotte would receive radiotherapy to 360 degrees of her brain and to her entire spine. The actual treatment itself would only take around three and a half minutes. But those three and a half minutes represented our hope.

We had to take the opportunity.
It felt like the only hope we had left.
Looking back now, I believe that without the radiotherapy, Charlotte would have died even sooner.
At the time, though, we weren't thinking that far ahead.
We were simply trying to keep Charlotte alive.
We had to believe that this treatment could give us more time.
More time with Charlotte.
More time to hope.
More time to find something else that might help her.

text:
The Abrahamic blessing, “I will bless those who bless you, and those who curse you I will curse,” raises questions that run through centuries of Jewish and Christian history: who carries Abraham’s blessing, and what does being chosen authorize? The formula moves from Abraham (Gen. 12:3), to Jacob (Gen. 27:29), to Israel as a people (Num. 24:9).

But that formula contains a tension from the start. Abraham is singled out, protected, and promised descendants and land. Yet in the same promise, all the tribes of the earth are to be blessed through him. Abraham is chosen in particular for a purpose that reaches beyond him.

Then, Isaac inherits this covenant while Ishmael is still explicitly blessed. God promises to bless Ishmael, multiply him, and make him a great nation, even while saying that the covenant will be established through Isaac (Gen. 17:20–21).

Now we get to the deep contention. With the next generation the line narrows again. Before Jacob and Esau are born, God tells Rebekah that two nations and two peoples are in her womb and that the greater will serve the lesser (Gen. 25:23 LXX). Jacob’s precedence is announced before the birthright sale, before the deception, and before either brother has done anything.

I’m using the Septuagint (LXX) here because it gives us a major pre-70 textual witness, and the LXX leaves Jacob’s moral problem right where it is. Jacob tells Isaac that he is Esau, and after the trick is exposed Isaac says that Jacob came μετὰ δόλου, “with deceit” (Gen. 27:35 LXX). Yet the blessing stands. Genesis 28 makes the point even harder to get around. Isaac now knows exactly who Jacob is and deliberately gives him “the blessing of Abraham” (Gen. 28:3–4). God then confirms the land, descendants, and the promise that all the tribes of the earth will be blessed through Jacob and his seed (Gen. 28:13–14).

So Jacob is the covenantal heir without becoming morally innocent. Election does not wash the deception. Esau receives his own divine grant as well. Israel is warned not to seize Seir because God has given that land to Esau’s descendants (Deut. 2:4–5). The result is an asymmetry of vocation: one line carries the covenantal calling, while the purpose announced with Abraham reaches beyond that line.

The early Christian church wrote a lot about Jacob and Esau, but Justin Martyr is my favorite because he goes straight at the name Israel itself. Writing in the second century, Justin reads the Jabbok encounter through the preexistent Son or Logos. In other words, the mysterious figure who wrestles Jacob, blesses him, and gives him the name Israel is, for Justin, Christ before the incarnation. In Dialogue with Trypho 58–61, the divine figure appearing to the patriarchs is the Son acting on the Father’s behalf. So when Jacob wrestles, is blessed, and receives a new name, Justin understands him to be encountering the one later revealed as Christ.

In chapter 125 Justin makes the claim explicit: “Israel was His name from the beginning.” Christ gives Jacob his own name. That is the hinge. Israel doesn’t originate with Jacob in Justin’s reading; Jacob receives the name from Christ. And once Justin has made that move, chapter 135 follows naturally. Christ is Jacob and Israel, and those who belong to Christ become the true Israelitic people. Justin even distinguishes a line of Jacob “by blood and flesh” from one “by faith and the Spirit.”

For Justin, then, the inheritance is relocated around Christ. The nations enter Abraham’s blessing through him because Christ is the source of the Israelite name, and those joined to him share in it. Dialogue 47 still allows Jewish Christians to keep Mosaic observance so long as they don’t impose it on Gentile believers, but ancestry by itself no longer decides who finally carries Israel’s identity.

Let's then fast forward a few centuries to discuss the Jewish POV on Esau-Jacob, and I think Rashi is ideal here. Rashi, or Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, 1040–1105, draws on later Talmud and midrash to build a defense of Jacob’s title that culminates at Jabbok. His reconstruction starts earlier. On Genesis 27:19, where Jacob tells Isaac, “I am Esau your firstborn,” Rashi reparses the sentence so Jacob isn’t directly lying: Jacob identifies himself as the one bringing the food, then separately identifies Esau as Isaac’s firstborn. On 27:35, Isaac’s charge that Jacob came through mirmah, deceit, becomes “with cleverness.” And on 27:36, Rashi supplies a conversation in which Isaac learns that Esau had already sold the birthright and realizes that he blessed the rightful holder. The Greek has the sale and the deception, but it doesn’t supply that validating conversation.

At Jabbok, all of that becomes an adjudication. Rashi follows earlier midrash in identifying the mysterious “man” as Esau’s guardian angel. Jacob’s demand, “bless me,” now means: acknowledge my right to the blessing Isaac gave me and which Esau still contests. The new name does legal work as well. “No longer Jacob, but Israel” means that Jacob’s possession of the blessing will no longer be attributed to supplanting and deceit. Esau’s own heavenly representative has been forced to concede the title.

Rashi then brings Hosea 12 into the case. Chullin 92a asks who wept and pleaded with whom and answers that the angel pleaded with Jacob. Rashi expands that into a scene where the angel asks Jacob to wait until Bethel for public confirmation, while Jacob refuses and demands acknowledgment immediately. But the Old Greek Hosea has ἔκλαυσαν καὶ ἐδεήθησάν μου, “they wept and implored me.” The verbs are plural, and God is the object. That grammar doesn’t furnish the defeated angel begging Jacob to recognize his title.

And Rashi carries the acknowledgment into Genesis 33. Esau’s offer that Jacob keep what is his becomes an admission that the blessings really belong to Jacob. Jacob’s remark that seeing Esau’s face is like seeing the face of God points back to Esau’s angel, and Rashi has Jacob invoke that victory partly to intimidate Esau. He still preserves a genuine moment of reconciliation in Esau’s kiss, but the reconciliation now sits inside a larger story of Jacob’s vindication.

The dispute over Jacob’s title did not stay a family dispute. Once Jacob and Esau became ancestors of rival peoples, their story could be used to read later political history. That is where Esau becomes Rome. Bereshit Rabbah 63:7 already reads Rebekah’s two nations as Jews and Romans, and by the medieval period Edom could stand for the Christian imperial world. Jacob and Esau now signified Israel and the civilization ruling over it.

Rome and Jerusalem later became a way of reading Jacob and Esau, but the political beginning is interesting and worth a little bit of expansion. Jewish rule had already come back under the Hasmoneans. When Salome died (67 BC), the house split between Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II. Rome was not occupying Judea. Pompey’s people were in Syria, taking over the old Seleucid east, when both brothers went to them and asked Rome to decide who should hold the country. They argued the case at Damascus before Pompey’s legate Scaurus. Aristobulus bought the first hearing with gifts, including money from the Temple, and Scaurus backed him. Then Aristobulus would not wait for Pompey himself. He pulled back to a fortress, armed, and strengthened Jerusalem while the judgment was still open. Pompey treated that as contempt, arrived in 63 BC, and chose Hyrcanus, the weaker brother and the safer client. Aristobulus’s people then shut the city against Roman troops. Pompey took that as revolt and took Jerusalem. Josephus’s later judgment is blunt here: the brothers’ war cost the Jews their liberty and subjected them to Rome. So, the Jewish state had returned, and two people who couldnt get along pulled in Pompey into an inheritance fight, double-dealed Pompey, and then lost that state.

Roman rule then became something much harder to reverse. Jerusalem and the Temple were destroyed in AD 70, and the defeat of the Bar Kokhba revolt in AD 135 devastated Judea again. It’s almost impossible to overstate the impact of the Second Temple’s destruction on later Judaism. For the argument here, one consequence is especially important: Roman domination gave the older Esau-Edom typology an increasingly concrete historical target. Rome could now become Esau.

After Jewish sovereignty disappeared, restoration increasingly moved into the realm of messianic expectation. Rabbinic traditions such as the Three Oaths could be read to restrain attempts to force the end of exile, and Sabbatai Zevi gave the danger of activated messianism a spectacular historical form. In 1665–66 a mass movement formed around him, mixing Kabbalah, prophecy, radical ritual innovation, and the conviction that human action below could participate in redemption above. His conversion to Islam shattered the movement, although some followers made even the apostasy part of the redemptive mystery. Anyway, the episode became a powerful warning about believing that the moment of redemption had arrived and that human beings were authorized to help force it.

Fast forward roughly a century and a half, and enter Tsevi Hirsch Kalischer. He brings human agency back into redemption from inside traditional Judaism, but in a material form. In Derishat Zion he proposes migration, pooled money for land purchases, agricultural colonies, and the rebuilding of Jewish life in the Land. Redemption begins through human action. Jews themselves can “take charge of ending” their exiled condition.

Kalischer’s Kabbalistic formula says exactly what is happening: “the awakening of the lower world will lead to the awakening of the upper world” (Derishat Zion). So, action below calls forth action above. He even says that “the beginning of redemption does not depend on repentance, but on returning to the land.” So Kalischer gives a 19th-century answer to the question running through the whole essay: if Israel carries Abraham’s blessing, what does that election authorize Israel to do? For Kalischer, it authorizes the covenant-bearing people to become an agent of their own collective restoration.

Kalischer did not settle the debate with the nineteenth-century quietists. The dispute was over who starts redemption: must Jews wait for God and the Messiah, or can Jewish action below begin the process and call forth the response above? His opponents could still say that settlement did not prove redemption had begun, and even the creation of Israel in 1948 did not end that theological dispute. For Kalischer’s later Kookian heirs, 1967 was the moment when history seemed to answer the objection.

Kalischer’s end is wider than Jewish resettlement. His messianic sequence eventually brings the nations to the Temple, where they receive divine teaching and share in the blessings of the messianic age.  Land and labor begin the process; the nations remain inside its final horizon.

Moses Hess similarly makes the modern Jewish nation the bearer of that vocation in Rome and Jerusalem (1862). He reaches directly back to Genesis 12:3: “In thee … shall all the families of the earth be blessed.”  For Hess, national restoration gives Israel the historical form in which that mission can operate again. In the messianic age, Hess says, “the Jewish nation and all the other historical nations” arise again to new life.  His “Sabbath of History” is the maturity of human development, when history reaches its messianic completion.  So, for Hess, Israel remains a distinct historical people inside that future. In the Eleventh Letter, Hess calls the returning Jews the “triumphal arch” under which the “great covenant of humanity” will be written and sealed.

Theodor Herzl then turns national restoration into an organized political program. Der Judenstaat (1896) gives the project machinery: the Society of Jews handles the political work, the Jewish Company handles property and economic organization, and sovereignty becomes something to be pursued through diplomacy, migration, finance, and land acquisition.

Fast forward a few decades, and we get to Rav Abraham Isaac Kook. He reads secular Zionist action back into providence. Settlers and political organizers may not understand themselves as religious agents, yet their work can still participate in a divine historical process. Kook also places a moral limit on the nation that acts. In his early essay “Israel’s Mission and Nationhood,” he describes Jewish nationalism as an ethical mission for the benefit of all humanity and warns that nationalism detached from that mission can become self-loving chauvinism and a pretext for immorality and xenophobic violence.

Back to Kalischer and the old debate with the quietists, 1967 looked to Kook’s activist heirs like the answer from above that Kalischer’s theology had anticipated. If Jewish action below could awaken redemption above, the Six-Day War seemed almost tailor-made as confirmation. And from this point of view, the irony was that the secular state and its leaders could be instruments of redemption without even recognizing what they were doing. In May 1967, R. Kook publicly lamented that Hebron, Shechem, Jericho, and other biblical territories still lay outside the Jewish state. Weeks later, Israel’s unexpectedly rapid victory brought East Jerusalem and the West Bank under Israeli control. Anyway, for his students, this looked like more than military success. The state they already understood as an instrument of redemption had acted, and history had placed the biblical heartlands in its hands. What Kalischer had described as an awakening below could now be read, by this camp, as having received an answer above.

I suppose we could keep going with Rome as Esau or Dispensationalism, but let’s leave it with Justin Martyr, Rashi, and 1967. The Old Greek still leaves a constraint on every later answer. Abraham is chosen for a blessing aimed beyond Abraham. Jacob carries the covenant without becoming morally innocent. Election is real, but it does not erase moral judgment.

Who carries Abraham’s blessing, and what does being chosen actually authorize?

If your will is to hurt, you will be hurt.

Crowley was sent to collect kindling for the fire. For there to be light, something must burn.

There's no better way to separate the wheat from the chaff that than to allow the chaff to throw itself into the fire.

Be careful what you wish for.

text:
ALAN ROSENBAUM
SEPTEMBER 20, 2026 
Two thousand years ago, as the high priest entered the Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur, Jews throughout the Land of Israel and across the Diaspora were fasting. But what else were they doing?
The Yom Kippur rituals and observances practiced in the Temple thousands of years ago are clearly enumerated in the Bible (Leviticus 16), the Mishnah (Yoma), and the Talmud.

During the Yom Kippur Service, the high priest (kohen gadol) offered a bull as a sin offering for himself and his household, and confessed his own sins and those of his household and the other kohanim.Advertisement
Two identical goats were placed before him, and lots were drawn: one “for the Lord” and one “for azazel.”
The first would be sacrificed; the second became the famous se’ir la’azazel, often translated as the “scapegoat,” which was sent into the wilderness. The Mishnah describes it being taken to a cliff and pushed to its death.
The day’s special status was highlighted by the high priest’s entry into the Holy of Holies, where he offered incense.
While many people undoubtedly came to Jerusalem to see the Temple Service, Yom Kippur is not one of the three pilgrimage festivals, like Sukkot, Passover, and Shavuot, and there was no special mitzvah to go to Jerusalem.

How did Jews living in Beit Shemesh, the Galilee, or Beersheba observe Yom Kippur? What did the Jews in Alexandria, Rome, and Babylonia do on that day?
While the biblical rules of fasting and the prohibition of labor applied to everyone, the major prayers of Yom Kippur that we are so familiar with today – Kol Nidrei, “Avinu Malkenu,” “Unetaneh Tokef” – had not yet been composed.
Did they pray at home? Did they hold prayer assemblies? Did they attend a synagogue? If they prayed, what did they say?
“On the 10th day the fast takes place, which they take seriously – not only those who are zealous about piety and holiness, but even those who do nothing religious the rest of the time. For all are astounded, overcome with the sacredness of it; in fact, at that time the wicked compete with the righteous in self-control and virtue.”
“The commentator here writes, ‘There is nothing new under the sun.’”
Jerusalem Post

text:
The first ballistic missile strike on Riyadh since this conflict cycle resumed has changed the strategic calculus in ways that go beyond the tactical details — the missile was intercepted, no casualties confirmed — but the political consequences are anything but modest.

On September 19–20, 2026, the Houthis crossed a threshold that qualitatively shifts Saudi Arabia's position. Absorbing a ballistic missile aimed at the capital is politically unsustainable for MBS in a way that previous Aramco facility strikes were not. Riyadh, which had earlier signaled it could manage the Houthi threat unilaterally, has reversed that position — with MBS reportedly lobbying Washington directly for US military action.

That pressure appears to be landing. Trump's early return from Camp David and reported Yemen strike deliberations constitute credible pre-decisional signals. But to be precise: deliberation is not decision. The White House offered no comment, and the evidence rests on reporting that remains circumstantially corroborated. The assessed probability of US kinetic action against the Houthis within seven days sits at *likely — 55 to 75%* — with a MODERATE validation process.

What complicates the calculation is Iran. Khatam al-Anbiya Central HQ has warned of "continuous, effective, and painful attacks" against US bases if strikes resume. Analysts treating that as rhetorical bluster would be mistaken — it is assessed as consistent with Iran's documented counter-escalation doctrine. At the same time, Iran is transmitting ceasefire conditions to Washington via Qatar. The dual-track posture reduces but does not eliminate the risk of direct US–Iran exchanges.

A structural problem also remains unresolved: any strike package leaves the following in place. The Houthis have already seized the Bab el-Mandeb coastline, Mocha port, and the Hanish Islands. Near-term US military action will not reverse that territorial reality. The strategic objective the Houthis are pursuing — control of Yemen and the strait — remains intact regardless of what happens in the next 96 hours.

An additional constraint worth noting: US munitions stocks in the region are reportedly under pressure, with weapons burn rates drawing documented external attention. That is a real variable in decisions about the scope of any expanded operation.

The next 72–96 hours represent the most acute escalation node since Operation Epic Fury began in February 2026. The direction of pressure is clear. The decision itself has not been confirmed. 6/6

text:
Trump Wants to Rename Artificial Intelligence, Offers Three Alternatives
Washington, Sept 20: US President Donald Trump has said the term "artificial intelligence" is inaccurate and proposed renaming it, inviting people to vote on social media. He offered three options: "Superior Intelligence," "Extreme Intelligence" and "Supreme Intelligence."
Calling AI's rise a "revolution," Trump said he would not allow efforts to weaken or destroy the industry and its data centers. He criticized liberals, saying they want "AI's destruction."
The president also announced plans for a new government "AI Force," which he said would be tasked with finding "bad" actors. He said an AI coordinator, or "czar," would be named soon but gave no further details.
Speaking to reporters at his golf club in Doonbeg, Ireland, Trump dismissed concerns about AI as a "hoax," comparing them to climate change, and said, "Whoever wins AI wins." He said guardrails could be put in place, but that many negative forces were pushing things that would not happen. On Truth Social, he wrote that AI only needed the "guardrails" of a "strong and smart" president.
Meanwhile, China's foreign ministry said all parties should work together on AI. Spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a press conference that "fear-mongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only damage global AI governance, benefiting no one."
The debate flared up again after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a three-part plan to manage the pace of frontier AI development. He argued that AI systems are increasingly able to help build more advanced models, raising concerns about how fast the technology could advance.

Simple negotiation principle BATNA - Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement:

A threat works only if it is worse for them than the deal, and walking away is better for you than a bad deal. Iran has already been through war with the United States. Repeating “or else war” is weaker unless the next war would clearly cost Tehran more than the last one. Washington therefore has to put an offer on the table that beats Iran’s Plan B — durable sanctions relief, reconstruction funds, Hormuz rules, and nuclear terms Iran can sell at home — while keeping a real alternative if Iran refuses. If either side’s fallback is stronger than the deal, talks stall.

This is the revolving door in full effect. The same people who run the country's most sensitive national security apparatus move seamlessly into advisory and board roles for the world's most powerful financial and corporate interests. The Final Irony

The people who ran the "poisonous" and "mad" Johnson government—Case, Sedwill, and their ilk—are now in the private sector, advising Rothschild and McKinsey, while condemning the very system they served.

And the people who were supposed to replace them—Starmer, McSweeney, and the Labour leadership—turned to Mandelson, a man whose entire career has been a masterclass in serving power, not principle.

You asked, earlier in our conversation: "Is it not the case of the company you keep?"

Yes. And Labour chose to keep company with Peter Mandelson. Now they are paying the price.

The question is whether the public—angry, exhausted, and abandoned by both major parties—will turn to Farage, Musk, and the "British friends of Trump" as the only alternative.

👇Trump says he is in “deciding mode” on Iran, with “very big things” coming soon.

But while US strategy remains unclear, Iran has tied its counter-escalation to explicit diplomatic goals: return to the June MOU and actually implement it.

For Tehran, the lesson of the original MOU was that de-escalation without coercive leverage did not produce reciprocal US restraint. It simply reduced Iran’s leverage while leaving Washington free to improve its position.

In the weeks after the MOU, attacks continued in Lebanon, the U.S. struck Iran multiple times, Iranian leaders faced renewed threats, Iran never gained access to the frozen assets promised under the deal, and Washington promoted an alternative shipping corridor through Hormuz that bypassed the Iranian transit arrangement the MOU had explicitly recognized.

That last point is arguably the most important. Tehran saw the U.S. as using the ceasefire to restore energy flows while building a new transit regime that would gradually strip Iran of its leverage over Hormuz. Iran would then be left dependent on reversible US promises while Washington improved its position for another war.

That helps explain Iran’s counter-escalation since July. Its aim has not been endless war, but a more durable deal backed by leverage Washington cannot simply take away.

The question for Trump now is what another military escalation can achieve that months of war have not, particularly as energy buffers have eroded and the U.S. has burned through substantial quantities of expensive munitions.

The UNGA could offer an off-ramp. Pezeshkian will reportedly be in New York, Iran’s terms are increasingly clear, and Trump says he is open to meeting him. China could also help anchor a broader regional arrangement around Hormuz and Persian Gulf security that is more durable than another bilateral ceasefire.

The ball is in Trump's court: He now has to decide whether to pursue serious negotiations with meaningful reciprocal concessions, or gamble yet again that another round of war can achieve what the previous ones could not.

text:
Good landing on the terms of the pact that is scheduled to be signed. As noted by Siaxares, Greenland keeps its internal life. Denmark keeps the flag. The United States hardens permanent access, basing, overflight, and a veto on adversary bases and sensitive investment — including after Greenlandic independence. That is the 1951 U.S.–Denmark–Greenland defense arrangement updated and restructured for 2026 and beyond. Not Alaska. Not a cartoon annexation. The map did not change. The security architecture did. Mining is not a title in this paper; the screen is meant to keep Chinese and Russian projects off the rock. American firms still have to compete like everyone else.
Two corrections, then the history the thread did not include.

I do not believe that Trump was cleaning up a Stephen Miller mess. Miller still has an office in the West Wing. Reporting on the talks put him on the quiet track with Rubio from February. Katie Miller’s flag-on-ice “SOON” (3 January) and the later “IT’S HAPPENING” graphic were the visual anchor, not a freelance coup. If the carnival had been internationally stupid on a staffer’s own authority, he would have been fired. He was not. IMHO, the ugly half and the close appear to be one file.

And this term did not invent the ask. After the Alaska purchase from Russia, Seward surveyed Greenland (1867–68) and got nowhere. In 1917 the United States did buy Denmark’s West Indies. In 1941, while Denmark was occupied, a wartime defense pact was signed in Washington so the United States could hold Greenland for the war. In December 1946 the Truman administration offered Denmark’s foreign minister $100 million in gold — a first-ask lowball by honor as much as by acre. Denmark refused. The 1951 defense treaty was the real price: U.S. defense areas, no deed. In 2019 Trump asked again in purchase language. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called it “absurd.” In diplo-speak that is not “we decline to haggle.” It is “this is not a serious conversation between allies.” He canceled the visit. That is why 2026 opened with the Big Ask instead of another quiet note. Copenhagen asked for the January working group after the public threats and the flag meme, not before. Rubio then said the quiet part out loud: they do not have the means to defend the island; we do.

Persuasion stack, not a tantrum — Art of the Deal plus Adams: Big Ask as anchor, then close on the instrument that was available in 1951 and was never locked for an independent Greenland. Two movies on the same screen: permanence and denial in one theater, sovereignty preserved in the other. You can hate the memes and still notice Denmark sat down after the price of refusal included the cartoon.

This deal is scheduled, but not yet done.  It was announced 18 September and signatures are expected at UNGA this week. Then parliaments. It appears the end of 2026 is a fair “no-later-than” for the instrument to be in force. Cuba is still the other item on that clock. Score the ink, not the flag overlay.

text:
Colonizing the Moon in the near term (roughly the next 10–20 years) would not solve most everyday Earth problems like poverty, climate change, or overpopulation. Logistics make large-scale migration impossible, and recent analyses show accessible lunar water ice could support only modest outposts of a few thousand people for centuries rather than million-person cities.

It could address a narrower set of technical and strategic problems:

Energy and high-tech materials: Lunar regolith contains helium-3, which is extremely rare on Earth and useful for fusion research, quantum-computer cooling, and certain medical/security applications. Commercial efforts already target robotic extraction in the late 2020s. Water ice at the poles could also be turned into rocket propellant, reducing the cost of deeper-space missions.

Technology proving ground: The Moon is close enough for relatively rapid resupply and communication. It lets engineers test closed-loop life support, radiation shielding, dust mitigation, and in-situ resource use under real conditions before attempting Mars. Those systems have spin-off value for remote or harsh environments on Earth.

Scientific access: The lunar far side is radio-quiet, making it valuable for low-frequency astronomy that is blocked on Earth. Polar sites also offer nearly continuous sunlight for power and nearby ice for operations.

The main near-term “problem” it actually solves is the engineering one of learning how to live off-world at all. Larger claims—backup civilization, unlimited resources, or geopolitical prestige—remain speculative and constrained by physics, biology (1/6 g effects are still poorly understood), and cost.

text:
A sportsbook makes money when gamblers lose. DraftKings trained a 2023 machine-learning system to rank online casino players by how much they were expected to lose after a free bet or bonus, then steered promotions at the highest scores.

Machine learning here means software that learns patterns from past bets instead of following a handwritten rule. Workers called the ranking an “elasticity” score: how much a customer is expected to lose after the perk lands. Higher meant chase with more free bets.

The Daily Caller and Tech Times, attributing a New York Times investigation, say former data analyst Jayden Butts tested the tool on thousands of casino players and told the paper: “We are looking for traits and features that we can target that indicate a good investment… The best investment would be a problem gambler.” A problem gambler is someone whose betting is compulsive and financially harmful.

Data scientist Nestor Hernandez began a 2024 model to flag gamblers sliding toward crisis. DraftKings shelved it. Chief Responsible Gaming Officer Lori Kalani said leaders reached a “collective decision” against predictive tools because the approach was not “evidence-based.”

DraftKings disputed the framing. The company says promotions go to customers with “sustained, engaged use,” not people singled out for losing, and called Butts’s test “preliminary and inconclusive.”

Roughly $8.7 billion in gross gambling revenue last year, about $3 billion handed out in promotions, per the Times citing Citizens Bank research.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (CT) and Rep. Paul Tonko (NY) introduced the SAFE Bet Act to forbid sportsbooks from using AI to track habits and serve personalized offers. Congress has not passed it.

The promo model learned addiction markers. The harm model got shelved.

text:
Robert Saleh just said he is putting his job on Cam Ward.

"This kid's not going to fail. Obviously, I put my job on that one, but he's not going to fail. He's special."

Here is what makes that wild.

Five years ago, nobody in America wanted Cam Ward to play quarterback.

Not a low-star recruit. Zero stars.

He grew up in West Columbia, Texas, a town of about 3,600 people between Houston and the coast. He played in a Wing-T offense, which is a run-first scheme where the quarterback is mostly handing the ball off and running option.

His senior season numbers:

45% completions. 948 passing yards. Eight touchdowns.

Nine hundred and forty-eight yards. In an entire year.

He was honestly better at basketball. He is still the all-time leading scorer in West Columbia High School history.

Every major program looked at that film and saw nothing, because there was nothing on it to see. You cannot evaluate a passer who never passes.

As Eric Morris later put it, all anybody needed was to see him "playing in the gun, running some RPOs and going through progressions."

Nobody bothered.

His one reported offer besides Incarnate Word was Texas Southern.

Then he went to a camp at Incarnate Word, an FCS school in San Antonio.

Eric Morris was the head coach there.

"The first time we noticed him was at a camp out at Incarnate Word. We didn't know who he was beforehand. The ball was just popping off his hand."

Morris kept him after the camp to throw more, and watched a 17 year old make throws that 17 year olds are not supposed to be able to make.

That was it. That was the entire discovery.

Ward went to Incarnate Word and in 19 games threw for 6,900 yards and 71 touchdowns.

Then he followed Morris to Washington State.

Then he went to Miami in 2024 and finished fourth in the Heisman voting.

In April 2025, the Tennessee Titans took Cam Ward with the first overall pick in the NFL Draft.

From zero stars and 948 high school passing yards to the first name called.

And now here is the part that should make you sit up.

That coach, Eric Morris, is now the head coach at North Texas.

Last season a kid walked on there with no scholarship. In high school in Austin he had not even been his team's starting quarterback. He was the punter. His all-district honors came for punting.

His name is Drew Mestemaker, and when Morris finally gave him the job, he led every quarterback in the country in passing yards.

So the same man who spotted a zero-star Wing-T quarterback at a camp in San Antonio also looked at a high school punter and saw a starter.

Two quarterbacks nobody else wanted. Both found by the same guy.

Robert Saleh is betting his job that the first one is special.

Given who found him, that is not the craziest bet in football.
