Designing charts can be hard. 

It is the ultimate balance of form and function.

We've all seen examples of bad charts. But it's difficult to describe what makes a chart good.

The key priorities when designing any chart are:

- it needs to be easy to interpret;
- it should be easy to scan, even at a distance; and
- it should not commit any chart crimes (poor axis, labels, legends, etc.)

And, ideally, it should match the rest of your brand's design language.

Recently, I've been working on a project where charts will be generated on-the-fly by AI agents.

I needed to design the style guide and design system that the agents will use to create each chart.

This led me to create a general set of principles, which I then codified inside a style.md file:

1. Color

You often need a distinct colour palette, purpose-built for your charts.

Why? Because it can be difficult to retrofit your existing palette to work for all eventual chart layouts.

This new palette should be an extension of your base design system, but specifically designed for displaying different series of data on the same chart.

The goal is to maximise contrast (ideally >3:1 contrast ratio) between neighboring sets of data, whilst being cohesive with the core brand.

Choose colors that aren't too vibrant or bright, especially if using any green, orange, or red hues, to avoid users interpreting these as status/warning colors.

For example, a modern, accessible set of colors could be the following:

Series 1: Navy (e.g. #183B56)
Series 2: Orange (e.g. #D9772A)
Series 3: Teal (e.g #378873)
Series 4: Purple (e.g. #765A9E)
Series 5: Vermilion/Red (e.g. #C94432)

Note 1: Ideally, we would limit charts to only include 3 series of data in a single visualisation. Because users can ask the agent to generate any chart, we needed to extend to a maximum of 5 series, to offer more versatility.

Note 2: Obviously, the above color palette is tailored towards a light mode UI. Most colors will still work on a darker background, except you would need to boost the vibrancy and brightness or the navy and orange.

text:
Hassett's $2 Hamburger Defense Blows Up in His Face
Kevin Hassett has a barometer for the American economy: the price of the meat he grills on weekends.
The White House chief economist offered it up Sunday on Fox News, where Peter Doocy pressed him on polling showing 62 percent of Americans now call grocery prices a major problem for their household. Hassett smiled through it.
"It's a really strong economy," he said, adding that he shops every weekend and had noticed his barbecue hamburger running two dollars cheaper than a few weeks earlier.
The anecdote landed badly almost immediately.
Andrew Weinstein, a former U.S. Public Delegate to the United Nations, called the remark offensively ignorant, noting that families aren't chasing a two-dollar discount on burgers - they're trying to cover the grocery bill at all. He pointed to roughly 40 percent of Florida households leaning on Buy Now, Pay Later services just to keep food on the table.
Retired Labor Department judge and Air Force colonel Moe Davis flatly contradicted the premise, pointing out that ground beef and diesel are both sitting at record highs.
The numbers back him. USDA Economic Research Service figures circulated by Zeteo's Justin Baragona show ground beef up 22 percent year over year to $6.92 a pound, beef steak up nearly 18 percent to $12.81, and sirloin up more than 21 percent to $14.36.
Even self-described constitutional conservative commentator ThePatrioticBlonde broke ranks, calling it astounding that the administration would say something so easily disproved while Americans struggle to make rent.
Commentator Jason Levin was blunter, describing the rest of the economy as a full-body house fire.
Texas House Democratic nominee Sara McGee saw an upside. Lying about things people witness with their own eyes at the checkout counter, she argued, exposes the lie instantly - and seeds doubt about everything else the administration says.
#Hassett #GroceryPrices #Economy #Trump

Shocking new court documents reveal that comedian Carrot Top (real name Scott Thompson) was the target of an alleged sextortion plot prior to his reported attempt at taking his own life on Friday.
According to a September 3 filing in Broward County, Florida, by Thompson's attorney, Ronnie Bitman, musician Brian Evans demanded $500,000 to resolve legal claims. Bitman alleged that Evans threatened to make a sexually explicit video of Thompson public if the funds were not paid immediately.
The Demands & The Response
In an email included in the court records, Evans wrote that he wanted the money in immediately available funds, threatening to introduce the footage into a public court docket where the press could access it.
"It is not a threat. I am not offering to create coverage, stop coverage, or trade silence for money," Evans wrote in the email, while also noting that if his deadline was missed, "it is not an offer your client will ever see again."
Evans claimed his email was meant to be confidential, insisted he never threatened to post a video in exchange for a settlement, and stated the video was deleted long ago. He added, "Thankfully he is still with us."
A Pattern of Legal Battles
Thompson’s representative, Jami Schlicher, pointed out that Evans has been officially declared a "vexatious litigant."
Federal Findings: A U.S. District Judge noted that Evans has filed at least 15 frivolous pro se cases in the district since 2025.
Judicial Pushback: Broward County Judge Shari Africk Olefson recently ruled that Evans improperly filed emergency motions, calling it an "abuse of the emergency motion procedure."
Record Sealed: Judge Olefson granted a motion to strike or seal irrelevant and unrelated sensitive material from the public record.
Thankfully, Carrot Top survived the incident and is recovering.

text:
🚨 Key points from the game against Fulham

• Fulham deserved more than a point. Manchester United were embarrassing for long spells, so we should be thankful and grateful to God for the draw.

• Carrick needs to be ruthless with his selections. Rashford was wasteful today. Had he converted some of the chances he got, United could have won this game.

• Mbeumo has little use as a winger because he rarely beats his marker. He spends most of the game running up and down like a headless chicken. The Cunha experiment has overstayed its welcome; it’s time to play him on the left. The equaliser came from that side, and I’m convinced Rashford wouldn't have taken that chance if he was in that position. He desperately needs to rediscover his shooting boots.

• Shaw is a liability. I repeat, Shaw is a liability and must be moved on.

• Bruno was in ghost mode all game. He needs to do better because, too often, when Bruno doesn’t perform, nothing positive comes out of a Manchester United game.

• Lacey performed well in the last game despite the defeat. The coach needs to learn how to appreciate and motivate players after good performances. I’m convinced Lacey would have offered more than Mbeumo did today.

• Lammens was excellent today and kept us in the game. Every day, he continues to show why he should be Manchester United’s No. 1 goalkeeper.

• Another excellent game from Kobbie Mainoo. He was United’s best midfielder today and, at times, looked like the only player trying to make something positive happen.

• Martinez needs to wake up and stay focused. He gave away a poor goal against Ipswich and has now scored an own goal. He has been a shadow of his former self this season. I’m certain he wouldn’t perform this way in an Argentina shirt. He needs to improve significantly, or he should make way for another defender.

• Maguire had a good game and even put in a better midfield shift than Bruno Fernandes. However, this should probably be his final season at the club to give younger defenders the opportunity to grow into the role.

• Thank God the international break is here. Carrick now has three weeks to go back to the drawing board, think deeply and strategise with his coaching staff. What we’ve seen so far is nowhere near as impressive as what we saw last season. We’re already out of the Carabao Cup after our first game, which is unacceptable. He needs to come back from this break with solutions and ensure we finish as high as possible this season.

text:
The UAE has a value that a lot of people don't understand.

They compare it to cities like Paris or London and say it lacks charm, history, culture and no seasons.

The reality is that you choose a city for what it gives you at a particular moment in your life.

What the UAE gives you is emotional stability, for people whose work already brings stress and intensity.

In Paris, you have to be ready to wake up to bad weather some days and beautiful weather others, to handle whatever the city throws at you, a bureaucratic system, and enormous taxes for entrepreneurs. In a city like that, you swing between feeling exceptional, feeling fine, and feeling like everything is falling apart.

In Dubai, you feel "good" all the time, all year round. No intensity or stress on the administrative side, on service quality, on any of it. The focus can go to the work, and the intensity goes where it belongs.

It's always a pleasure to walk the streets of Paris and take in the architecture and the culture the city offers, when the weather allows.

Dubai offers something else. A certain serenity, with the desert there to clear your head.

That's what makes the city so attractive to entrepreneurs from all over the world, and what makes meeting people there so easy. 
The sense of safety makes it possible to grab a coffee with a founder who would have thought twice before meeting a stranger in person in his home country.

You have to have lived it to understand it

text:
Reminds me of this story... 

There was once a businessman who was sitting by the beach in a small Brazilian village.

As he sat, he saw a Brazilian fisherman rowing a small boat towards the shore having caught quite few big fish.
The businessman was impressed and asked the fisherman, “How long does it take you to catch so many fish?”
The fisherman replied, “Oh, just a short while.”

“Then why don’t you stay longer at sea and catch even more?” The businessman was astonished.

“This is enough to feed my whole family,” the fisherman said.

The businessman then asked, “So, what do you do for the rest of the day?”

The fisherman replied, “Well, I usually wake up early in the morning, go out to sea and catch a few fish, then go back and play with my kids. In the afternoon, I take a nap with my wife, and evening comes, I join my buddies in the village for a drink — we play guitar, sing and dance throughout the night.”

The businessman offered a suggestion to the fisherman.

“I am a PhD in business management. I could help you to become a more successful person. From now on, you should spend more time at sea and try to catch as many fish as possible. When you have saved enough money, you could buy a bigger boat and catch even more fish. Soon you will be able to afford to buy more boats, set up your own company, your own production plant for canned food and distribution network. By then, you will have moved out of this village and to Sao Paulo, where you can set up HQ to manage your other branches.”

The fisherman continues, “And after that?”
The businessman laughs heartily, “After that, you can live like a king in your own house, and when the time is right, you can go public and float your shares in the Stock Exchange, and you will be rich.”

The fisherman asks, “And after that?”
The businessman says, “After that, you can finally retire, you can move to a house by the fishing village, wake up early in the morning, catch a few fish, then return home to play with kids, have a nice afternoon nap with your wife, and when evening comes, you can join your buddies for a drink, play the guitar, sing and dance throughout the night!”

The fisherman was puzzled, “Isn’t that what I am doing now?”

text:
12/ Post Race

Athletes got ushered into a section where we were offered recovery shakes and drinks, got finisher photos taken, and had access to a banger of a buffet

I started chatting with a guy at the start of the queue. Asked him if I was the only one questioning whether I shat in my tri suit. We hit it off right away. Turns out he did one year as a pro triathlete in the 80s (the first Ironman was held in Hawaii in 1978!)

We had common views on life, which I expect are shared by most other athletes at the event. The shared goals naturally lead to similar outlooks. Pretty cool

Anecdotally, I wouldn't be surprised if 10% of athletes don't drink. By no means am I stomping on booze, but it puts the larger goal at risk, so lots of folks - myself included - simply decide to cut it out entirely

Bike pickup was nice and easy. Went over a few hours after I finished and got in and out without any traffic

Illinois Governor 𝐉𝐁 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐳𝐤𝐞𝐫 was asked a simple question on camera: does he worry that Democratic Socialists of America candidates are increasingly winning his party's primaries, energy that could cost Democrats swing seats in November? His answer wasn't reassurance. It was an admission.

“𝘓𝘰𝘰𝘬, 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘋𝘦𝘮𝘰𝘤𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘴 𝘴𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘪𝘯 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘮𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘸𝘦 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘢 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘮𝘰𝘯 𝘮𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘢𝘨𝘦. 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘪𝘳𝘴𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘸𝘦'𝘳𝘦 𝘧𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘨𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘴𝘵 𝘋𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭𝘥 𝘛𝘳𝘶𝘮𝘱 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘙𝘦𝘱𝘶𝘣𝘭𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘯𝘴,” Pritzker said, waving off concerns about the DSA's momentum by insisting “𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞𝐧'𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐲” of its candidates winning and that the ones who do "get highlighted too much."

Notice what's missing from that answer: a policy. Not a jobs plan, not a border position, not an inflation fix — just a shared enemy. Pritzker, one of the most talked-about 2028 hopefuls in his party, couldn't offer voters anything Democrats are actually 𝐟𝐨𝐫, only what they're against.

Democratic Socialist-aligned candidates keep winning primaries in blue strongholds, and the party's governors keep shrugging it off as noise. Voters heading into the midterms are left to wonder what exactly they'd be voting to support.

text:
INTUIT $INTU SPENT THURSDAY REPEATING ITS FORECAST. FRIDAY TOOK ANOTHER 3% OFF:

Intuit INTU at $304.00 (after hours), -$9.13 / -2.92% Friday. The Mountain View company owns TurboTax, QuickBooks and Credit Karma.

Rank the six Len5es by what a dollar of last year's profit costs and the board runs from about 7 times to 151. That spread is not a ranking of quality. It is a ranking of how much of each company's future the market believes it already knows.

Intuit is the loudest case. Profit per share rose 20% last year, its own forecast for the year now running calls for 22% to 24% more, and the price has been halved. Nobody disputes the results. What is being sold is the belief about what follows them - that AI does the filing and the bookkeeping for nothing.

Fiscal 2026 ended July 31, reported August 25:

- Revenue $21.4B, +14%; profit per share $16.46, +20% - counted strictly, nothing stripped out
- $5.5B spent retiring its own shares, nearly double the prior year; the dividend raised 15%, to $1.38 a quarter

The forecast set that day and repeated at Thursday's September 17 investor day: revenue $23.28B-$23.51B, +9% to +10%; profit $20.12-$20.36 a share, +22% to +24%. Sales growth slows from 14% to 9%. Profit per share climbs faster anyway, on a shrinking share count and widening margins.

Friday closed at $303.15, -3.2%, on 7.7M shares against a 3.6M two-week average. Against $705.08 last September 22 that is -57.0% - about 18.4 times what it earned, near 15 times the floor of its own guide.

Two Len5es watch it at once, the dislocation below and Quality-Value 42nd of 59, where the accountant lock-in earns the quality half but the discount reads modest. WHEN: first-quarter results tentatively Thursday, November 19 after the close, not company-confirmed, guided to revenue of $4.294B-$4.313B, +11%. VERDICT: a company beating its numbers, priced on a forecast about a product that has not shipped.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
Baldwin Insurance Group, ticker BWIN, at $31.93 (after hours), -$0.02 / -0.06% Friday. The Tampa firm brokers insurance for businesses and families - paid a commission, carrying none of the claims. This Len5 wants a price near its one-year high with the short and long climbs agreeing: $32.705 on September 15, double February 12's $15.88. Read why before calling it strength. On September 14 the board agreed to sell the company for $32.50 a share in cash to Sequence Holdings and Michael Dell's family investment office, an 88% premium to the June 17 price. CHANGE IT: the deal. Friday sits $0.57 under that offer, which is where a bought price sits. VERDICT: the best chart here, and the least of it earned.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
Illinois Tool Works at $269.42 (after hours), +$1.91 / +0.71% Friday. The Glenview, Illinois company makes welding gear, kitchen equipment and car fasteners. This Len5 wants a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought under its worth; the fifth name on it has only the first half. July 28 quarter: revenue $4.30B, +6.1%, with organic revenue - sales leaving out deals and currency - up 4.5%; operating income $1.15B, +7.4%, the most profitable quarter of its 114 years. It raised the year to $11.45 a share. CHANGE IT: the price, about 23.5 times that, a discount to nothing. WHEN: October 23, tentative; $2.98 against $2.81. VERDICT: the one business here nobody argues about, and it is charged for.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
Intuit, sixth of 90, on a Len5 hunting a sound business knocked down by a fixable problem. The 57% is the knock-down. The problem is inside the August 25 report, a line per business: QuickBooks Online Accounting +23%, Credit Karma +20%, Consumer +11%, TurboTax +7%. The AI argument is about TurboTax - the slowest line Intuit owns, and about a quarter of the company at $5.3B of $21.4B. CHANGE IT: whether the fear spreads. Small businesses deciding a chatbot can keep their books, and QuickBooks slowing off that 23%, turns a discount into a correct price. VERDICT: $21.4B of revenue priced on the trajectory of the $5.3B piece that frightens people.

GROWTH LEN5:
ServisFirst Bancshares at $41.45 (after hours), +$0.50 / +1.23% Friday. The Birmingham, Alabama bank lends to companies across the South with 666 staff and almost no branches - deposits arrive through bankers, not buildings. This Len5 wants profit growth the price has not charged for; the first name on it costs about 14 times profit. July 20 quarter: net income $85.8M, +40%; loans up $533M, a 15% annual pace; net interest margin - what loans earn minus what deposits cost - 3.63%, wider by 0.53 of a point on the year. CHANGE IT: that 0.53 was earned through a year of Federal Reserve cuts, and on September 16 the Fed went the other way, to 3.75%-4.00%. Savers reprice before borrowers do. WHEN: October 19, tentative; $0.83 against $0.65. VERDICT: real growth at a fair price, on the one number Washington sets.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
Palantir Technologies at $177.32 (after hours), +$1.08 / +0.61% Friday. The Aventura, Florida company builds software that pulls an organization's scattered data into one place so people can act on it. This Len5 wants very fast growth on a base big enough to matter, and the first name on it has both: the August 3 quarter brought revenue of $1.94B, +93%, US commercial sales $764M, +149%, and the year lifted to $8.15B-$8.16B. Then September 2, the Army moved its TITAN battlefield ground stations out of prototype and ordered eight for $127M - about 1.6% of the revenue Palantir guides to this year. CHANGE IT: the price, and nothing else. About 151 times reported profit is dearer than anything here by a factor of six. WHEN: November 2, tentative; $0.40 against $0.21. VERDICT: growth nobody disputes, at a price needing all of it and years more like it.

INCOME LEN5:
Ardmore Shipping at $19.15 (after hours), +$0.15 / +0.79% Friday. The Bermuda company owns mid-size tankers carrying refined fuel - petrol, diesel, jet fuel - and chemicals. This Len5 wants cash reaching owners that the business itself pays for, and Ardmore's arrives by formula: two-thirds of each quarter's adjusted profit. So the last check was $0.79 a share, paid September 15, and multiplying it by four is the wrong instinct. The June quarter, reported July 29: revenue $116.2M, profit $1.48 a share against $0.22 a year earlier, tankers earning $51,870 a day, close to three times what it costs to run them. Europe is short diesel and buying it from further away, and distance is what a tanker is paid for. CHANGE IT: the formula runs both ways - analysts model $0.62 for September against $1.18 in June, and two-thirds of that is about $0.41. WHEN: November 4, tentative. VERDICT: roughly 7 times profit and about 7.2% of the price paid out over the past year, on the only payout here that is a calculation rather than a promise.

Baldwin's price was settled by contract on September 14 and will not move again. Ardmore's gets recalculated on November 4, by arithmetic anyone can follow. Intuit's rests on something nobody can check: a machine that has not shipped, doing a job worth $5.3B a year. November 19 counts a quarter. It will not settle that.

Not investment advice.

The Invention of the Palestinian People
Alan Meyer

The other day the question was put to me why so many keep saying that Palestinians are an invented people.
A simple question with a complex answer.
Until the late 19th century, the term Palestinian was used as a regional term.
Residents living in the region between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean identified themselves primarily in terms of religion: Muslims felt far stronger bonds with remote co-religionists than with nearby Jews and Christians. Living in that area did not imply any sense of common political purpose or sense of discrete peoplehood or nationhood.
An identity as a people is one precursor to nationhood. And nationhood is the presence of common identity together with the three key elements of sovereignty, self-determination and self-sufficiency.
The “Palestinians” have never had this, and they still don’t have it. The concept that such a people exists is being forced on the world to achieve a base political goal.
In actual fact, the deliberate creation of the “Palestinian people” as a discrete entity in 1967, and the political group known as the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) in 1964 was for the political purpose of destroying a sovereign and legally mandated Jewish state.
Till that point in time, nor, it will be shown, after that time, was there ever ANY sense or mention of a “Palestinian” people or nation.
The term Palestinian was ALWAYS followed by a descriptive noun – Arab;  ie Palestinian Arab.
According to Palestinian historian Muhammad Y. Muslih, during the entire 400 year period of Ottoman rule (1517-1918), before the British set up the 30-year-long Palestine Mandate, “There was no political unit known as Palestine.”
When the Islamic armies conquered the Levant, they adopted the administrative name used by the Byzantines and dubbed part of Palestina Prima (“the first Palestine”) – more or less today’s Jerusalem area and the Shfela [coastal plain] – as “Jund Filastin.” Jund means “army;” Jund Filastin means “the Palestine military command.” In other words, the name did not signify the national identity of a “Palestinian people” who lived in the land, but instead, a military district, in line with the Byzantine nomenclature.
Until Israel was re-established as a nation in 1948, Palestine was the term for the territory between the Mediterranean Sea and the Jordan River. The word Palestinian was applied to anyone living in that area.
As late as 1909 the first recorded Arab to use the term “Palestinian” was Farid Georges Kassab, a Beirut-based Orthodox Christian who, in 1909, espoused sympathy for Zionism. Kassab’s 1909 book stated that “the Orthodox Palestinian Ottomans call themselves Arabs, and are in fact Arabs.” Even Kassab decried the use of the term “Palestinian” Arab. Nevertheless, apart from the ancient indigenous Jews in the Levant, the largely Muslim Arab population identified only as Arab and ONLY with the start of the British mandate, was the term used to describe both Jew and Arab. So, the term Palestinian did not take on its current popular meaning until the mid-20th century and was used as a regional reference.
On a related tangent, in 1948, the invasion of Israel by 6 pan-Arab armies had NOTHING to do with creating an Arab Palestinian state but ALL to do with a classic imperialist Muslim scramble for Palestinian territory. Had they succeeded, as the first secretary-general of the Arab League, Abdel Rahman Azzam, admitted to a British reporter, Transjordan “was to swallow up the central hill regions of Palestine with access to the Mediterranean at Gaza. The Egyptians would get the Negev. The Galilee would go to Syria, except that the coastal part as far as Acre would be added to Lebanon.”
Had Israel lost the war, its territory would have been divided among the invading Arab forces. The name Palestine would have vanished into the dustbin of history.
So, are the “Palestinians” an invented people for purely political (anti-semitic) purposes?
Well, even Mandate Palestinian Arab leaders during the British mandate era (1920-48) who, as products of the Ottoman imperial system where religion constituted the linchpin of the socio-political order of things, had no real grasp of the phenomenon of nationalism. Hence, they had no interest in the evolution of a distinct Palestinian nation, or acknowledging a Palestinian “people”, because there simply wasn’t one.
As an example that there was no concept of “Palestinian” nationhood or peoplehood, the April 1920 pogrom in Jerusalem was not in the name of independence of the “Palestinian people” of the Mandate area, but under the demand for its incorporation into the (short-lived) Syrian kingdom, headed by Faisal ibn Hussein of Mecca….
In 1926, the Arab Executive Committee still referred to Palestine as the unlawfully severed southern part of “the one country of Syria, with its one population of the same language, origin, customs, and religious beliefs (emphasis mine), and its natural boundaries, as I pointed out earlier.
In July 1937, the Arab Higher Committee (AHC) justified its rejection of the Peel Commission’s recommendation for the partition of Palestine on the grounds that “this country does not belong only to [the] Palestine Arabs (that qualifying noun again….) but to the whole Arab and Muslim Worlds (emphasis mine).”
And finally, as late as August 1947, three months before the passing of the U.N. resolution partitioning Mandate Palestine into Arab and Jewish states, the AHC’s mouthpiece, al-Wahda, advocated the incorporation of Palestine (and Transjordan) into “Greater Syria(emphasis mine).”
No, there was no concept of a “Palestinian people” but rather, always one of Palestinian Arabs who were part of the wider Arab Muslim ummah.
How did they then suddenly appear as homogeneous ethnic group in 1967 when not even the Arab High Commission had ever heard of them?
There are undereducated misconceptions too that pan-Arabism was of no consequence in the dialogue surrounding the authenticity of the “Palestinian” “people”. This is untrue.
Even the younger generation of post 1948 Arab activists supported this ideal as evidenced by Ahmad Shuqeiri, a Lebanon-born politician of mixed Egyptian, Hijazi, and Turkish descent who served as the Arab League’s deputy secretary-general. As he put it, “Palestine is part and parcel in the Arab homeland.”
Asked to clarify which part of the “Arab homeland” this specific territory belonged, he added that Palestine “is nothing but southern Syria.”
And so, it is no surprise that Yasser Arafat, the (Egyptian born and educated) father of the “Palestinian people” followed this pan-Arab line. The 1964 PLO charter defined the Palestinians as “an integral part of the Arab nation”, rather than a distinct nationality (emphasis mine) and vowed allegiance to the ideal of pan-Arab unity – that is, to Palestine’s eventual assimilation into “the greater Arab homeland.”
In 1996, even that bastion which proclaims itself as the leader in the “struggle” for the Palestinian “people”, Hamas, said this, “Islamic and traditional views reject the notion of establishing an independent Palestinian state … In the past, there was no independent Palestinian state. … [Hence] our main goal is to establish a great Islamic state, be it pan-Arabic or pan-Islamic… This…land…is not the property of the Palestinians…. This land is the property of all Muslims in all parts of the world.”  (senior Hamas leader Mahmud Zahar, 1996)
And finally, on this line of reasoning, it is not possible to go past the words of Azmi Bishara, founding leader of the nationalist Balad Party (with seats in the Israeli parliament since 1999). In a statement he made in 2002 he said: “My Palestinian identity never precedes my Arab identity…. I don’t think there is a Palestinian nation, there is [only] an Arab nation…. “
Not much more needs to be said; the concept of a Palestinian “people” engaged in a struggle of “liberation” from a colonial Jewish “oppressor” is a purposely misleading one, invented solely for the purpose of de-legitimising the Jewish state and its people.
The Levantine Arabs, up to and including 1948 , ALWAYS identified firstly on the basis of religion and secondly on the basis of ethnicity. Thus the Levant contained Christian ARABS, Muslim ARABS but only and always, Jews. In other words, the identity of those Arabs who today would like to be known as an ancient “Palestinian “people” have in actual fact NO distinguishing markers of a discrete peoplehood (ever) given that their identity is mostly based on shared customs and beliefs of their Arab Muslim brothers, ALL of them mediated by Islam.
Till 1967, nobody had ever heard of the “Palestinians” as a people, let alone a “people” steeped in antiquity. Its subsequent use is merely a political tool to delegitimise the Jewish claim to what was left of the division of the British Mandate into two projected Arab Muslim entities and one Jewish one.
However, there are those who will use meaningless terms like endogenesis and ethnogenesis in an attempt to pointlessly philosophise with words that have no concrete impact on the issue to hand.
Besides, the concept of a homogeneous, ethnic and disparate “Palestinian people” (endo/ethno genesis) is frankly ludicrous when one considers that through centuries of Muslim imperialism right down to the end of Ottoman Empire in 1918, caliphs and other rulers brought in hundreds of thousands of soldier slaves loyal to their pay masters.
The Tulunides brought in Turks and Negroes.
The Fatamids introduced Berbers, Slavs, Greeks, Kurds, and mercenaries of all kinds.
The Mamelukes imported legions of Georgians and Circassians.
Saladin brought in 150,000 Persians who were given lands in Galilee and the Sidon district for their services.
In the fourteenth century, 18,000 Yurate Tartars from the Euphrates were brought in, soon followed by 20,000 Ashiri and 4,000 Mongols who occupied the Jordan Valley and settled from Jerusalem south!! Mongols…
In 1830, as a further example, Mehemet [Muhammad] Ali colonized Jaffa and Nablus (Jewish Schem before the arab invasion and occupation…) with Egyptian soldiers and their Sudanese allies. So much so that british estimates of the 13,000 inhabitants of Jaffa, for example, ran at 8,000 Turco-Egyptians, 4,000 Greeks and Armenians, and 1,000 Maronites. The british did not consider that there were any Arabs at all in that city. ….
For her/his part, it would be a brave soul who would deny the constancy of the presence of the Jewish PEOPLE in the Levant over the past 3,000 years.
No, the whole concept of a “Palestinian people” is a base political strategy invented not to build a state but to destroy a neighbouring one. For this reason, many who are knowledgeable on this issue will continue to say they are an invented “people”.
Today, while the term Palestinian is applied to the Arabic-speaking residents of what is largely the State of Israel, this usage is purposely misleading because for most of human history, a “Palestinian” was simply a person born or living in that land with no connotation of being a “people”.
When used in reference only to non-Jews, it implies an historical claim to the territory in opposition to Israel. In reality, the concept of Palestine as a nation-state in opposition to Israel or as a racial group ( a “people”) predating the presence of Jewish inhabitants is historically false and is currently pushed as part of a broader strategy of delegitimising Jewish connection to the Land of Israel.
The tactic of the myth of a “Palestinian people” is simple yet sophisticated: preaching and dispersing lies and distortions of reality. History proves that the bigger the lie and the more common its reiteration, the more it is accepted as authentic and genuine.
After all, who can believe that an entire national leadership would dare to totally distort and fabricate history in full?
But the notion of a “Palestinian people” has been forced on Europe and America through the ploy of telling all players what they want to hear.
To a guilty Europe, where there is a high level of guilt and remorse about its own colonialist past, the creation of Israel is pitched as an excess of a bygone European colonialist era where Europe is directly blamed for the creation of the Jewish state.
To the Americans, where many feel guilt and remorse over historic racism, the Palestinians depict Israel as a racist state, which treats them in the same way as African Americans were treated.
And for the broader international community and for human rights organizations, Israel is a cruel occupier that violates all human rights and freedoms of the Palestinians.
But no matter the myth of a Palestinian “people”,  ANY Palestinian national identity is overwhelmingly founded, and heavily predicated, on the negation of Jewish and Israeli identity, rather than on positive attributes or real history.
Arguably, the international community’s enabling and legitimizing of the wishes of a group of people with such an open hatred of a neighbouring sovereign state may be down to simple things: Oil, wilful naiveté, anti-semitism, and a politically correct unwillingness to offer any challenge to such falsehoods.
In the end though, it matters little. The modern re-constituted Jewish State of Israel and the Jewish people are celebrating 71 years of existence as contributing members of the family of nations; without the need to revise, falsify or fabricate its 3000 year old history.
The same cannot be said for the Palestinian “people”.
Shabbat Shalom.

Alan Meyer is a retired educator with an interest in the Arab-Israeli conflict, photography and Australian road trips.
Marking the Fault Lines in Israel’s War on Terror
The firing of the first shots by Hamas at 6:29 a.m. on October 7, 2023, triggered not only a bloody kinetic war in which a lot of Gaza was, and continues to be, flattened, but also a war of narratives which roiled the West much more so than the Middle East itself.
The Israel-Hamas war split open societal fault lines in the West, polarized relations between countries, embedded itself into domestic divides, and accelerated trends such as the growth of far-right movements and anti-immigrant sentiment.
Even so, governments, historically leery of civil chaos no matter their politics, shifted closer to Israel’s point of view, even as public opinion, especially the younger generations and shaped by a large Muslim minority across Europe, shifted in favour of the Palestinian (sic) cause. This is evidenced by the huge public protests across Europe highlighting the split between public opinion and governments.
But those huge public protests are only superficially about the human cost of the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, or even about the seeming power imbalance between a violent, messianic terror group in Gaza wedded to wiping out a neighbouring sovereign state because it is Jewish, and a ME military heavyweight determined to prevent a repeat of the atrocities and massacres perpetrated on it by Hamas in 2023.
Across Europe, in America, and even in the Antipodes in Australia, mass protests sprang up protesting, it seemed initially, Israel’s robust military response to the Hamas terrorists embedded deep inside Gaza’s civilian infrastructure.
Within a couple of months, that changed into something else: blatant antisemitism coupled with a wide ranging cultural war aimed at the very roots of Western traditions.
But not only traditions, even the language of ideas was under attack as words no longer meant what they had, until recently, meant.
Thus, Israel, with 2.1 million Israeli Arab citizens with equal rights, was an “apartheid regime”; targeting and killing Hamas terrorists purposely embedded amongst nominally innocent civilians was a “genocide” albeit pointedly not framed as such by seventeen judges from the ICJ; Jews in and out of Israel were “racists” even as the mass protestors screamed at Jews to go back to Poland/Russia/Ukraine in open racist taunts; and placards demanding “justice” seemed more to demand merely revenge.
Revenge on Israel through a range of measures including sanctions, cancel culture where Jewish and Israeli authors, as one example, were boycotted and where their books may not be sold or even translated from Hebrew to another language.
This was accompanied by a slow-walking of military parts requirements from various European countries and vitriolic public speeches by Muslims and Islamophiles which seemed to have stunned governments around the world into bewildered silence.
Tent cities sprang up across campuses. As Seth Mandel (Commentary, 8 October, 2024) pointed out: “The tent isn’t the point of the tentifada. The point is the violence, the normalization of second-class citizenship for Jews, the loyalty oaths, the street mobs outside Jewish-owned restaurants smashing windows. It’s the evil energy that can’t be re-corked.”
But, while notionally protesting “Gaza”, it was actually Western culture, and Israel as its “Western European” “colonising” standard bearer in the region that generated the most vitriolic hate speech and where Western achievements in thought, art, philosophy and culture were under sustained attack as an embarrassment and the product of “dead white males”.
This irony has not been lost on either Diaspora Jews who were expelled to the Diaspora because they were not white and on Israelis where the population census figures show that 45% of Israelis are Mizrahim, 15% are Russian immigrants, 20% are Arab Israelis, 2.2% are Ethiopian, and 25-30% are Ashkenazi Jews and others. Meaning that 55-60% of the Israeli population is ‘non- white’……
Thus, in America, as in Europe, the Israel-Hamas war led to a selective moralism where international NGOs from Amnesty to MSF refused to hold Islamist terror entities in Gaza to account for a plethora of documented war crimes and crimes against humanity and where that moral blindness, growing unchecked, allowed despotic and corrupt regimes like South Africa to bring charges of genocide against a democratic sovereign state and where the chief prosecutor at the ICC indicted the PM and MoD of a country fighting for its existence on seven fronts against declared terror entities, for “crimes against humanity”.
Further, together with the tidal wave of mainly Muslim migrants from Syria to Europe in 2015-16, the Israel-Hamas war threw into sharp relief the fault lines across Europe of resentment not only against Hamas for its atrocities, but also against Arabs and Muslims in general. The emotions triggered by the Hamas atrocities in Israel and its massacre of Israeli civilians no doubt ended up conflating terrorists, illegal migrants, and asylum-seekers in the minds of Europeans who generally have no detailed knowledge of the politics of the Middle East.
For better or for worse, this fed into Europe’s voting demographic and may well explain the political gains of more right wing parties based as they are on both the fears this mass immigration created among their followers as well as the concerted academic push to re-locate loci of power in Western society through things like Critical Race Theory accompanied by aggressive activism as seen through that lens.
Closer to home, Israel’s war on terror in both Gaza and Lebanon led to an accentuating of local fault lines.
Egyptian officials were worried about the possibility that Palestinians in the coastal strip would stream into the Sinai Peninsula through the Rafah crossing on the Egyptian border.
While they may publicly profess that this would mean the death blow to a cherished “Palestinian State”, such “endangered” “statehood” did not seem to be part of their calculus when they illegally occupied the Strip between 1948 and 1967 with never a single peep made about Palestinian statehood.
The real reason, apart from the country’s economic woes, why Egypt feels the fault line should not widen is altogether less altruistic: Egyptian President Abdelfattah al-Sisi has been has been battling jihadist cells in the Sinai. He has outlawed the Muslim Brotherhood, a designated terrorist organisation in Egypt, of which Hamas is the Gazan branch. His concern is that should a significant number of Gazans infiltrate the Sinai, and Palestinian jihadist groups establish logistical, ideological and operational links and bases there, it would be difficult, if not impossible, to separate Palestinian militants from the mass of new refugees. These militants could very well try to launch attacks on Israeli targets from Egyptian territory, inviting retaliation from Israel and unsettling its relations with Egypt.
For its part, Jordan fears that Israel plans to force West Bank Palestinians into the kingdom. Jordanians have taken to the streets across the country to protest on a daily basis and the government’s major concern is that this feared mass displacement into Jordan would be economically ruinous, where the new demographic reality of Jordan becoming the de facto Palestinian state would almost certainly destabilise the political order, which has historically privileged Jordanians of non-Palestinian origin.
And finally, in this brief overview of how Israel’s war on terror is exacerbating fault lines old and new, we have the renewal of the civil war in Syria.
With the fall of Haleb (Aleppo) to Turkey-backed Syrian groups and al Qaeda linked groups like Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham, Turkey’s influence in the region has risen greatly while complicating prospects for reconciliation between Erdogan and Assad.
For Israel, Iran’s wish to rush arms to Syria which no longer has Hezbollah to fight alongside it, will be met (IS being met) with a clear deterrence by Israel which will not allow an arms build-up so close to its border, arms which may be used against it now that Assad has fallen.
It remains to be seen if Turkey’s Sunni Muslim Brotherhood affiliated militia(s) or Iran’s Shia IRGC and local Shia militias will win out in the end and what will be its implications for Iraq, Lebanon and Syria and for a weakened Iran itself.
In Gaza, Yahya Sinwar dreamed of, and planned for, a huge Middle East conflagration and chaos.
It’s happening.
Just not in quite the way he envisaged.

NIGERIAN CONTINGENT COMMANDER PRESENTS LEARNING MATERIALS AND FOOD ITEMS TO THE WIDOWS AND CHILDREN OF GAMBIAN ARMED FORCES FALLEN HEROES

The Nigerian Contingent of the ECOWAS Mission in The Gambia (ECOMIG), led by the Contingent Commander, Lieutenant Colonel Yahaya Mohammed Abdullahi, has presented learning materials and other essential items to more than 20 children and family members of fallen personnel of the Gambia Armed Forces (GAF).

The presentation, initiated by Intake 28 Alpha as part of efforts to support the welfare and educational development of the children of their departed colleagues, was held at the Defence Camp, Yundum Barracks, on Saturday, 19 September 2026.

Speaking at the event, the Contingent Commander expressed his heartfelt condolences to the families of the fallen personnel and commended Intake 28 Alpha for the thoughtful initiative, describing it as a meaningful demonstration of military comradeship, compassion and responsibility.

Lieutenant Colonel Abdullahi noted that the initiative was particularly significant because it resonates with the Nigerian Armed Forces’ longstanding commitment to the welfare of families of personnel who have paid the supreme sacrifice in service to their country.

This gesture is in line with the Chief of Defence Staff, General Olufemi Oluyede, and the Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shuaibu’s core value of sustained emphasis on the welfare of personnel and the families of fallen heroes, particularly through initiatives designed to support their dependants and provide opportunities for the children of fallen personnel to continue their education and pursue their aspirations.

According to him, the support provided to the children of fallen GAF personnel reflects the same values of care, responsibility and solidarity that underpin such welfare initiatives within the Nigerian Armed Forces.

He said, “The sacrifice made by our fallen colleagues does not end with their passing. It is our collective responsibility to ensure that their families, particularly their children, continue to receive the support, encouragement and opportunities they deserve.”

The Contingent Commander further offered prayers for the beneficiaries, wishing them strength, wisdom and success in their education and future endeavours. He expressed hope that the children would grow into responsible citizens who would contribute meaningfully to the development of The Gambia.

Lieutenant Colonel Abdullahi described his participation in the initiative as a privilege, stressing that military service transcends national boundaries and that the welfare of fallen personnel and their families remains a shared responsibility within the military profession.

He commended the Commanding Officer, 1 Infantry Battalion, Yundum Barracks, Lieutenant Colonel Ambrose Dacosta, and the organising committee for their initiative and continued commitment to the welfare of the beneficiaries.

Earlier in her opening remarks, the Chairperson of Intake 28 Alpha, Captain Sainabou Jatta, explained that the initiative was organised to provide essential educational materials and other items to the children of their departed colleagues.

She assured the beneficiaries that the sacrifices of their parents would never be forgotten and encouraged them to uphold the values of courage, discipline, sacrifice and service exemplified by their parents.

Captain Jatta urged the children to remain focused on their education, study diligently and strive for excellence, while also commending the caregivers for their dedication, love and commitment to raising the children.

Also speaking, the Commanding Officer, 1 Infantry Battalion, Yundum Barracks, Lieutenant Colonel Ambrose Dacosta, observed that the loss of military personnel often creates emotional, social and economic challenges for the families and dependants they leave behind.

text:
🚨 A 14-YEAR MYSTERY: Why Are Autistic People Dying So Much Earlier?

What if a person’s life expectancy could be shortened not because of their condition, but because the world around them fails to provide the care they need?

A new study published in JAMA Network Open has uncovered a troubling gap in the lives of people with autism in the United States. Researchers found that autistic individuals receiving Medicaid had an estimated life expectancy of just 64.9 years, compared with nearly 79 years for the general U.S. population. That represents a difference of almost 14 years.

Why is this gap happening? Is autism itself responsible, or are other factors quietly shortening lives?

Researchers from Columbia University and the University of Colorado Anschutz analyzed data involving more than two million autistic Medicaid beneficiaries between 2000 and 2020. Their findings suggest that the problem is connected to several preventable health and safety risks rather than autism alone.

For autistic women, the difference was even greater, with life expectancy estimated to be around 16 years shorter than that of women in the general population.

Behind these statistics are everyday dangers that many people might never expect to become life-threatening. The study highlighted increased risks associated with illnesses such as influenza and pneumonia, malnutrition, and accidental injuries, including drowning. Influenza mortality was reported to be more than ten times higher among autistic individuals in the study population.

But why would a common illness or accident become so much more dangerous?

The answer may involve several overlapping challenges, including access to healthcare, communication difficulties, social support, and the ability to recognize or respond to medical emergencies. These factors can vary greatly from one person to another, and the study does not suggest that every autistic individual faces the same risks.

Lead author Dr. Guohua Li emphasized the importance of improving healthcare and support systems. Instead of focusing primarily on autism diagnosis during childhood, healthcare services also need to address the long-term health, safety, and well-being of autistic adults.

Better primary care, stronger social support, and targeted home- and community-based services could help address some of the risks identified by researchers.

This study raises an important question for society: Are we doing enough to help autistic people live longer, healthier lives?

Autism is a lifelong condition, but that does not mean a shorter life should be accepted as inevitable. Understanding the causes of health disparities is an important step toward building systems that offer people the support they need throughout their lives.

Source:
Li, G., DiGuiseppi, C. G., Blanchard, A., Russell, M. T., & Ing, C. (2026). Autism Spectrum Disorder and Life Expectancy Among Medicaid Beneficiaries. JAMA Network Open, 9(9), e2633251.

text:
Trump Scores a Win in Greenland

His pact will secure the Arctic even if the territory becomes independent of Denmark.  The Wall Street Journal 

President Trump’s announced deal with Denmark to ensure permanent U.S. access to Greenland brings to an end the  nearly two-year contretemps over America’s interest in the world’s  largest island. More important, it resolves a security challenge that  has bedeviled American presidents since the 1860s and, in the process,  strengthens the U.S. and European position in the Arctic in the face of  Russian and Chinese ambitions.

While  additional details are needed, the outline of Friday’s deal among the  U.S., Denmark and Greenland solves the most pertinent security issues.  By ensuring U.S. military access to Greenland in perpetuity, expanding  the U.S. military presence on the island, and restricting other  countries’ military and economic access to Greenland, Washington has  achieved the goals Mr. Trump set out when he called for the acquisition  of Greenland. Mr. Trump has improved on the work of presidents from Andrew Johnson to Harry S. Truman, who sought to improve the U.S. security position in the High North from the great-power adversaries of their eras.

Until Mr. Trump’s deal, the glaring weakness of the U.S. strategic position was the long-term viability of the 1951 Defense of Greenland Agreement between the U.S. and Denmark and its lack of buy-in from  Greenland itself. With Greenland’s prime minister stating as recently as last year a desire for independence from Denmark, the agreement governing U.S.  military access, which was negotiated only with the island’s colonial  master, offered a poor long-term basis for addressing U.S. security  concerns in the North Atlantic. Mr. Trump’s new agreement, negotiated  both with the Danes and with the Greenlanders themselves, explicitly  preserves U.S. military access even if Greenland eventually becomes  independent.

The  new agreement also resolves America’s concern about restricting other  countries’ military access to Greenland and investment in sensitive  economic sectors. The “right of denial” is a key feature in the Compacts  of Free Association the U.S. maintains with the Pacific nations of  Micronesia, Palau and the Marshall Islands, which have been discussed as  a possible model for Greenland. Under Mr. Trump’s deal, the U.S. will,  in consultation with Denmark, enjoy a version of this diplomatic tool in  sensitive areas. Given rising Chinese and Russian interest in the  Arctic, such a guarantee of consultation on adversary involvement in  Greenland is essential.

Finally,  Mr. Trump appears intent on remedying his predecessors’ failure to  maintain a robust U.S. presence in Greenland, which has declined since the Cold War. The president has indicated a desire to expand the  U.S. military presence, including new bases and elements of the Golden  Dome missile-defense system, in Greenland. Mr. Trump should take  advantage of existing and new agreements with Denmark and Greenland to  establish a serious U.S. naval presence on the island, both as an Arctic  base for the future and to patrol the Greenland-Iceland-U.K. Gap that  separates Europe from North America and is the principal Russian  submarine route to the U.S. East Coast.

The  Trump administration wisely connected Greenland’s security to America’s  broader strategic position in the Western Hemisphere and the North  Atlantic. The new agreement improves Washington’s strategic position as  well as that of its European partners, which will benefit from a  strengthened northern flank. The pact makes America and its partners  safer and puts China and Russia on notice that the U.S. and its Arctic  partners will stand shoulder to shoulder against their malign behavior  in one of the world’s most dynamic regions.

text:
In January 1806 the Lewis and Clark expedition climbed a mountain in the rain to buy 300 pounds of fat, and the people who had it did not want to sell.

They were wintering at Fort Clatsop on the Oregon coast, 33 of them, and it had rained on all but 12 days. The woods were full of elk. That was the problem. Winter elk is lean as a fence post, it spoiled in the wet, and the men were living on it boiled, with roots and dried fish, getting thinner and more miserable on full stomachs. Lewis noted that the best food they had was dog and the marrow out of the elk bones, and that the party had been healthier on dog than at any time since they left the buffalo country. Dog is fatty. Marrow is fat. Winter elk is neither.

Then word came up the coast. A whale had washed ashore near a Tillamook village.

On the 5th two men came back from the salt works with a sample of the blubber. Lewis had it cooked and wrote that it was "very pallitable and tender", white like pork fat. By nightfall Clark had a dozen men and two canoes ready.

One more person wanted to go. Sacagawea had carried a baby across a continent for these people, and she told the captains, in Clark's spelling, that "She had traveled a long way with us to See the great waters, and that now that monstrous fish was also to be Seen, She thought it very hard that She Should not be permitted to See either." She went, with the boy, who was not yet one.

It took three days, over a headland so steep they hauled themselves up by roots. On the beach they found a skeleton Clark paced out at 105 feet, and nothing else. The Tillamook had stripped every ounce in under a fortnight and were rendering it in wooden troughs with hot stones, storing the oil in the whale's own bladders and guts. Clark laid out everything he had to trade. They parted with 300 pounds of blubber and a few gallons of oil, grudgingly, like people being asked to sell their savings.

Lewis was overjoyed. He thanked providence for being "much more kind to us than he was to jonah, having sent this monster to be swallowed by us in stead of swallowing of us."

Thirty-three people standing in a forest of lean meat crossed a mountain for fat. A whole village, offered good trade goods, would barely let it go. Nobody on that beach, on either side of the deal, was under any illusion about which part of an animal is the food.
